Abstract: District heating systems (DHS) are increasingly required to support low-carbon building energy supply; however, conventional fossil-fuel-based DHS suffer from high energy consumption, thermal losses and limited flexibility under variable solar availability and heating demand. Solar air-source heat pump systems improve renewable heat utilization, but their practical operation is challenged by intermittent solar irradiance, nonlinear coupling among the solar collector, heat pump, thermal storage and load-side distribution loop and the need for accurate real-time state estimation and control. Existing rule-based and proportional–integral–derivative (PID) strategies lack predictive capability, while conventional model predictive control (MPC) and digital-twin approaches often rely on simplified linear or quasi-static models that cannot fully capture heat-pump nonlinearities, model uncertainty and thermodynamic constraints. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a physics-informed digital-twin district heating system (PI-DT-DHS) based on a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for a solar air-source heat pump. The proposed framework models the solar air heater, evaporator, condenser, thermal storage tank and load-side loop using coupled thermodynamic energy-balance equations, while the PINN embeds supervised reference-data fitting, physics residuals, boundary conditions, energy conservation and operational constraints into the learning process. The trained digital twin is further combined with a constrained optimization layer to minimize compressor power, auxiliary heating, load-temperature deviation and storage-temperature fluctuation under operational limits. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed PI-DT-DHS reduces compressor energy to 19.7kWh, auxiliary heating to 8.9kWh, storage loss to 2.4kWh and distribution loss to 2.0kWh, while increasing useful heat delivery to 39.5kWh compared with other district heating configurations. Title: A digital twin approach for aircraft fatigue crack prediction considering overload retardation effect

Authors with affiliations: Zhang H., College of Aerospace Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China; Li W., College of Civil Aviation, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China; Li Y., College of Aerospace Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China; Li H., College of Aerospace Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China
Abstract: Aircraft structures endure variable flight loads and environmental conditions that promote fatigue-crack initiation and propagation at critical locations, thereby threatening structural reliability. Accurate crack-growth prediction is challenged not only by uncertainties in material properties and load histories but also by overload retardation, in which an overload-induced plastic zone temporarily reduces the subsequent crack-growth rate. To address these challenges, this paper develops a digital-twin framework named DPUP, which integrates Data, Physics, Uncertainty, and Prediction modules to enable real-time tracking and prognosis of fatigue cracks under overloads. Specifically, the Data module collects and processes flight-load data, physical-test data, and inspection data; the Physics module incorporates global-local multiscale finite-element modeling with three-dimensional M-integral analysis to obtain crack length dependent stress-intensity factors, and then couples the NASGRO model with the Modified Generalized Willenborg model to capture overload retardation effects; the Uncertainty module characterizes variability in fatigue crack-growth parameters and the overload factor, while the Prediction module assimilates crack-inspection observations through a particle filter to dynamically update the crack state and uncertain parameters. The DPUP framework is validated using fatigue crack-growth data from a 2024-T3 aluminum-alloy lower-wing-skin specimen subjected to TWIST spectra truncated at Levels I and III. Results show that the NASGRO-MGW model captures spectrum-dependent overload retardation, while particle-filter assimilation progressively improves crack-growth predictions and updates the uncertain material and overload parameters. Overall, the DPUP framework provides a physically interpretable approach for aircraft-specific crack-growth tracking under variable-amplitude loading and offers a practical basis for remaining-life assessment, adaptive inspection planning, maintenance decision-making, and mission planning. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Digital twin-driven hybrid fuzzy Bayesian simulation framework for dynamic green credit risk assessment in manufacturing enterprises
Source title: International Journal of Modeling, Simulation, and Scientific Computing
Affiliations: Hunan International Economics University, Business School, Changsha, Hunan, 410205, China
Authors with affiliations: Yang N., Hunan International Economics University, Business School, Changsha, Hunan, 410205, China
Abstract: Green credit risk assessment for manufacturing enterprises is a dynamic and complex problem affected by operational states, environmental uncertainty, financial conditions, information quality, and interactive risk evolution. Traditional assessment methods depend heavily on low-frequency financial and disclosure data and therefore have limited ability to capture early risk signals arising from production operations, energy consumption, environmental performance, and supply-chain disturbances. In addition, conventional machine-learning models provide limited interpretability for causal dependence and uncertain risk propagation. This paper proposes a digital twin-driven hybrid fuzzy dynamic Bayesian network (DT-FDBN) framework for dynamic green credit risk assessment and scenario simulation in manufacturing enterprises. The framework integrates multi-source information covering financial solvency, production and equipment operation, energy consumption and emissions, green transition, environmental disclosure and information credibility, and the external environment into a unified enterprise digital-twin representation. Fuzzy evidence transformation is used to represent incomplete and imprecise observations, while credibility correction and group-level sensor reliability reduce the influence of unreliable digital-twin evidence. The DT-FDBN further models hierarchical risk dependence, temporal evolution, and probabilistic uncertainty propagation, supporting dynamic inference, key-factor diagnosis, multi-period prediction, and intervention-scenario simulation. Based on a semi-synthetic dataset containing 2160 enterprise-month observations from 60 manufacturing enterprises, the proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 0.881, recall of 0.893, (Formula presented)-score of 0.869, AUC of 0.943, and Brier score of 0.079. It outperforms XGBoost and conventional fuzzy dynamic Bayesian networks in overall predictive and calibration performance and identifies operational and environmental deterioration earlier than financial-only assessment. The proposed framework provides an interpretable and dynamically adaptive modeling paradigm for manufacturing green credit risk management. © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract: Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries combine a high theoretical specific energy with low-cost active materials, yet their development remains constrained by coupled reaction pathways, mobile intermediates, lithium-metal instability, and a large design space that changes with loading, electrolyte inventory, temperature, format, and cycling history. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a way to connect these variables, but most published demonstrations remain isolated within small computational datasets, literature-derived tables, or single-laboratory cell series. This review develops an evidence-first, closed-loop framework for AI-enabled Li–S research that links observation, learning, decision, validation, and model updating. It critically examines data infrastructure, text and multimodal extraction, descriptor learning, catalyst and electrolyte design, physics-informed state inference, degradation prognosis, autonomous experimentation, and digital twins. The available evidence shows that machine learning (ML) can compress high-dimensional calculations, recover useful structure–property relations, and predict selected cell outcomes within bounded domains. However, ML has not yet demonstrated robust transfer across laboratories, cell formats, or practical operating conditions. The main barriers are incomplete metadata, non-independent data splits, uncertain labels, weak uncertainty calibration, and limited prospective validation. To address these gaps, the review introduces a minimum data schema, an evidence-fidelity pathway that separates proxy prediction from decision-grade evidence, task-specific benchmarking requirements, and a minimum viable digital-twin architecture for Li–S cells. The central conclusion is that AI becomes decision-grade only when its predictions are physically credible, uncertainty-aware, experimentally actionable, and iteratively validated. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Mechanism–AI fusion in refining simulation software: A module-level review
Affiliations: Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China; China Petrochemical Corporation (SINOPEC), Beijing, 100728, China
Authors with affiliations: Han J., Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China; Zhao X., China Petrochemical Corporation (SINOPEC), Beijing, 100728, China; Han L., Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China
Abstract: Refining simulation software has remained functionally static for decades: property calculation, reaction kinetics, unit-operation modeling, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solving modules are hard-coded, unidirectional, and cannot be calibrated online against drifting plant conditions. Purely mechanistic approaches provide irreplaceable rigor but are constrained by computational cost; purely data-driven approaches offer speed and adaptivity but lack the interpretability, generalization, and physical guarantees required for safety-critical deployment. This review examines how mechanism–AI fusion—encompassing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), reduced-order models (ROMs), operator learning, and closure-model augmentation—is reshaping these functional modules at the architectural level. We propose a module-level taxonomy that maps each fusion strategy to the specific simulation module it transforms, and we distinguish this paradigm from related concepts (hybrid modeling, physics-informed machine learning, grey-box modeling, and digital twins) by specifying the bidirectional information flows between mechanistic and AI components. A systematic literature survey following PRISMA-style methodology identified 133 references from Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore (2000–2025). We provide enhanced comparative tables that include training cost, data requirements, extrapolation ability, uncertainty quantification (UQ), scalability, and industrial maturity for each method class. Industrial software benchmarking is presented as a qualitative comparison rather than a subjective ranking. Three industrial case studies (gasifier, FCC unit, distillation column) are analyzed with explicit baselines, deployment durations, and performance indicators, clearly identifying vendor-reported versus independently verified data. We discuss emerging topics—AI-native scientific software, foundation models for scientific computing, autonomous engineering agents, trustworthy and explainable AI, verification & validation (V&V), and MLOps for scientific applications—that will shape the next decade. The review concludes with graded findings (verified, supported, emerging, conceptual, and policy-level) to clearly distinguish established results from industrial observations and conceptual proposals. The central finding is that mechanism–AI fusion transforms refining simulation software from a fixed-algorithm tool into an adaptive multi-fidelity platform, but the transition from advisory and optimization applications to safety-critical closed-loop control requires standardized V&V protocols, UQ frameworks, and process-industry-specific safety governance that do not yet exist. Abstract: The limited availability of labelled gamma-radiation data constrains the development and evaluation of machine-learning methods for radiation-monitoring applications, particularly under shielded or otherwise difficult-to-reproduce conditions. This study presents a physics-guided Digital Twin framework integrating Geant4-based Monte Carlo radiation transport, automated scenario orchestration, detector-response aggregation, structured synthetic-data generation, and multiple explicitly separated levels of assessment. Eight radionuclide-labelled source classes were represented by characteristic monoenergetic gamma emissions ranging from 0.051 to 2.610 MeV. Simulations covered four shielding materials-lead, stainless steel, concrete, and polyethylene-at thicknesses of 0, 1, 2, 5, and 10 cm, resulting in 160 source-material-thickness configurations. The simulated detector responses reproduced the expected dependence of photon transmission on energy, shielding material, and absorber thickness. After incorporating counting-statistical uncertainties, the fitted linear attenuation coefficient for 1.25-MeV 60Co-labelled photons in lead was 0.618 ± 0.042 cm-1, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.535 - 0.700 cm-1. The corresponding NIST XCOM reference value of 0.680 cm-1 lies within this interval. A limited detector-level experimental assessment was performed using independently acquired NaI(Tl) spectra. A multi-peak blind spectrum was assigned to material containing the 232Th decay chain before disclosure of the source identity, and the assignment was subsequently confirmed by the data provider. This result is reported as a proof-of-concept case rather than a statistical estimate of identification accuracy. An independent UAV radiation-survey dataset containing 3,722 observations across ten flight transects was additionally analysed. It demonstrated a strong and spatially stable relationship between integral gamma activity and estimated 137Cs activity r=0.990, R2=0.980. These UAV results provide an application-level reference but are not interpreted as direct validation of Geant4-generated spectra. The proposed framework provides a transparent and extensible basis for physics-guided synthetic-data generation while explicitly distinguishing attenuation verification, limited detector-level spectral assessment, and application-level consistency analysis. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Abstract: This study synthesizes the rapidly expanding evidence base on machine learning that links renewable variability to green-hydrogen production optimisation and proposes an integrated PM–CFL–OPT architecture that embeds uncertainty handling, safety constraints, and interpretability across the decision chain. The architecture represents a synthesis-derived and testable functional hypothesis rather than a quantitatively validated superior pipeline. Because the included studies use heterogeneous datasets, horizons, system boundaries and performance measures—and only three studies are primarily classified as CFL—the present corpus cannot support a pooled estimate of the framework’s incremental performance over standalone alternatives. A PRISMA-aligned, feedback-loop workflow was executed across Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, and SpringerLink, yielding 244 records; 48 duplicates were removed, and 129 critical studies were retained for synthesis. Bibliometric profiling revealed a transition from early exploratory contributions during 2016–2019 to a marked acceleration after 2022, with publication output peaking in 2025 and expanding geographically across established research economies and emerging regions. A systems-map synthesis organises the literature using an Energy/System Vector–Machine-Learning Method–Application/Decision Domain (E–M–A) framework and overlays it with three functional roles: predictive modelling (PM), clustering and feature learning (CFL), and optimisation and control (OPT). E–M–A locates each study by physical context, computational method and decision task, whereas PM–CFL–OPT identifies how ML contributes to the forecast–representation–action chain. Persistent gaps include limited transferability across climates and grids, weak decision-focused learning pipelines, and under-specified safety cases for real-time and market participation. The review concludes with a deployment-oriented roadmap for climate-robust, privacy-preserving, and auditable ML that can scale hydrogen-integrated renewable operations. Findings clarify maturity, trust, and transferability bottlenecks for deployment. © 2026 The Author(s).

Abstract: To address the growing complexity between the built environment and urban life, modern urban planning has increasingly relied on digital technologies for decision-making, including City Information Modeling (CIM). While CIM has matured from standards and data integration to real-time analytics and digital twins, most initiatives optimize physical systems while struggling to incorporate “intangible” citizen-generated data. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a replicable methodology to embed a customized Environment, Social, and Governance (ESG) framework with a CIM workflow by joining both tangible and intangible city layers to inform planning. The general methodology includes: (1) identifying a French priority neighborhood (QPV) and prioritizing local ESG indicators with a focus group, (2) conceptualizing and designing a data model that integrates urban geometry with subjective human perceptions, and (3) prototyping and developing the CIM model. This approach allows for a multi-scale assessment of socio-environmental sustainability, accounting for uncertainty in human perception. The novelty of this research lies in creating a replicable CIM method that converts non-geocoded citizen perceptions into spatially weighted and probabilistic indicators. Future work will complete the CIM workflow, detailing the integration of the ESG indicators in a practical CIM tool designed to inform decisions through reporting and recommendations. © 2026 The Author(s)

Abstract: Digital dentistry increasingly reports high-performing computational models, yet a central knowledge gap remains: existing reviews often catalogue technologies or deployment concerns without a common framework that distinguishes analytical performance from transportability, clinical validity, clinical utility, and lifecycle safety. Consequently, it remains unclear what level of real-world use is actually justified by a reported benchmark result. This systematic scoping review critically appraised literature available through July 2026; 147 records were screened and 56 studies were included for evidence synthesis. Rather than pooling incomparable accuracy values, the review evaluated data provenance, partitioning and leakage, reference standards, external validation, calibration and uncertainty, fairness, human factors, cybersecurity, prospective impact, and lifecycle monitoring across imaging, natural-language processing, multimodal and foundation models, robotics, AR/VR, tele-operation, synthetic data, and digital twins. The synthesis identifies an accuracy-to-deployment gap: evidence is comparatively mature for selected two-dimensional imaging and segmentation tasks, whereas multimodal assistants, generative systems, robotics, teleoperation, and digital twins remain limited by external, prospective, human-factor, or lifecycle evidence. The novelty of this review is an integrated evidence-to-deployment taxonomy, an M0-M5 clinical utility ladder, minimum reporting requirements, and staged evidence gates. The new knowledge created is that evidence maturity, not nominal accuracy alone, determines the defensible level of clinical use, and that the validation burden increases as autonomy, multimodality, generative behaviour, and post-deployment change increase. These outputs provide a practical basis for designing, reviewing, and governing clinically credible digital-dentistry research. © Little Lion Scientific

Title: Decision-centered wearable biosensors for personalized rehabilitation: integrating multimodal monitoring, artificial intelligence, and closed-loop intervention

Abstract: Personalized rehabilitation requires repeated assessment of movement, physiological tolerance, fatigue, and adherence, yet conventional clinic-based measurements provide only intermittent snapshots. The convergence of wearable biosensors with artificial intelligence, edge-cloud computing, and connected data infrastructures creates an opportunity to convert continuous multimodal signals into timely rehabilitation decisions. This critical narrative review synthesizes physiological, biochemical, electrophysiological, biomechanical, and behavioral sensing within a monitoring–interpretation–feedback–adaptation–outcome framework. We first evaluate analytical validity, real-world robustness, biocompatibility, wearability, calibration drift, and power continuity. We then examine signal-quality control, multimodal fusion, digital biomarkers, federated learning, digital twins, and predictive models according to latency, uncertainty, generalizability, privacy, and decision utility. The review follows biosensor-derived information across a graded spectrum of action, from clinician-reviewed monitoring and real-time biofeedback to assist-as-needed adaptation, functional electrical stimulation, and state-responsive neuromodulation. Applications include motor and physiological assessment, fatigue-aware dose adjustment, musculoskeletal and neurological rehabilitation, posture correction, sensor-rich prosthetics, and Internet of Things–enabled home rehabilitation. Across these settings, greater autonomy increases the evidence and safety requirements: models should expose confidence, systems should degrade safely when signal quality falls, and digital infrastructures should preserve interoperability, version traceability, privacy, and accountable clinician oversight. The central translational gap is not sensor sensitivity alone but whether an integrated biosensor system produces a reliable metric, supports an explicit and proportionate decision, and improves an outcome important to the patient. Decision-centered evaluation can help move wearable biosensing from fragmented technology demonstrations toward secure, personalized, continuous, and clinically accountable rehabilitation. Title: Digital twins in medicine: between simulating the future and clinical uncertainty.; [Gemelos digitales en medicina: entre la simulación del futuro y la incertidumbre clínica.]
Source title: Revista de la Federacion Argentina de Cardiologia
Affiliations: Hospital Nacional de Itagua, Paraguay
Authors with affiliations: Lesme G.L.E., Hospital Nacional de Itagua, Paraguay
Abstract: It is an undeniable fact that science has evolved extraordinarily. Each discovery and new tool has served as a foundation for the next, enabling us to better understand the world and solve problems that until recently seemed impossible. Yet, it faces a paradox today: never before has so much information about patients been available, and at the same time, never has it been so difficult to integrate that information into a truly coherent representation of their biology. The next step for artificial intelligence seems almost natural: constructing an individualized, dynamic, and predictive virtual representation of a patient, organ, or biological system; in other words, a digital twin. More than just a computer copy, it aims to be a model updated with data from its real-world counterpart, capable of simulating trajectories and exploring responses to various interventions. In cardiology, this concept has already driven the development of models for phenotyping, prediction, electrophysiology, and therapeutic selection. © 2026, Federacion Argentina de Cardiologia. Abstract: Background: Personalized digital twins for type 1 diabetes (T1D) can simulate future glucose responses under different therapeutic conditions, but their probabilistic outputs require structured interpretation before supporting clinician-facing reasoning. We introduce retrieval-augmented simulation (RAS), a modular framework connecting probabilistic digital-twin simulation with guideline-grounded report generation. Methods: Retrieval-augmented simulation summarizes simulated glucose trajectories, converts them into structured clinical descriptors, retrieves relevant guideline evidence, and generates uncertainty-aware reports for clinician review. We evaluated RAS using data from 35 individuals with T1D in a controlled ablation study involving 2 locally hosted large language models (LLMs) (LLaMA 3.1:8b and Qwen 3:8b). Two independent LLM-based evaluators, GPT-5.5 Thinking and Kimi 2.6 Thinking, assessed report quality using a standardized rubric. Results: Structured clinical descriptors were essential for guideline selection: their removal substantially altered the retrieved evidence, demonstrating that qualitative clinical framing influenced evidence selection more strongly than numerical values alone. For LLaMA, the full RAS pipeline achieved the strongest overall performance, maintaining high numerical faithfulness (NumCov: (Formula presented) ) and consistent guideline coupling. In contrast, Qwen exhibited substantial model-specific safety risks and frequently distorted simulation-derived numerical values (NumCov: (Formula presented) ). Directional bias analysis showed that Qwen systematically under-reported time in range by a mean of (Formula presented) percentage points and over-reported time below range, thereby inflating hypoglycemia risk. These safety findings were consistent across both independent evaluators, with a mean score difference of (Formula presented) points. Conclusion: Retrieval-augmented simulation provides a reproducible framework for the expert-supervised interpretation of digital-twin simulations. However, aggregate framework scores alone are insufficient for clinical validation. Downstream language models must be rigorously evaluated for numerical faithfulness and directional bias to prevent unsafe, hallucinated clinical narratives. © 2026 Diabetes Technology Society

Title: AI based next generation industry 6.0 and industry 7.0 nanotechnology in pharmaceutical sectors with toxicological challenges, safety concerns, sustainable perspectives and strategies to overcome these barriers
Affiliations: Department of Chemistry, Dean ORIC, University of Management and Technology (UMT), Lahore, Pakistan; Department of Biotechnology, University of Management and Technology (UMT), Sialkot Campus, Lahore, 51310, Pakistan; Applied Botany Lab, Department of Botany, Government College University Lahore, 54000, Pakistan; Institute of Biology, Leiden University, Netherlands

Abstract: Nanoparticle drug delivery systems are reshaping pharmaceutical development by enabling programmable control over biodistribution, cellular uptake & release kinetics beyond the limits of conventional formulations. Advances in lipid, polymeric, inorganic and hybrid nanocarriers now support delivery of small molecules, biologics, nucleic acids and gene editing cargos across oncology, cardiometabolic, infectious and neurodegenerative disease domains. Materials level engineering, spanning interfacial chemistry, supramolecular assembly and stimuli responsive matrices has enabled improved solubilization of poorly bioavailable drugs, enhanced tissue targeting and reduced systemic toxicity. Despite these therapeutic advantages, translation from laboratory systems to commercial pharmaceutical products remains constrained by manufacturing reproducibility, sterilization compatibility, endotoxin control, long term stability and regulatory uncertainty regarding nano specific safety endpoints. Industrial implementation therefore requires tight control of critical quality attributes, integration of continuous manufacturing routes and adoption of predictive modelling tools for formulation design and lifecycle risk assessment. Emerging Industry 6.0 aligned technologies including AI assisted formulation optimization, digital twin process modelling and real time process analytical technologies are beginning to transform nanomedicine from a formulation challenge into a data driven manufacturing discipline. In parallel, safe by design materials engineering and integrative nanotoxicology frameworks are improving regulatory confidence by linking physicochemical properties to biodistribution, clearance and immunological responses. These developments indicate a transition from first generation nanocarriers toward intelligent, scalable pharmaceutical systems capable of supporting precision therapeutics. The convergence of advanced materials chemistry, automated smart/ intelligent manufacturing and predictive safety science is expected to accelerate clinical translation, reduce development risk, and establish nanomedicine as a core platform across the future pharmaceutical landscape. © The Author(s) 2026. Title: SOMA: a preventive health governance framework for adaptive, consumer-facing digital health guidance
Affiliations: Bratislava University of Economics and Management (BUEM), Bratislava, Slovakia
Authors with affiliations: Mueller M.R., Bratislava University of Economics and Management (BUEM), Bratislava, Slovakia
Abstract: This paper introduces SOMA, a conceptual preventive health governance framework for adaptive, consumer-facing digital health guidance, designed to support everyday preventive health self-governance. Non-communicable and lifestyle-sensitive chronic diseases account for the majority of global mortality, yet existing consumer-facing digital health tools rarely provide coherent, governed preventive guidance that integrates multimodal personal health data, scientific evidence, user-defined goals, real-world feasibility, relational support, and explicit safety constraints within a unified architecture. SOMA conceptualizes preventive health self-governance as the iterative, user-governed process through which individuals interpret their evolving health state, define goals and feasibility constraints, receive evidence-informed guidance, and act within boundaries that reduce the risk of unsafe or inappropriate digital health guidance. The framework theorizes an architecture of five interdependent components: a Digital Twin Core synthesizing a multimodal Health State Vector across biological, wearable, subjective, behavioral, and contextual layers; a Scientific Intelligence Core evaluating evidence quality, uncertainty, and applicability; a Relational Avatar Core supporting disclosure, trust calibration, and user-facing communication; a Personal Health Governance Profile embedding user-defined goals, feasibility constraints, and autonomy preferences; and a Continuous Learning Engine updating the model based on outcomes, evidence, and user feedback, all bounded by non-negotiable Safety and Medical Escalation Boundaries. The theoretical contribution lies in integrating previously siloed approaches (digital health twin logic, evidence-weighted scientific intelligence, relational guidance, behavioral self-governance theory, and personal health governance) into a unified preventive architecture whose governance properties emerge from the structured interdependence of its components. Five testable hypotheses are derived from the architecture to guide a staged empirical validation programme. SOMA is a conceptual framework that has not been empirically validated and makes no claims regarding clinical effectiveness, disease prevention, or deployment readiness. © 2026 Mueller.

Abstract: Product volatility and market uncertainty are driving manufacturing companies toward highly customized products and increasingly flexible, reconfigurable production systems. To address these challenges, advanced technologies such as Digital Twins (DT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and eXtended Reality (XR) are being adopted to enhance engineering design processes and reduce time-to-market. While Concurrent Engineering has historically improved product development efficiency, limited attention has been given to production system design, which remains critical to introduce new products rapidly. This research investigates how the Industrial Metaverse (IM), a comprehensive environment integrating DT, AI, and XR, can support production system design while aligning with Industry 5.0 principles of human centricity. The study focuses on the detailed design phase, where both hardware and software components are verified and tested. In this context, the IM is explored as a platform to actively engage human stakeholders through immersive and collaborative environments, enhancing the interaction in the virtual worlds for design reviews and training. The findings are based on lessons learned from the METABRAKE project, a collaborative academia-industry project aimed at developing and testing IM applications for product-production system concurrent engineering. Through a laboratory demonstration, the study highlights the capability of immersive technologies to improve design review and virtual training, while also identifying key challenges and lessons learned on technical integration and organizational processes. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Abstract: The electrification of public transport has introduced new challenges in managing lithium-ion battery degradation, operational efficiency, and lifecycle sustainability. While battery digital twins (BDTs) have emerged as a promising solution for monitoring and prediction, most existing approaches remain limited to short-term state estimation and do not exploit lifecycle data for circular decision-making. This paper proposes a Circular Battery Digital Twin (CBDT) framework that integrates aging-aware operation, predictive lifecycle modeling, and circular value retention within a unified architecture. The framework combines real-world operational, environmental, and maintenance data to continuously calibrate a semi-empirical degradation model supporting multiple use cases, including route reassignment and second-life assessment. The framework is demonstrated using a multi-year dataset from a real electric bus operating in Sweden. The bus operates with a 60 kWh LFP battery pack and relies exclusively on pantograph charging at terminus stops. The results show that CBDT enables consistent degradation estimation, supports cost-aware operational decisions, and provides a pathway toward circular battery management. The framework successfully identified an optimal reassignment threshold at 70% load that extends operational life by 45%. The study demonstrates how integrating multi-source data and lifecycle intelligence enables the transition from reactive battery management to proactive and circular decision-making. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Abstract: Steel heat treatment is governed by coupled heat transfer, diffusion, phase transformation, and stress development, yet industrial practice still relies on empirical diagrams and trial-and-error. This review critically examines machine learning and advanced simulation as design tools for that practice, spanning physics-based simulation, supervised learning, computer vision, physics-informed learning, surrogate modeling, inverse design, and digital twins. Quenching and tempering, thermochemical carburizing, localized induction and laser processing, press hardening, and additive-manufacturing post-processing are analyzed as separate mechanism-specific families rather than pooled as one process class. The evidence base is uneven: most studies rely on simulation or retrospective internal validation, only isolated reports include prospective component-scale tests, and none documents sustained closed-loop production control. Tree ensembles and kernel methods are strong baselines for the small, structured datasets typical of heat-treatment research, but no model family is universally superior. Validation design matters more than architecture: in one vision study, yield-strength R2 rose from 0.43 under specimen-grouped validation to 0.97 under a leaky image split, and equation-generated targets merely emulate encoded correlations rather than validate physics. Hybrid models improve data efficiency and physical consistency, but evidence for extrapolation and plant transfer remains limited. A six-level validation hierarchy is proposed to separate random-holdout accuracy from grouped, external, temporal, prospective, and closed-loop evidence. Critical gaps persist in multimodal data integration, uncertainty quantification, causal process understanding, benchmarks, and safety-constrained control. © IMechE 2026

Abstract: Underground hydrogen storage is increasingly positioned as a long-duration flexibility option for renewable-dominated energy systems. Dependable deployment, however, is constrained by coupled uncertainties spanning multiphase flow, pore-scale interfacial physics, reactive transport, and potential microbiological effects. To improve the applicability and generalisability of physics-informed artificial intelligence for underground hydrogen storage, we conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic literature review of studies published from 2020 to 2026. The Scopus and Google Scholar searches retrieved 1071 records. After deduplication, 872 unique records remained, and 676 full texts were assessed for eligibility. From these, 51 primary studies relevant to PI-AI for UHS were retained for synthesis after an evidence-quality appraisal gate, comprising 49 UHS-explicit studies and 2 methodologically adjacent studies, retained for transferable PI-AI insights. We examined the complexity of applying physics-informed learning across pore-to-field scales and how this complexity contributes to barriers to transferability, reproducibility, and decision readiness. Specifically, we synthesised evidence across five themes: pore-scale interfacial physics; reactive transport, sorption, and biogeochemistry; reservoir-scale surrogate architectures; uncertainty and data assimilation readiness; and multi-objective design and operational optimisation. Each study was also coded by task, model family, uncertainty practice, and validation strength. Only 9 of the 51 included studies (17.6%) reported predictive intervals or distributions consistent with quantified predictive uncertainty (UQ-A), and just one of these reported fully calibrated empirical-coverage checks, identifying uncertainty quantification as the most consequential evidence gap in the reviewed corpus. Title: Phase-Guided Bayesian Model-Based Imputation for Missing Sensor Data in Mass-Spring-Damper Systems
Source title: Conference Record - IEEE Instrumentation and Measurement Technology Conference
Affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States
Authors with affiliations: Bouraima M.O., Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States; Zawodniok M., Missouri University of Science and Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, Rolla, United States
Abstract: Missing sensor data severely degrades parameter estimation in dynamic systems. In digital-twin applications for mechanical equipment, gaps in vibration or displacement measurements corrupt phase estimates, causing the virtual twin to diverge from the physical system and undermining both real-time monitoring and predictive-maintenance decisions. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Phase-Guided Bayesian Model-Based Imputation (PGMI-Bayesian) that uses a physics-guided two-stage scheme for reconstructing missing samples and refining phase estimation in a mass-spring-damper system. The approach first generates model-consistent estimations and then applies a weak Bayesian shrinkage update. Monte Carlo results show that PGMI-Bayesian consistently achieves lower variance, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Mean Squared Error (MSE) than both observed-only estimation and standard imputation strategies. Although it does not reach the complete-data Cramér-Rao Lower Bound, the method remains well below the Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) CRLB for missingness up to 30%. Entropy analysis further confirms that PGMI-Bayesian produces the lowest-uncertainty reconstructions, demonstrating that physics-guided reconstruction can meaningfully enhance estimator efficiency under missing data. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The increased occurrence of extreme weather events, cyber-physical disturbances, and electrification requires distribution systems to sustain critical services and recover quickly under adverse conditions. Meanwhile, the penetration of DERs, digitally controlled assets, and decentralized energy markets is transforming the traditional distribution networks into active and flexible systems. Virtual power plants (VPPs) and peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading are two types of complementary flexibility, but their coordinated role in resilience-oriented distribution systems operation has not been sufficiently synthesized. This review investigates the incorporation of distribution systems resilience, VPP aggregation, DER and battery energy storage system (BESS) coordination, and centralized/decentralized energy trading based on around 160 peer-reviewed studies. This review offers an in-depth synthesis of the resilience metrics, VPP architectures and control strategies, P2P and transactive-energy mechanisms, and optimization approaches for the distribution systems with DERs. Besides the synthesis of the literature, a scenario-based numerical assessment of the coordinated operation of DERs and BESS under single and multi-fault conditions is performed utilizing the IEEE 33-bus radial distribution system (RDS). The four optimization methods GA, GWO, HPOA, and COA are evaluated using 30 matched experimental runs, and the difference of performance is compared by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests. The results show that the coordinated VPP operation enhances the load restoration and decreases the energy not served (ENS), while it provides voltage support and accelerates the recovery during the outage conditions considered. The integrated resilience-aware operation further shows the complementary role of DER/BESS coordination and P2P energy trading in enhancing the technical and economic performance. The review highlights important gaps in coupled uncertainty and cascading-failure modeling, network-aware transactive-energy coordination, cyber-secure VPP operation, scalable multi-VPP control, resilience-oriented market valuation, interoperability and experimental validation. Future research should target integrated and scalable cyber-physical-economic frameworks with AI-assisted adaptive control, digital twins, distributed and federated VPP coordination, resilient P2P markets, larger-system validation, and hardware-in-the-loop and field demonstrations. © 2026 The Authors.

Abstract: The design of intelligent manufacturing equipment still relies on manual CAD iteration and ergonomic assessment after making geometry decisions, leading to unnecessarily long development cycles and operator well-being trade-offs being buried. We fill this gap by a novel human-machine ergonomics loop, where per-modality attention weights are computed within a Multimodal Confidence-Weighted Fusion (MCWF) module, with aleatoric uncertainty weights obtained from a learned head, which automatically down-weight unreliable CAD, telemetry or pose channels, and where the reward directly couples surrogate variance σ f and PDE/Kienzle residuals R_phys into the policy gradient, ensuring physically-feasible parameter updates in the Policy-Core, Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm (Physics-Constrained Soft Actor-Critic, PC-SAC). A closed loop system that integrates a physics-informed digital-Twin surrogate system with a conditional latent-diffusion generative design head is encased in the two cores. The SAC agent has a 24-D continuous action space, entropy target =-24, discount γ=0.99 and Polyak coefficient τ=5 × 10-3. The gains are made through the MCWF and PC-SAC cores, not just integration, as shown by ablations and parameter-sensitivity testing across three operating conditions of the device. The results place the framework among repeatable, human-centric designs of Industry 5.0 equipment. © 2026 IEEE.

Source title: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
Affiliations: Politecnico di Torino, Department of Electronics and Telecommunications, Turin, 10129, Italy; NTT Network Innovation Laboratories, Kanagawa, Yokosuka, 239-0847, Japan; NEC Laboratories America, Princeton, 08540, NJ, United States

Abstract: Polarization-dependent loss (PDL) makes the post-equalization signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of a coherent optical lightpath stochastic, with an outage-relevant lower tail that depends on the longitudinal interleaving of PDL elements and amplified-spontaneous-emission (ASE) noise sources. Under a finite-hinge representation, the inverse-SNR is a weighted sum of correlated exponentials of a random walk, whose exact evaluation is too costly for repeated quality-of-transmission assessment in an optical network digital twin (ONDT), where physical-layer models are continuously combined with network data to predict transmission feasibility and support network operation. We model the PDL magnitude of each element through a Maxwell prior in dB and compare five efficient approximations: gamma moment matching, recursive moment-matched lognormal, correlated Fenton–Wilkinson lognormal, delta-cumulant log-skew-normal, and third-moment recursive log-skew-normal. Their descriptors can be accumulated element by element or exchanged as a constant-size moment state across vendor and operator domains, while allowing different PDL statistics in different network portions. Monte Carlo validation based on 10^{9} realizations, with N\in \{2,10,40\} and \sigma _{\mathrm {PDL}} from 0.1 to 1.5 dB, shows that no approximation is uniformly best. In the practically relevant sub-1 dB range, the third-moment recursive log-skew-normal model is generally the most accurate global approximation and provides the best overall outage-tail prediction, with outage-probability errors typically within a few tenths of a decade and outage-quantile errors of about 0.2 dB or less. Realistic core–metro and metro–access examples further show that propagation direction, received optical power, and transceiver SNR jointly alter both the reference SNR and the distribution shape. The scope is limited to ASE-dominated links, independent per-element Maxwell priors, and ideal zero-forcing polarization equalization; Kerr nonlinear noise, non-ideal receivers, and correlated or telemetry-conditioned PDL models remain for future work. © 2020 IEEE.

Title: Predictive Digital Twin-Assisted Geometry-Aware Uncertainty-Adaptive Beamforming for ISAC
Affiliations: RVCE, Department of ETE, Bengaluru, India
Authors with affiliations: Vishwanath A., RVCE, Department of ETE, Bengaluru, India; Amaresh H., RVCE, Department of ETE, Bengaluru, India; Saroha H., RVCE, Department of ETE, Bengaluru, India; Shanthi P., RVCE, Department of ETE, Bengaluru, India
Abstract: Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) is becoming an important part of sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks, where the same radio resources are used for both data transmission and environmental sensing. In practical systems, however, beamforming performance depends strongly on accurate and frequently updated channel state information (CSI). This requirement increases signaling overhead and makes the system vulnerable to mobility, blockage, and multipath effects. To address this problem, this paper presents a Predictive Digital Twin-Assisted Geometry-Aware Uncertainty-Adaptive Beamforming (GA-UAB) framework for robust ISAC operation when digital twin information is imperfect. The proposed system uses a geometry-aware digital twin with ray-tracing-based line-of-sight (LoS) and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) path inference for a 16 × 16 MIMO indoor ISAC scenario. Dual Kalman filters are used to separately track and predict the future states of the user and target, enabling the framework to account for mobility and outdated environmental information. The predicted state covariance is then used to estimate geometry uncertainty, which drives adaptive steering-angle correction and beamwidth control. The framework is evaluated through 2000 Monte Carlo realizations incorporating obstacles, reflections, mobility, and measurement dropouts, with conventional digital-twin beamforming, uncertainty-aware beamforming (UAB), and a Full-CSI (genie-aided) benchmark used for comparison. The proposed predictive GA-UAB achieves a median sensing SNR of 22.24 dB, compared with 14.04 dB for conventional digital-twin beamforming and 18.99 dB for UAB. The proposed method reduces the outage probability to 23.40%, compared with 87.15% for conventional digital-twin beamforming and 61.20% for UAB. The Full-CSI benchmark achieves a median sensing SNR of 23.99 dB, placing GA-UAB only 1.75 dB below the genie-aided reference. These results demonstrate that combining predictive geometry estimation, uncertainty adaptation, and geometry-aware beamforming improves sensing reliability and robustness in dynamic DT-assisted ISAC environments. © 2013 IEEE.

Title: Hybrid Digital Twin Framework for Predictive Maintenance and Operational Optimization of Marine Propulsion Systems
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, AMET University, Chennai, India; Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, SSN School of Engineering, Shiv Nadar University, Chennai, India; Faculty of Data Science and IT, INTI International University, Nilai, 71800, Malaysia

Abstract: Marine propulsion systems operate under highly variable environmental and mechanical conditions, making conventional threshold-based monitoring and calendar-based maintenance insufficient for early degradation detection and operational optimization. This study proposes a hybrid Digital Twin framework for a Panamax-class container vessel equipped with a MAN B&W ME-GI propulsion system. The framework integrates multi-rate operational and sensor data, time synchronization and preprocessing, a physics-based Mean Value Engine Model, machine-learning residual analysis, anomaly detection, Remaining Useful Life estimation, uncertainty quantification, and PMS/EMS-based decision support. A twelve-month simulated dataset was generated to represent variations in engine load, vessel trim, draft, sea state, hydrodynamic resistance, and progressive machinery degradation. The proposed framework was evaluated against a baseline Planned Maintenance System using Specific Fuel Oil Consumption, unplanned maintenance events, advisory latency, and false-alarm rate. Results show that the Digital Twin reduced Specific Fuel Oil Consumption from 184.6 to 176.9 g/kWh, equivalent to a 4.17% improvement. Unplanned maintenance events decreased from 11 to 9 per year, advisory latency was reduced from 20.0 to 8.5 seconds, and the false-alarm rate declined from 6.1% to 2.1%. The framework also enabled earlier identification of scavenge-cooler fouling, cylinder leakage, injector-response delay, turbocharger deterioration, and bearing degradation. These findings demonstrate that combining physics-based modelling with temporal residual analysis can improve propulsion-performance estimation, diagnostic reliability, and condition-based maintenance planning. However, further validation using real shipboard data and multiple vessel configurations is required before operational deployment. © Authors retain all copyrights.

Title: A Monte Carlo enhanced agent based model for Tokenized BIM Twin (TBT) resource reallocation in construction projects
Affiliations: School of Engineering, Cardiff University, Cardiff, United Kingdom; Department of Architecture, Artvin Coruh University, Artvin, Turkey; Department of Statistics, Cumhuriyet University, Sivas, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Celik Y., School of Engineering, Cardiff University, Cardiff, United Kingdom, Department of Architecture, Artvin Coruh University, Artvin, Turkey; Cadirci M.S., Department of Statistics, Cumhuriyet University, Sivas, Turkey
Abstract: Construction projects involve a complex relationship of interdependence among numerous parties, which often leads to delays and significant coordination costs among contractors. While approaches based on Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies have enhanced monitoring and visualization capabilities, they remain limited in their ability to enable autonomous, decentralized, and tamper-proof resource reallocation. This paper proposes and computationally evaluates a three-layer Tokenized BIM-Twin (TBT) framework under controlled simulation conditions. The framework combines a static IFC-based BIM layer for resource tokenization, a real-time Digital Twin layer to detect anomalies and measure deviations, and a blockchain-based smart contract layer that has the potential to minimize disputes and reallocate resources automatically and transparently under the modelled conditions. The framework is evaluated using an agent-based simulation model defined on an eight-parameter uncertainty space. A total of 150 Monte Carlo iterations per scenario (n = 450 observations) are performed across three configurations: Baseline (traditional management), Centralized BIM + DT, and the TBT framework. The results are assessed using one-way ANOVA, Welch’s t-tests, and effect size analysis (Cohen’s d), indicating statistically significant differences across all evaluated performance dimensions under the modelled conditions. Schedule overrun is reduced within the simulation environment from a mean of 38.90% (± 6.24) to 3.30% (± 1.38) (F = 2672.5, p < 0.001, d = 7.88). Resource idle rates decline from 35.52% (± 3.22) to 20.04% (± 3.02) (d = 4.96), while disruption response time is reduced from 5.45 days (± 1.23) to 0.44 days (± 0.17) (d = 5.69). In addition to its conceptual contribution, the framework has practical implications, as the framework demonstrates the potential to improve coordination efficiency, reduce disputes, and increase transparency under the modelled conditions. The results suggest that the approach has potential for projects characterized by high uncertainty and complex stakeholder interactions, although empirical validation is still required before real-world performance can be confirmed. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Uncertainty-aware digital twin-driven fault-tolerant control for autonomous underwater vehicles using temporal fusion transformer-based fault diagnosis
Affiliations: Electrical Engineering Department, College of Engineering, Najran University, Najran, 61441, Saudi Arabia; Science and Engineering Research Center, Najran University, Najran, 61441, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Irfan M., Electrical Engineering Department, College of Engineering, Najran University, Najran, 61441, Saudi Arabia, Science and Engineering Research Center, Najran University, Najran, 61441, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operate in challenging marine environments. The actuator faults, propulsion degradation and environmental disturbances can significantly compromise mission safety and tracking performance. Existing studies have primarily focused on either fault diagnosis or fault-tolerant control as separate tasks. A limited attention has been given to integrating fault diagnosis, predictive digital twins and uncertainty-aware control within a unified framework. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel uncertainty-aware digital twin-driven fault-tolerant control (UA-DT-FTC) framework that integrates the Temporal Fusion Transformer with Confidence-Aware Learning (TFT-CAL) for fault diagnosis; a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) based Digital Twin for one-step-ahead state prediction; dual-source uncertainty estimation; and a severity-confidence-adaptive predictive fault-tolerant control strategy. The proposed controller continuously adjusts the digital twin compensation according to both the estimated fault severity and the confidence of the fused uncertainty measure through a severity-confidence adaptive gain and fault-adaptive predictive gains, thereby improving tracking performance under uncertain operating conditions. To the best of the authors' knowledge, publicly available studies using the selected AUV benchmark dataset have primarily focused on fault identification, whereas its integration into a complete digital twin-assisted fault-tolerant control framework has not been previously reported. Experimental evaluation on a publicly available AUV dataset comprising five operating conditions demonstrates that the proposed diagnosis module achieves approximately 97.57% classification accuracy and 97.43% macro-F1 score. The performance was also validated through five-fold cross-validation. The LSTM-based Digital Twin provides one-step-ahead state predictions whose reliability is explicitly quantified through prediction residuals. In closed-loop control, the proposed UA-DT-FTC framework achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated controllers, reducing the tracking root mean square error (RMSE) and integral absolute error (IAE) by approximately 6.7% and 6.5%, respectively, compared with the conventional digital twin-based fault-tolerant controller, while maintaining robust performance under Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis. These results demonstrate that the proposed integration of TFT-CAL fault diagnosis, an LSTM-based Digital Twin, dual-source uncertainty estimation, and a severity-confidence adaptive predictive fault-tolerant control strategy provides an effective and reliable solution for improving the fault tolerance, robustness, and operational safety of autonomous underwater vehicles. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Design of large-scale floating offshore wind turbines: A review of advances and challenges
Affiliations: School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China; Huaneng Clean Energy Research Institute (CERI), Beijing, 102209, China
Authors with affiliations: Gu Q., School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China; Li H., Huaneng Clean Energy Research Institute (CERI), Beijing, 102209, China; Cheng Z., School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China; Huang D., School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China
Abstract: Reliable design of floating offshore wind turbines requires balancing energy production, structural reliability and cost under coupled interactions among aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, structural dynamics and turbine control. This review examines horizontal-axis floating turbines, focusing on how blade, floater, mooring and control design affect system response. Physical tests, numerical models and data-assisted methods are evaluated in terms of predictive accuracy, computational cost and validation evidence. Platform motion alters the relative rotor inflow, while control strategies that suppress platform motion can increase fatigue loads under certain operating conditions. Reported fatigue changes therefore remain specific to the turbine configuration, environmental conditions and operating state. Environmental uncertainty, experimental scaling and limited field data constrain validation; predictive accuracy depends on the representation of the governing physical mechanisms and the reliability of environmental and structural inputs. A validation procedure is proposed comprising five groups of cases covering basic model checks, aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, coupled response and field comparisons. Machine learning and digital twins can support load estimation and maintenance planning, with performance evaluated under conditions excluded from calibration and training. Research priorities thus include coordinated structural and control optimization, uncertainty propagation in lifetime fatigue prediction, and independent model validation under fault and shutdown conditions. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A physics-informed simulation-based digital twin framework for condition monitoring and health assessment of automotive suspension systems
Affiliations: School of Mechanical Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), Vellore, 632014, India
Authors with affiliations: Rajamohan V., School of Mechanical Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), Vellore, 632014, India
Abstract: In the present study, a physics-informed simulation-based digital twin framework for an automotive suspension system exposed to transient and stochastic road excitations is formulated for health monitoring and prognostics. A physics-based quarter-car dynamic model is considered for the development of governing equation of motion and integrated with the state estimation and online damping parameter tracking to synchronize the virtual model with the simulated degrading physical system. Further, the proposed framework is assessed through obtaining the response data under controlled road excitations, where the prescribed road displacement and velocity serve as excitation inputs during the state estimation process. A normalized suspension health index (SHI) is obtained continuously from the estimated damping coefficient to quantify its degradation in real time. Initially, remaining useful life (RUL) of the suspension system is evaluated using the conventional slope-based degradation approach. The numerical instability of the slope-based approach is evident from the presence of artificial spikes and projection of unreliable life. However, this limitation is overcome through developing a cumulative damage-based prognostic of suspension system such that the life degradation is expressed in terms of integral of degradation of intensity of the damping coefficient, obtained through SHI. The comparative analysis under half-cosine bump and stochastic road inputs demonstrates that the proposed damage-based RUL approach provides stable, interpretable, and monotonic prognostic estimates. Further, the robustness of the proposed framework against the various uncertainties in vehicle loading is investigated through performing a mass sensitivity analysis. The various uncertainties such as the variation in the sprung mass depending on passenger occupancy, payload, and operating conditions are considered for the investigation. Further, the results demonstrate that the proposed digital twin framework enhances the robustness and reliability of suspension life prediction through integrating the time-varying damping coefficient, SHI, and cumulative damage modelling. It can be concluded that the proposed simulation-based digital twin framework yields a scalable foundation for the physics-informed health monitoring, prognostic studies and offers a extensible basis for future real-world implementation. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors with affiliations: Bhatt T., School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, 639798, Singapore; Sharma D., School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, 639798, Singapore; Ng E.Y.K., School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, 639798, Singapore; Le Ferrand H., School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, 639798, Singapore, School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, 639798, Singapore
Abstract: Global cold-chain logistics relies heavily on energy-intensive and hard-to-recycle materials that offer excellent thermal insulation, but are often made using highly polluting materials and are vulnerable to punctures. Here, we developed mycelium-bound bio-fiber envelopes (BFEs) obtained by growing Ganoderma lucidum mycelium on discarded lignocellulosic cardboard, rice husk, and oats. The hyphal fiber network bonds the waste substrates into a mechanically robust (yield strength = 0.72 MPa), thermally insulating (thermal conductivity = 0.05 W/m.K), hydrophobic (contact angle = 121.4°), fire-resistant, and fully biodegradable composite in tropical ambient outdoor climate. The BFE delivers thermal insulation comparable to foams, while achieving 6× lower carbon emissions and 4.2× lower energy demand than other cold-chain materials. To overcome the issue of performance uncertainty, a digital twin framework is integrated for real-time monitoring. Combining bio-based materials with digital tracking can reduce risks and make them reliable for demanding applications such as cold-chain logistics. Unlike prior mycelium composites, which are typically characterized in isolation from real-time performance monitoring, this work couples a living bio-based insulation material with a physics-based digital twin, turning biological variability into a bounded and monitored quantity and offering a practical route to qualify bio-based materials for regulated cold-chain logistics. This study is limited to prototype-scale envelopes and to a digital twin validated on a bounded set of payloads, geometries, and ambient profiles, and wider qualification is the subject of ongoing work. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Accurate prediction of transient pore-water pressure (PWP) is essential for reliable assessment of levee performance and decision-making, as seepage-driven processes directly influence failure mechanisms such as slope instability, uplift, and internal erosion. Physics-based numerical seepage models are widely used in engineering practice, but their predictive accuracy is often limited by model parameter uncertainty, simplified boundary conditions, and unmodeled processes, particularly under transient hydrologic forcing. These limitations introduce uncertainty in evaluating levee performance under extreme events. This study develops a hybrid modeling framework that enhances predictive accuracy while preserving the physical consistency of numerical seepage models. The framework integrates transient finite-element (FE) seepage modeling, sensitivity-guided parameter calibration, and a data-driven residual-learning layer based on a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. The LSTM is trained exclusively to learn structured residual errors between FE predictions and field measurements and operates as an additive correction without modifying governing equations. Application to a field-instrumented levee demonstrates that while calibration improves overall agreement, systematic discrepancies persist under transient conditions. The residual-learning layer reduces prediction error by approximately 70%, lowering the RMSE from about 11 cm to approximately 3. Interpretability analysis using TimeSHAP confirms that residual corrections are governed primarily by physically meaningful drivers, including hydrologic forcing and recent system state. By reducing structured model discrepancy, the proposed framework improves transient seepage predictions while retaining a physics-based predictive baseline and providing transparency into the factors governing residual correction. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future sensor-integrated digital-twin applications as additional validation data become available. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Toxicology has accumulated many predictive tools - physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models, quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) frameworks organ-on-chip systems, quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models, adverse outcome pathway (AOP) networks and machine-learning approaches. Yet predictive practice remains fragmented. Each tool captures a slice of biology; few capture the whole; none captures the patient. We argue that the concept of a digital twin - a continuously updated, mechanistically grounded, data-driven digital representation of an individual biological system - offers the missing organisational layer. We first trace the origin of digital twins from aerospace engineering through biomedicine into toxicology, emphasising how the defining properties (dynamic data assimilation at the pace a decision requires, multi-scale integration, hybrid mechanistic-statistical architecture, personalisation, predictive simulation) map onto existing toxicological methods. We then position PBPK and QSP as mature proto-twin components and name the architectural gaps - continuous data flow, uncertainty quantification, feedback-driven recalibration and regulatory-grade validation - that separate today's best models from a working twin. A four-layer architecture is proposed: data, mechanistic, AI and simulation. Six published systems are tested against the five conditions; none satisfies all five. We examine applications in drug development, personalised risk assessment, mass-poisoning response, chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear (CBRN) preparedness and antidote discovery for unknown toxins. Finally, we confront the translational gap: data heterogeneity, validation standards, interpretability, regulatory acceptance and ethical custody of patient-level models. Toxicology, we conclude, has most of the ingredients needed for digital-twin implementation; what remains is the integration work, two unresolved scientific problems and the institutional willingness to address them. Abstract: Flexible operation subjects coal-fired utility boilers to distinct but interacting combustion, emissions and equipment-safety constraints at low load and during rapid load changes. This review synthesises 203 publications on sensing, prediction, dynamic modelling, optimisation and system integration, linking operating problems to measurements, model resolution and validation requirements. Low-load operating points are better documented than plant responses during ramps. Low-load assessment centres on ignition, burnout and heating-surface conditions; ramping also requires attention to fuel delivery, steam/water dynamics and selective catalytic reduction. Low-order dynamic models support load-tracking analysis, whereas spatially resolved or coupled models address local heat transfer and tube-wall constraints. Validation must distinguish steady regression, transient forecasting and control, and test transfer across relevant fuels and operating conditions. Predicted optimisation gains require independent evaluation before they support claims of plant benefit. For plant application, selected settings must be linked to operating constraints and measured responses, with benefit attribution accounting for fuel and load differences and uncertainty. System integration, physical implementation and repeated automatic feedback remain distinct. Future work should combine complementary measurements with task-appropriate models and independently evaluate the resulting operating actions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Non-CO2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from urban wastewater resource recovery facilities (WRRFs) are spatially heterogeneous at the meter scale, introducing large uncertainties in national inventories and process-level control. We establish SMART-GHG (Spatially explicit Monitoring, Assessment, and Reduction Technology for Greenhouse Gas management), combining unmanned-aerial-vehicle (UAV) concentration mapping with floating-chamber flux measurements to reconstruct continuous CH4 and N2O emission fields. The framework quantifies sampling requirements and validates an activated-sludge model as a facility-specific digital twin. At a full-scale anaerobic/anoxic/oxic WRRF (300,000 m3 d–1), seasonal surveys of the monitored basin in one of four parallel treatment trains yielded CH4 emissions of 3.15–13.08 kg d–1, dominated by influent stripping, and N2O emissions of 4.74–28.64 kg d–1, with mid-train peaks corresponding to aeration transitions. Numerical sub-sampling indicated that stable emission estimates required approximately 30 measurement points per lane (5 m spacing) in this basin; sparser sampling induced errors up to ±30%. Validation against longitudinal dissolved-oxygen and nitrogen profiles yielded mean absolute percentage errors of 3.6–17.5%. Model-guided optimization of zoned dissolved-oxygen set points predicted approximately 12% lower N2O emissions and 9% lower aeration energy use than a simulated conventional-aeration baseline, while maintaining effluent compliance in the model. SMART-GHG supports spatially explicit emission inventories and model-based aeration optimization in WRRFs. © 2026 American Chemical Society

Title: Flood evacuation models: A simplified probabilistic approach with application to a case study in Rome
Source title: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction

Abstract: Flood events clearly induce significant impacts in urbanized regions. Over the last decades, advances in computational capacity, high-resolution digital elevation data, and open-access geospatial datasets have enabled the development of Evacuation Models (EM). However, many EMs are often not so suitable for operational use by civil protection authorities, due to their significant data requirements, high computational burden and complex parametrisation. In this context, this work aims to bridge this gap by proposing a screening-level, operational tool based on a simplified probabilistic methodology, that integrates pedestrian movement under uncertainty with a streamlined representation of flood arrival time, and then produces evacuation-time distributions and spatially explicit estimates of floodwater-pedestrian interaction probability. The approach is applied to a flood-prone urban area in Rome (Italy). Results highlight the role of network topology, route branching and behavioural variability in determining evacuation performance, revealing critical areas where existing Evacuation Plans (EPs) may require revision. Finally, we state the need for integrating simplified evacuation models into emergent decision-support frameworks, including Digital Twins for urban flood management. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors with affiliations: Li Y., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States; Wang X., Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, United States; Yang X., Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, United States; Ding J., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States; Hu R., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States; Huang Y., Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, United States; Tao C., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States
Abstract: Distributed fiber optic sensing (DFOS) provides spatially continuous strain measurements and is increasingly used in infrastructure monitoring applications. However, structural deformation, a key response parameter for performance assessment, is not directly available from measured strain data alone. To enable deformation evaluation from distributed strain measurements, this study develops a curvature integration deformation reconstruction framework based on Kirchhoff-Love plate theory specialized for DFOS applications in thin plate structures. This study is designed to accommodate the intrinsic measurement characteristics of DFOS, in which strain data are obtained along discrete fiber paths. Given the number restriction of DFOS, the reconstruction formulation is modified to enable strip-based calculations compatible with DFOS layouts. The reconstruction is formulated as an inverse problem grounded in Kirchhoff-Love plate theory. DFOS measured surface strains are converted into bending curvatures and subsequently integrated along Kirchhoff-Love strips to recover full field displacement. Spline interpolation and boundary correction are incorporated to enhance numerical stability and mitigate measurement uncertainty. To verify the reliability of the method, multiple representative loading conditions on thin plates are conducted, including bending, impact, and buckling. The results are validated through comparison with finite element analysis (FEA) and experimental measurements. In the bending test, the predicted transverse deflection closely matches the imposed displacement, with a relative error of less than 9%. For the impact and buckling conditions, the reconstructed peak transverse deflections also show strong alignment with FEA outputs. These results indicate that the Kirchhoff-Love strips method (KLSM) framework, leveraging DFOS measurement data, provides a reliable and efficient solution for deformation reconstruction in thin-plate structures with limited sensor coverage, supporting potential applications in real-time structural health monitoring and digital twin systems. © 2026 Institution of Structural Engineers.
