Title: Integrating Digital Twin technology in Quality 5.0 and operational excellence: a Fuzzy COPRAS and Monte Carlo uncertainty simulation approach
Affiliations: International Business Management, International School of Management (ISM), Paris, France
Authors with affiliations: Bagherian A., International Business Management, International School of Management (ISM), Paris, France
Abstract: Existing literature on the topic of Digital Twin (DT) integration in Quality 5.0 predominantly focuses on technical performance indicators, including predictive maintenance and efficiency in the process, and ignores the essential real requirement of alignment with human-centric values, the necessity of sustainability, and the interdependencies of factors of implementation success. This study compares the integration of Digital Twin (DT) in Quality 5.0, which is based on human-centric and sustainability-driven operational excellence. It allocates implementation criteria and alternatives in priority using a three-level Fuzzy COPRAS model with Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification and Sobel sensitivity analysis. A participation of 74 experts and a case study on the automotive industry reveal that Sustainability in Quality Improvement (SQI) is the best driver of improvement, in addition to conventional efficiency. Major sub-criteria are MES/ERP integration (MEI) and risk management (RM-DTQ) as well as root cause analysis (RCAE). IoT (Internet of Things)-based applications, in particular, continuous improvement, were the highest ranked. Composite sensitivity was high in hybrid (AI+IoT) strategies (0.991). Validation of cases showed a reduction of 25% defects and 18 percent energy saving. The research offers a statistically proven decision model to match the adoption of DT with sustainability, IoT-based enhancement, risk management, and human collaboration. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Benbouzid M.
Author full names: Benbouzid, Mohamed (7003437800)
Title: Are Digital Twins Ready for Diagnosis and Prognosis in Power and Energy Systems?: An Application-Driven Readiness and Validation Perspective
Affiliations: University of Brest, Brest, 29238, France; Shanghai Maritime University, China
Authors with affiliations: Benbouzid M., University of Brest, Brest, 29238, France, Shanghai Maritime University, China
Abstract: Digital twins (DTs) are increasingly being considered as enabling technologies for advanced condition diagnosis and prognosis in power and energy systems. By combining physical models, operational data, and synchronization with physical assets, DTs can potentially support physically consistent fault diagnosis, degradation assessment, and remaining useful life (RUL) estimation in electrical machines, power electronic systems, renewable energy plants, energy storage systems, and power networks. However, the engineering maturity of DTs for these capabilities remains heterogeneous, and some reported implementations might be more accurately interpreted as monitoring-oriented digital shadows, periodically updated models, or application-specific analytical tools. This perspective critically examines the readiness of DTs specifically for condition diagnosis and prognosis in power and energy systems. Rather than providing another systematic review of DT technologies, it evaluates the DT layer itself against the functional requirements imposed by diagnosis and prognosis. Particular attention is given to model adequacy, synchronization and state updating, degradation representation, uncertainty handling, validation credibility, and lifecycle integration. An application-driven distinction among digital models, digital shadows, and DTs is established, followed by a readiness framework that relates these representations to diagnosis- and prognosis-oriented decision support. Representative power and energy applications are then examined to identify the gap between demonstrated capability and engineering-ready deployment. The resulting perspective highlights the validation evidence and research advances required to move DT-based diagnosis and prognosis from research demonstrations toward validated and scalable engineering deployment. © 2007-2011 IEEE.

Title: Identifying and characterising uncertainty in digital twin engineering
Affiliations: IRT SystemX, Palaiseau, France; Université Paris-Saclay, ENS Paris-Saclay, LURPA, Gif-sur-Yvette, France
Authors with affiliations: El Bouzaidi Tiali B., IRT SystemX, Palaiseau, France, Université Paris-Saclay, ENS Paris-Saclay, LURPA, Gif-sur-Yvette, France; Creff S., IRT SystemX, Palaiseau, France; Kallel A., IRT SystemX, Palaiseau, France; Anwer N., IRT SystemX, Palaiseau, France, Université Paris-Saclay, ENS Paris-Saclay, LURPA, Gif-sur-Yvette, France
Abstract: Digital twin technologies are increasingly deployed in complex industrial systems where uncertainty management is critical to ensure their reliability, robustness, and resilience. However, there is currently limited literature on the management of uncertainties for digital twins, and even less a structured framework for a better understanding of the uncertainties, focusing on the identification and characterisation of uncertainties within the context of digital twin engineering. In this work, a conceptual framework is proposed, structured around three key pillars: a conceptual model, a lifecycle, and maturity levels of the digital twin. A systematic literature review, following the PRISMA methodology, is conducted to identify and map four major categories of uncertainty across these pillars. The findings show how uncertainty types correspond to the 5D conceptual model of the digital twin, at which lifecycle stages they become most critical, and how they evolve as the digital twin progresses towards higher maturity levels. The proposed framework positions uncertainty characterisation as a core engineering principle of digital twins, paving the way for future research on structuring uncertainty management across digital twin engineering practices. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: A digital twin-based method for predicting the burst speed of discs
Affiliations: School of Energy and Power Engineering, Dalian University of Technology, Liaoning Province, Dalian, China; Taihang National Laboratory, Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China
Authors with affiliations: Chen G., School of Energy and Power Engineering, Dalian University of Technology, Liaoning Province, Dalian, China; Wei G., Taihang National Laboratory, Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China; Xu S., School of Energy and Power Engineering, Dalian University of Technology, Liaoning Province, Dalian, China; Zhao H., School of Energy and Power Engineering, Dalian University of Technology, Liaoning Province, Dalian, China; Li C., Taihang National Laboratory, Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China; Ni C., Taihang National Laboratory, Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China; Xu M., Taihang National Laboratory, Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China
Abstract: Overspeed burst is a critical failure mode of discs, for which experimental validation is costly and destructive, while conventional finite element analysis (FEA) is computationally expensive and often inaccurate. To address these challenges, this study proposes a digital twin-based method for disc burst speed prediction by integrating multi-source uncertainty modelling, surrogate-based prediction, and adaptive model correction. A fracture strain criterion combined with FEA is used to estimate critical burst speeds, and a high-precision Kriging model is constructed via sequential sampling to improve prediction efficiency. Experimental data are incorporated to enable online correction of geometry and model parameters. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed method improves prediction accuracy by 16.99% compared with conventional FEA, with the relative error of the actual burst speed reduced to 3.26%, while the computational time is reduced by approximately two orders of magnitude. The developed digital twin framework further supports the real-time updating of strain fields and the dynamic visualisation of the disc burst process. This method provides an accurate and efficient solution for disc burst prediction, supporting disc safety design and reliability assessment. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: A digital twin-based probability-interval hybrid uncertainty quantification method
Affiliations: Department of Frontier Technology Research, AVIC China Aero-Polytechnology Establishment, Beijing, China
Authors with affiliations: Peng W., Department of Frontier Technology Research, AVIC China Aero-Polytechnology Establishment, Beijing, China; Chen S., Department of Frontier Technology Research, AVIC China Aero-Polytechnology Establishment, Beijing, China; Xue K., Department of Frontier Technology Research, AVIC China Aero-Polytechnology Establishment, Beijing, China; Li K., Department of Frontier Technology Research, AVIC China Aero-Polytechnology Establishment, Beijing, China
Abstract: The credibility of digital twin predictions is contingent upon their capacity to manage uncertainty. Conventional methods typically characterise all uncertainties via unified probability distributions; however, in scenarios involving sparse data or conflicting expert knowledge, imposing precise distributions upon epistemic uncertainty may yield misleading results. This article proposes a probability-interval mixed uncertainty digital twin framework (PI-DTF) that constructs a dual-channel representation and propagation model. It employs probability distributions to characterise inherent aleatory uncertainty, whilst introducing a ‘belief-plausibility’ structure to describe epistemic uncertainty. The framework computes response probability bounds or belief functions via a nested, double-loop strategy, combining outer-loop Monte Carlo sampling with inner-loop interval optimisation. Abstract: This study presents a digital-twin (DT) framework for real-time condition monitoring and fault diagnosis of industrial turboshaft engines. The proposed architecture employs physics-based semi-empirical models as the core of the twin, which are calibrated using operational data collected under both nominal and off-design conditions. Given that gas turbines are prone to diverse faults with varying onset times, magnitudes, and signatures, a time-windowed residual embedding (TWRE) method is introduced to enhance the temporal representation of diagnostic features. In addition, a data-driven dynamic adaptive thresholding scheme is applied to improve robustness against environmental variations and uncertainties. By providing a comprehensive fault table, feature spaces are systematically linked to distinct fault scenarios using pattern recognition classifiers. Finally, a decision fusion mechanism is implemented to integrate diagnostic outputs based on fault types and their severities. To assess the performance of the proposed system, four sample faults are considered for simulation studies. The results indicate that the system reliably tracks fault progression and accurately detects both evident and latent anomalies, providing clear fault timelines for early alarm generation. The effectiveness of integrating semi-empirical modelling and advanced signal processing in a digital twin framework is confirmed for real-time fault monitoring and diagnosis of industrial gas turbines. © 2025 The Author(s). Abstract: Background: Digital Twin (DT) has proven to be one of the most promising technologies for routine monitoring and management of complex systems with uncertainties. Methods: Our work, which is mainly concerned with heterogeneous spatial-temporal data, focuses on exploring data utilization methodology in DT. The goal of this research is to summarize the best practices that make the spatial-temporal data analytically tractable in a systematic and quantifiable manner. Some methods are found to handle those data via jointly spatial-temporal analysis in a high-dimensional space effectively. We provide a concise yet comprehensive tutorial on spatial-temporal analysis considering data, theories, algorithms, indicators, and applications. The advantages of our spatial-temporal analysis are discussed, including model-free mode, solid theoretical foundation, and robustness against ubiquitous uncertainty and partial data error. Finally, we take the condition-based maintenance of a real digital substation in China as an example to verify our proposed spatial-temporal analysis mode. Results: Our proposed spatial-temporal data analysis mode successfully turned raw chromatographic data, which are valueless in low-dimensional space, into an informative high-dimensional indicator. The designed high-dimensional indicator could capture the ’insulation’ correlation among the sampling data over a long time span. Hence it is robust against external noise, and may support decision-making. This analysis is also adaptive to other daily spatial-temporal data in the same form, for example in a digital substation such as Cai Lun. Conclusions: This exploration and summary of spatial-temporal data analysis may benefit the fields of both the engineering and data science. © Copyright: © 2022 He X et al.

Abstract: Digital-twin (DT) systems have emerged as critical enablers of intelligent cyber–physical interaction, yet their effectiveness is limited by static modelling and non-adaptive optimisation mechanisms. This article presents a co-evolutionary framework that simultaneously evolves the DT model and its optimisation strategy, achieving self-correcting performance in dynamic environments. The framework integrates a Multi-Task Genetic Algorithm (MTGA) that unifies three concurrent evolutionary processes model calibration, decision optimisation, and uncertainty-guided exploration within a closed feedback loop. A formal theoretical foundation is developed to describe the coupled fitness landscapes and feedback–response operators that govern reciprocal adaptation between model and optimiser. The architecture incorporates an uncertainty-aware selection mechanism, where predictive variance from the surrogate model dynamically influences evolutionary pressure, thereby improving both model fidelity and solution robustness. Experimental validation on a Grid ALU Processor configuration problem demonstrates that the proposed MTGA achieves up to 60% reduction in model prediction error, 22% improvement in Pareto-front hypervolume, and enhanced stability under nonstationary conditions compared with NSGA-II, SPEA2, and CNSGA-II. These findings confirm that co-evolutionary coupling yields superior convergence and sustained reliability, positioning this framework as a foundation for next-generation self-learning, adaptive DTs in complex engineering domains. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors with affiliations: Anonto H.Z., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Shufian A., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Pathik B.B., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Hasan M., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Hazari M.R., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Mannan M.A., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, American International University-Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh
Abstract: This study develops a confidence-aware synchronized digital-twin deep deterministic policy gradient (CA-SDT-DDPG) energy-management system for a battery–ultracapacitor electric vehicle. In contrast to a generic simulation-labelled twin, the proposed architecture separates the physical, data/communication, virtual-model and twin-service layers; synchronizes state of charge (SOC), power demand, battery temperature and resistance estimates; and uses a short-horizon demand forecast, uncertainty-aware battery-stress penalty and safety projection before commands reach the bidirectional direct current-to-direct current (DC/DC) converters. Performance was assessed with a matched, repeated-seed benchmark rather than single-run comparisons. Five dataset-informed driving-profile families were each evaluated with six independent seeds (30 runs per method) using identical delivered wheel-energy demand and explicit ultracapacitor terminal-energy normalization. The comparator set comprised rule-based control, the equivalent consumption minimization strategy (ECMS), Q-learning, model predictive control (MPC), standalone deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), twin delayed DDPG (TD3), soft actor–critic (SAC) and proximal policy optimization (PPO). CA-SDT-DDPG achieved 94.95±0.40% mean conversion efficiency and a 0.0248±0.0140% monotonic equivalent battery-stress/degradation index with zero constraint violations. Relative to standalone DDPG, the digital-twin and confidence-aware extensions reduced the degradation index by 18.6% while changing mean efficiency by +0.11 percentage point; the 95% paired-bootstrap interval for the efficiency change crossed zero, whereas the interval for the degradation change remained entirely below zero. Against MPC, mean efficiency was statistically indistinguishable and the mean degradation proxy was about 4.0% lower, although this difference was not statistically clear. A 9,000-sample dataset-informed synthetic telemetry set, bounded by a 2025 one-second real-world battery-electric-vehicle (BEV) dataset, is additionally used for diagnostic correlation, three-dimensional (3D) stress-surface, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and classifier analyses; the light gradient-boosting machine (LightGBM) obtained a macro-F1 of 0.977 for the derived battery-stress classes. These machine-learning diagnostics are presented as interpretability checks rather than independent proof of controller superiority. The study remains simulation based; hardware-in-the-loop and vehicle validation are identified as the next validation stage. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Multiscale Digital-Twin Modeling of Energy-Storage Materials by Integrating First-Principles Calculations and Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
Source title: EAI Endorsed Transactions on Energy Web
Affiliations: Department of Physics and Information Engineering, Cangzhou Normal University, Cangzhou, 061001, China
Authors with affiliations: Li Y., Department of Physics and Information Engineering, Cangzhou Normal University, Cangzhou, 061001, China; Tang D., Department of Physics and Information Engineering, Cangzhou Normal University, Cangzhou, 061001, China
Abstract: Conventional modeling of energy-storage materials is constrained by the computational cost of first-principles calculations, limited electrochemical-state awareness in machine-learning interatomic potentials, and weak coupling between materials-scale models and online battery decision-making. This study proposes a first-principles-constrained electrochemically conditioned machine-learning interatomic potential (FP-EMLP) integrated with a multiscale digital-twin framework (FP-EMLP-DT). A multistate configuration space spanning ion concentration, temperature, defects, strain, and phase boundaries is combined with active learning based on committee uncertainty, structural novelty, and physics-based risk. The equivariant graph model incorporates electrochemical-state gating, charge-conserving projection, and differentiable long-range electrostatics, and is trained using energies, forces, stresses, equilibrium voltages, and migration barriers. Predicted diffusion coefficients, free energies, elastic tensors, and chemical expansion coefficients are transferred to an electrochemical-mechanical-thermal-damage model. The resulting model is further integrated with a physics-based reduced-order network, uncertainty-gated residual learning, online data assimilation, and degradation-aware control. FP-EMLP achieves mean absolute errors of 6.5meV atom-1, 33meV Å-1, 0.051V, and 0.038eV for energy, force, voltage, and migration barrier, respectively, with a 4.8 aggregate relative error across multiscale fields. Active learning reduces required first-principles labels by 33.3 while covering 91.2 of high-risk configurations. FP-EMLP-DT achieves mean absolute errors of 0.93 for state of charge and 1.21 for state of health. Degradation-aware control reduces maximum material stress and damage increment by 16.5 and 36.8, respectively, demonstrating an effective multiscale pathway from electronic structure to online battery management. © 2026 Yan Li et al., licensed to EAI. Title: AI-, DIGITAL-TWIN-, AND QUANTUM-ENABLED ROLLING-HORIZON OPTIMIZATION FOR YARD ALLOCATION AND GATE APPOINTMENT COMPLIANCE IN MODULAR CONTAINER TERMINALS
Source title: International Maritime Transport and Logistics Conference
Affiliations: Department of Political and International Sciences, University of Genoa, Piazza Emanuele Brignole 3A, Central Tower, Genoa, 16126, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Revetria R., Department of Political and International Sciences, University of Genoa, Piazza Emanuele Brignole 3A, Central Tower, Genoa, 16126, Italy; Rozhok A., Department of Political and International Sciences, University of Genoa, Piazza Emanuele Brignole 3A, Central Tower, Genoa, 16126, Italy
Abstract: Container terminals operate under increasingly tight capacity, energy, and service-level constraints, while facing growing uncertainty in arrival patterns, handling operations, and hinterland interactions. This paper proposes a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates advanced Artificial Intelligence techniques, Digital Twin modeling, and quantum-inspired optimization to address yard planning and operational optimization in container terminals. The core problem is formulated as a block-to-area assignment under soft and hard capacity constraints, priority rules, and rolling-horizon forecasts. The problem is mapped to a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation and solved using both classical and quantum-inspired approaches, including the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). Two alternative modeling strategies are investigated: a one-hot encoding with deterministic feasibility repair, and a feasibility-by-design binary encoding that reduces the number of decision variables and enforces assignment constraints structurally. A Digital Twin of the container yard acts as a truth model and constraint oracle, translating abstract optimization decisions into operational Key Performance Indicators such as reshuffling effort, crane interference, and truck waiting times. Computational experiments on a modular yard scenario highlight the trade-offs between encoding choice, feasibility, solution quality, and computational cost under time-bounded quantum-inspired optimization. The results demonstrate that quantum-inspired methods can effectively support combinatorial decision-making in port operations when combined with appropriate encodings and simulation-based validation. Rather than replacing existing planning tools, the proposed framework positions quantum optimization as a complementary accelerator within a scalable, explainable, and industry-ready Digital Twin-based decision-support architecture. Title: Exploring the metaverse: integrating emerging technologies for Industry 5.0 advancement
Affiliations: Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Faraji A., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran, Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia; Homayoon Arya S., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Ghasemi E., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Abagheri Mahabadi H., Khatam University, Tehran, Iran; Perera S., Western Sydney University, Sydney, Australia
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to explore the application of the Metaverse in the construction industry through an in-depth literature review. It highlights the core enabling technologies and investigates how they contribute to creating immersive, intelligent and sustainable construction practices in line with Industry 5.0 ideals. Design/methodology/approach – This study utilizes a systematic literature review methodology, examining 194 peer-reviewed articles published from 2015 to 2024. The papers were selected from top academic databases using specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. The review centers on Metaverse applications, the foundational technologies involved and their influence on various aspects of the construction industry. Findings – The results highlight the growing scholarly interest in the application of Metaverse technologies in the building sector, which has grown significantly since 2021. Key technologies identified include augmented reality, virtual reality, mixed reality, extended reality (XR), building information modeling, Digital Twin, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence and blockchain technology (BCT). These technologies facilitate real-time collaboration, immersive visual environments, secure data exchange and smart decision-making processes. Seven major areas of the construction industry – project management, architectural design, urban planning, construction education, civil engineering, energy management and supply chain coordination – are seeing a surge in innovation because of the Metaverse. Full integration is nevertheless hindered by persistent issues with data privacy, interoperability and regulatory uncertainty, despite its potential. Practical implications – This study provides practical insights for industry stakeholders aiming to leverage Metaverse technologies for digital transformation in construction. It emphasizes the need for integrated frameworks, skilled workforce development and consideration of environmental and economic impacts. Originality/value – This paper offers a novel synthesis of current literature at the intersection of Metaverse technologies and construction, highlighting research gaps and suggesting directions for future exploration. It contributes to the theoretical and practical understanding of how Metaverse adoption can drive smart, sustainable and human-centric innovation in the construction industry. © 2025 Emerald Publishing Limited

Title: Sparse measurement correction for full-field displacement prediction of nonlinear structures using reduced-order models and Gaussian process regression

Abstract: Online full-field displacement reconstruction from sparse measurements is an important task in nonlinear structural analysis, monitoring, and digital-twin applications. Direct finite element simulations are often too expensive for repeated online use, whereas input-only reduced-order model–Gaussian process regression (ROM-GPR) surrogate models may produce biased full-field predictions when the target structural state is insufficiently represented by offline training data. Sparse displacement measurements provide current-state information, but observation-only reconstruction is usually underdetermined or noise-sensitive under limited sensing conditions. To address this issue, this work develops a probabilistic correction strategy for ROM-GPR full-field displacement predictions by statistically weighting the input-informed surrogate estimate and sparse measurements according to their respective uncertainties. The Gaussian process regression (GPR) prediction provides a low-dimensional estimate with quantified regression uncertainty, while the measurement constraint uses an observation error covariance that accounts for sensor noise and the observation-space projection of reduced-order reconstruction residuals. Sparse measurements are incorporated through an error-covariance-weighted correction in the reduced-order space, with the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) and unscented Kalman filter (UKF) adopted as sampling-based implementations. Tests on two nonlinear 2D finite element examples and a 3D liver model show that the proposed correction reduces the mean reconstruction error by 55.92%–73.51% for autoencoder-based ROM-GPR and 72.48%–93.10% for proper orthogonal decomposition-based ROM-GPR. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Forest Carbon Sink Estimation under Smart Forestry: Progress, Challenges, and Prospects; [智慧林业背景下森林碳汇估算：进展、挑战与展望]

Authors with affiliations: Yuhua J., College of Resources and Environment, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, 712100, China; Qingfeng Z., College of Resources and Environment, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, 712100, China; Chuanlong Z., College of Resources and Environment, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, 712100, China; Jincheng L., College of Resources and Environment, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, 712100, China
Abstract: ： Forests constitute the largest carbon reservoir in terrestrial ecosystems, and accurately assessing their carbon sink capacity is essential for maintaining the global carbon balance. However, forest ecosystem carbon sinks exhibit pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity, making their accurate quantification highly challenging. By integrating multisource information technologies, smart forestry provides new opportunities to overcome the limitations of conventional static monitoring and to support dynamic simulation and precision management. This study systematically reviews the major methods used for forest carbon sink estimation, summarizes their development trends and research hotspots, and provides a comprehensive review of the opportunities and challenges associated with the development of smart forestry. The study results showed that the number of publications on forest carbon sink estimation has increased exponentially worldwide, forming a research landscape centered on China and the United States, with Western Europe and East Asia as major supporting regions. Forest carbon sink estimation has evolved from early reliance on field surveys and empirical statistical methods toward the integrated application of process-based models, remote sensing-driven models, ecosystem service models, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches. There are clear differences in research priorities are observed between international and Chinese studies: international research focuses more on climate-response mechanisms at the global scale, while research in China places greater emphasis on high-resolution regional mapping in support of the national carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals. Forest carbon sink assessment has entered a new stage characterized by multi-technology integration and cross-scale coordination. Future research should focus on reducing uncertainties associated with scale transformation and improving model interpretability by applying edge computing to dynamic carbon sink monitoring and risk early warning, strengthening the coupling of ecological process mechanisms with deep learning, and promoting the coordinated use of satellite, airborne, and ground-based observations within digital twin platforms. These advances will help improve the timeliness, accuracy, and decision-support capacity of forest carbon sink estimation. © 2026, Chinese Society of Forestry. All rights reserved.

Title: C³M-OMMT twin: A causal process–structure–property digital twin for morphology-aware mechanical optimization of OMMT-Modified PLA in fused-filament fabrications

Abstract: Mechanically reliable fused-filament-fabricated (FFF) PLA/OMMT parts depend not only on filler fraction and nominal printing settings, but also on the coupled evolution of clay dispersion, melt rheology, thermal healing, void topology, and strain localization. This study develops C³M-OMMT Twin, a six-stage causal process-structure-property digital twin comprising ExfoRheo-MAP, ThermoBond-Sense, MorphoFrac-3D, CauPSP-Net, ConBayes-Pareto, and CounterTwinV. Approximately 60 D-optimal material-process combinations were used for model development and 20 Bayesian-selected trials were reserved for experimental closure. The design space covered 0–5 wt% OMMT, 195–225 °C nozzle temperature, 0.10–0.25 mm layer height, 25–55 mm s⁻¹ print speed, raster orientation, and infill. A directly characterized condition at 2 wt% OMMT, 215 °C, 0.15 mm, and 35 mm s⁻¹ produced 62.5 MPa tensile strength and approximately 2.2% void fraction. On held-out data, CauPSP-Net achieved R²= 0.974, RMSE= 1.72 MPa, MAE= 1.29 MPa, and MAPE= 2.53%; 90% conformal intervals achieved 90.7% empirical coverage with a 4.46 MPa mean width. Model-based multi-objective optimization identified the same operating neighborhood, with predicted Young's modulus of 3.82 GPa, flexural strength of 94.1 MPa, and CVIFSI of 0.162, while CounterTwinV reported a 3.1% validation discrepancy. The originality lies in retaining physically interpretable intermediate states from exfoliation and rheology through thermal bonding and three-dimensional defect morphology, then separating direct and morphology-mediated effects under calibrated uncertainty. The resulting manufacturing window is intended for reproducible, morphology-aware optimization of lightweight PLA/OMMT FFF components rather than unrestricted extrapolation beyond the validated material and process domain. © 2026 The Authors

Abstract: Chemical research spans multiple scales from molecules to processes and industrial systems, and is inherently characterized by high dimensionality, strong coupling, and pronounced nonlinearity. Traditional research paradigms relying on empirical heuristics, isolated simulations, and iterative experimentation are increasingly inadequate to meet the emerging demands for green transformation, intelligent manufacturing, and sustainable development. In this work, we systematically review a state-of-the-art “four-dimensional integrated” intelligent research paradigm driven by large language models (LLMs), and elucidate its theoretical foundation, technical architecture, and implementation pathways for reconstructing the chemical research framework. Centered on LLMs as the cognitive core, the proposed paradigm integrates four key dimensions: knowledge engine, molecular reasoning, process simulation, and intelligent decision-making. At the knowledge level, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and knowledge graph technologies are synergistically combined to construct a dynamic and computable knowledge infrastructure that semantically unifies literature, patents, and experimental data. This enables the transition from conventional information retrieval to evidence-based knowledge discovery and reasoning-oriented scientific research. At the molecular level, generative foundation models, multi-objective optimization models, and multimodal molecular representation learning are integrated with physical constraints and chemical ontologies, forming a closed intelligent loop from molecular conception and structure generation to reaction planning, energy verification, and synthesizability assessment. This framework significantly accelerates the discovery of functional molecules and advanced materials while mitigating chemical hallucination risks. At the process level, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), neural operators, and digital twin technologies are introduced to bridge mechanistic models with data-driven surrogates, enabling cross-scale, high-fidelity, and computationally efficient modeling of complex multiphase transport, reaction, and energy conversion processes. In parallel, LLM-driven multi-agent automation frameworks enable end-to-end workflows for CFD/ FEM model generation, simulation execution, and intelligent post-analysis, substantially lowering the technical barrier for high-level process simulations. At the decision-making level, ontology engineering serves as the semantic foundation that formalizes chemical entities, equipment, unit operations, and control logic into a unified machine-interpretable structure. On this basis, reinforcement learning and uncertainty-aware optimization construct an interpretable, traceable, and transferable knowledge-driven decision loop, enabling semantic-level integration of process control, alarm diagnosis, batch optimization, and system-wide sustainable operation. The four dimensions work synergistically to form an intelligent cognitive chain that links molecules, processes, and systems, driving the transformation of chemical research from experience-driven to inference-driven paradigms. Furthermore, we propose the emerging concept of an ontology-driven multi-agent collaborative system (OD-MAS), which envisions a transition from isolated task-level intelligence toward system-level collaboration and knowledge-level autonomy. OD-MAS enables multiple specialized intelligent agents to operate within a unified semantic space for coordinated discovery, simulation, optimization, and safety evaluation. This framework provides a fundamental semantic infrastructure for the interoperability of data, models, and decisions, and establishes methodological and strategic foundations for the deep integration of green chemistry, intelligent manufacturing, and autonomous scientific discovery. © 2026 Science Press. Abstract: Modal parameters are increasingly used in vibration-based Structural Health Monitoring (SHM), Finite Element Model Updating (FEMU), and Digital Twin (DT) applications; however, nominally identical structures can exhibit different modal properties due to physical variability and uncertainties associated with modal identification. This study presents an experimental-statistical framework for characterizing these sources of variability through a large-scale repeated testing campaign comprising 400 vibration experiments on an Axial Piston Pump (APP) sub-assembly. Modal parameters were identified using input–output covariance-driven Stochastic Subspace Identification (SSI-IOCOV), combined with automated modal parameter extraction and tracking. Variability associated with component, assembly, and operator effects was characterized from repeated experimental measurements, while bootstrap resampling was used to quantify identification induced uncertainty under nominally fixed physical conditions. The resulting modal parameter distributions enable explicit comparison between experimentally induced variability and identification induced uncertainty, providing a statistically characterized baseline of nominal modal behavior. The results show that, for the investigated configurations, experimentally induced variability is consistently larger than the bootstrap derived identification uncertainty. Natural frequencies exhibit relatively consistent behavior and are primarily influenced by component variability, whereas damping ratio estimates show substantially greater dispersion and sensitivity. Accurate characterization of these uncertainty sources provides a basis for distinguishing structurally significant changes from normal variability arising from repeated testing and measurement conditions. Although demonstrated on an APP sub-assembly, the proposed framework is applicable to other mechanical structures and provides an experimental uncertainty basis for vibration-based SHM, subsequent probabilistic FEMU, and DT applications. © 2026

Title: Digital Twins for Nuclear Reactor Monitoring and Operational Intelligence: A Systematic Scoping Review
Affiliations: Department of Computer Systems and Technologies, Technical University of Sofia, Sofia, 1000, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Gancheva V., Department of Computer Systems and Technologies, Technical University of Sofia, Sofia, 1000, Bulgaria
Abstract: Digital twins (DTs) are increasingly proposed for nuclear-reactor monitoring, diagnosis, prediction, control, and decision support, but the maturity of reported systems is difficult to compare because DT realization, physical anchoring, synchronization, adaptation, validation, real-time execution, and trustworthiness are often conflated. This systematic scoping review maps substantive DT research for nuclear fission reactors and nuclear power plants using a strict substantive-DT definition and a multidimensional evidence-coding framework covering DT realization, physical anchoring, adaptation, validation, real-time capability, and trustworthiness. Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore yielded 845 database records and 590 unique records after deduplication. A multi-pass title/abstract workflow classified 182 records as Include, 397 as excluded from the primary-study stream, and 11 as Uncertain, yielding 193 reports sought for retrieval. Despite iterative multi-source retrieval attempts, 96 reports could not be retrieved. One additional Uncertain conference report was linked to an already retained journal report and was not treated as an independent report; 96 retrieved reports underwent primary full-text eligibility assessment. Seventy-one retrieved and eligible peer-reviewed primary reports met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 44/71 (62%) were Tier A implemented or integrated DT systems. Physical anchoring ranged from P0 simulation-only realization (39/71, 55%) to P3 operating-reactor or plant evidence (9/71, 13%); within P3, four reports used retrospective/offline operating data and five demonstrated live or near-live reactor/plant linkage. Validation evidence comprised 40/71 reports (56%) with development-linked validation (V1), 26/71 (37%) with separated empirical or benchmark validation (V2), and 5/71 (7%) with prospective, challenge-based, or independently confirmed validation (V3). Adaptation was limited: 51/71 reports (72%) demonstrated no adaptation (A0), 3/71 (4%) episodic or intermittent recalibration (A1), 5/71 (7%) online state synchronization/estimation (A2-S), 12/71 (17%) online parameter/model adaptation (A2-P), and none met the A3 criterion. Computational real-time capability was supported in 42/71 reports (59%), whereas integrated real- or near-real-time execution was demonstrated in 27/71 (38%); live physical-data ingestion, explicit recurring physical-to-digital synchronization, and automatic DT-to-physical actuation were demonstrated in 11/71 (15%), 5/71 (7%), and 1/71 (1%), respectively. Hybrid modelling was the dominant paradigm (34/71, 48%). Trustworthiness was asymmetric: calibration and robustness/OOD assessment were much more common than uncertainty quantification, explainability, cybersecurity, traceability, human oversight, or demonstrated regulatory readiness. A targeted data audit identified only four reports linked to clearly open and reusable benchmark or downloadable resources. Family-aware, quality, physical-evidence, temporal, and data-access sensitivity analyses did not materially change the central conclusions. Nuclear-DT maturity is best understood as multidimensional; future progress requires staged physical validation, bounded adaptive synchronization, trustworthy decision support, reproducible data/model provenance, and independent deployment-oriented validation. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Multi-Criteria Decision-Making and Digital Twins for Sustainable Environmental Planning and Management: Methods, Applications, and Limitations: A Review
Affiliations: School of Agriculture and Food Sciences, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, 4072, QLD, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Dayananda B., School of Agriculture and Food Sciences, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, 4072, QLD, Australia
Abstract: Environmental planning and management must reconcile multiple sustainability objectives, uncertain impacts, and diverse stakeholder priorities, often under data-rich but fragmented information environments. Multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) offers structured approaches for comparing alternatives, while digital twins and related smart tools (e.g., GIS, BIM, IoT monitoring, and decision support platforms) can represent system behaviour and support scenario testing. This article is a comprehensive narrative review (not a registered systematic review or meta-analysis). It synthesises a documented evidence base of 68 sources identified through Scopus/Web of Science-style Boolean strings, citation chasing, and a reproducible OpenAlex retrieval executed on 2 September 2026. Coding of that evidence base shows AHP/ANP as the most frequent MCDM family emphasis, GIS as the most frequent digital layer, and GIS/spatial MCDM (Pattern A) as the most frequent explicit coupling path; fully operational bidirectional twins and closed adaptive ranking loops remain uncommon. The typology contribution is an organising lens that jointly classifies (i) decision structure, (ii) digital representation class (conventional smart tool, partial twin, or fully operational twin), and (iii) coupling Patterns A–D; this differs from method-only MCDM surveys and architecture-only twin reviews by making coupling the unit of synthesis. Recurring limitations include uneven uncertainty treatment and validation, interoperability and cost barriers, governance and equity gaps, and rare monitoring-to-ranking loops. Priorities are transparent data lineage, uncertainty-aware and equity-conscious coupling, interoperable decision layers, and post-implementation learning. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Semantic-Guided Adaptive Gaussian Segmentation
Affiliations: College of Information Engineering, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, 201306, China
Authors with affiliations: Zhou Y., College of Information Engineering, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, 201306, China; Zhou F., College of Information Engineering, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, 201306, China
Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time photorealistic scene reconstruction, yet its segmentation tasks suffer from two critical flaws: poor 3D consistency (e.g., blurred instance boundaries and unstable cross-view semantic association) and insufficient structural awareness near ambiguous object boundaries. To address these issues, this paper proposes a semantic-guided 3D Gaussian segmentation framework. We first process multi-view RGB images and semantic masks to generate 2D semantic codes and initial Gaussian parameters. We then build a Gaussian-level joint representation by combining flow-aligned appearance cues, CLIP-derived semantic descriptors, and explicit Gaussian geometry. Semantic-guided adaptive decomposition identifies boundary-sensitive Gaussians through cross-view boundary statistics and semantic uncertainty, while multi-view voting further refines instance boundaries. Finally, 3D global optimization unifies instance association and labeling. Experiments on ScanNet and SPIn-NeRF show improved results under the reported evaluation protocol and the stated subset definitions. In particular, on the ScanNet benchmark, compared with the evaluated 3DGS baseline InstanceGaussian, SG-AGS improves mAcc@0.25 by 16.2 points for category-agnostic 3D instance segmentation and by 25.6 points for text-query-based open-vocabulary labeling of segmented 3D instances. These results support the usefulness of SG-AGS on the two evaluated benchmarks and suggest potential value for object-level scene querying and digital-twin inspection, while broader generalization to external captures and other scene domains still requires further validation. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Dwelling Refurbishment: A Bibliometric and Systematic Review

Abstract: Growing recognition of climate-related challenges and increasingly ambitious sustainability goals have raised the urgency of improving the energy performance of existing buildings. At the same time, emerging technologies, including advanced materials, artificial intelligence (AI), Building Information Modeling (BIM), Digital Twins (DTs), and Internet of Things (IoT)-based systems, are transforming refurbishment practices. However, research on emerging technologies in dwelling refurbishment remains fragmented, limiting a comprehensive understanding of current developments and future research directions. To address this gap, this study employs a combined bibliometric and systematic literature review to analyze the evolution of research on emerging technologies in dwelling refurbishment. Through quantitative knowledge mapping and qualitative thematic synthesis, the study identifies major research trends, collaboration patterns, and technological developments in dwelling refurbishment. The findings reveal growing research interest in new envelope materials, smart building technologies, advanced urban-scale refurbishment modeling, and participatory approaches within human-centered cyber-physical systems. Despite significant progress, persistent challenges include high implementation costs, scalability limitations, data interoperability issues, policy constraints, climate-related uncertainties, and socio-behavioral barriers. The results of this study offer a strategic research agenda for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers to support technology-driven, sustainable, energy-efficient, and resilient dwelling refurbishment. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Artificial-Intelligence-Enabled Wind-Grid Intelligence Systems: A Systematic Review of AI Evolution, Functional Intelligence Layers, and Deployment Readiness

Abstract: The accelerated adoption of renewable energy (RE) systems has heightened the complexity of electricity grid operations, primarily due to the uncertainty, variability, and distributed nature of wind power generation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative tool for addressing these challenges by facilitating advanced forecasting, adaptive control, optimization, and intelligent decision-making. Nevertheless, the maturity of AI-enabled Wind-Grid Intelligence Systems (WGIS), encompassing functional capabilities, methodological development, and practical deployment readiness, remains inadequately characterized. This systematic review assesses the current landscape of AI-enabled WGIS by synthesizing findings from 56 empirical studies. The literature was categorized using a structured framework that examined each study’s evidence source, AI methodologies, WGIS layer, target application, and validation maturity. The analysis indicates that WGIS research encompasses both wind-specific applications and transferable intelligent-grid technologies. Specifically, 48.2% of studies focus on wind-related challenges, while 51.8% address broader intelligent-grid solutions. Methodological trends reveal a shift toward advanced AI architectures, with deep learning as the predominant approach (50.0%), followed by reinforcement learning (33.9%) and traditional machine learning (8.9%). Although techniques such as graph intelligence and physics-informed AI are currently underrepresented, they offer considerable potential to enhance the reliability and contextual awareness of WGIS architectures. Analysis using a five-layer WGIS intelligence framework demonstrates that layer 2, predictive intelligence, is the primary research focus, accounting for 51.8% of studies, followed by layer 4, adaptive control intelligence, at 21.4%. In contrast, layer 5, strategic intelligence, is underexplored, with only 7.1% of studies addressing this area. This distribution indicates that current research prioritizes prediction and operational support rather than autonomous strategic decision-making. Furthermore, the validation maturity assessment reveals a substantial gap between AI development and practical implementation. Of the studies reviewed, 60.7% were classified at V1 using offline/stored-dataset validation, 37.5% at V2 using software simulation or co-simulation, and a single study (1.8%) reached V3 dedicated real-time hardware-coupled laboratory validation. No study satisfied the predefined criteria for pilot-scale demonstration or full operational deployment. Methodological-quality appraisal classified 39 studies (69.6%) as Higher-confidence and 17 (30.4%) as Moderate-confidence, with no Lower-confidence studies; restriction to the Higher-confidence subset did not alter the principal rank order conclusions. Accordingly, 98.2% of the evidence remained within the V1–V2 stages, while no study reached pilot-scale (V4) or operational (V5) deployment, underscoring the need for more robust validation pathways and industry-scale demonstrations. This review proposes a future WGIS development roadmap focused on integrated AI architectures, trustworthy AI, digital twin technologies, physics-informed learning, and real-world validation frameworks. The findings indicate that progress in WGIS will require a shift from prediction-oriented AI models to adaptive, explainable, and operational intelligent energy infrastructures that can support resilient renewable energy integration. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Molten Salt Thermal Energy Storage for Flexible Operation of Coal-Fired Power Plants: Integration Configurations, Operating Strategies, and Future Perspectives
Affiliations: China Resources Power (Changshu) Co., Ltd., Changshu, 215513, China; Xi’an Thermal Power Research Institute Co., Ltd., Xi’an, 710054, China; School of Energy and Environment, Southeast University, Nanjing, 211189, China

Abstract: Coal-fired power plants are increasingly required to operate flexibly in power systems with high shares of variable renewable energy. Molten-salt thermal energy storage (MSTES) offers a promising retrofit option because it can be coupled with the steam-water cycle, boiler-side heat sources, flue gas, or electric heaters to decouple heat generation from electricity output. This review summarizes recent progress in MSTES-assisted flexible operation of coal-fired power plants from the perspectives of integration configurations, operating strategies, performance evaluation, and engineering challenges. The main charging routes include electric heating, main-steam extraction, reheat-steam extraction, flue-gas heat recovery, and hybrid heat sources, while the main discharging routes include feedwater heating, condensate heating, and steam generation. Representative studies show that MSTES can reduce minimum net load, enhance power-boosting capability, improve ramping performance, and support frequency regulation; however, reported efficiencies and economic indicators depend strongly on system boundaries and market assumptions. Dynamic modeling and coordinated control are essential for practical implementation, particularly for mode switching, heater-group reserve allocation, pump-flow coordination, and safety-limit management. Major challenges remain in salt freezing, corrosion, thermal decomposition, heat-exchanger inertia, field validation, and revenue uncertainty. Future research should focus on modular design, control-oriented models, digital-twin-assisted validation, standardized performance reporting, and multi-service economic optimization. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Generative adversarial networks with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification for structural health monitoring: Fibre Bragg grating data augmentation comparison in Hawk T1A aircraft
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Peiro A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom; Impraimakis M., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom
Abstract: The signal generation capabilities of a novel data augmentation framework are examined in aerospace structures. First, the framework learns class-conditional temporal and spectral characteristics of the measured structural responses. It uses conditional generative adversarial network training and Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification as a Bayesian approximation. This step enables stochastic signal synthesis and uncertainty quantification. Second, the generated responses are rigorously compared against experimental measurements across time, frequency, uncertainty, variability, and feature domains to assess physical realism, statistical consistency, and distributional fidelity. Finally, the synthetic data are evaluated to determine whether they should be incorporated into a supervised damage classification workflow. The framework is validated on the full-scale benchmark dataset from a BAE Systems Hawk T1A aircraft tested at the University of Sheffield’s Structural Dynamics Laboratory for Verification and Validation. The test involves acceleration, fibre Bragg grating strain, and nonlinear dynamic response measurements. The results demonstrate that the model accurately captures dominant structural dynamics, it guides on signal use for classification improvement based on uncertainty characteristics, and it provides meaningful uncertainty estimates linked to signal complexity and excitation characteristics. Importantly, the framework offers a realistic generative modelling plan as a robust digital twin component for data-driven structural health monitoring, supporting resilient decision-making for condition assessment in safety-critical aerospace systems. © 2026 The Author(s).

Affiliations: Department of Urban and Regional Planning, Faculty of Architecture, Center of Excellence in Urban Strategies and Healthy Cities, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand; Center of Excellence in Green Tech in Architecture, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand; Department of Materials Science, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand

Abstract: This study conducts a systematic review and thematic analysis to explore how physics-informed machine learning (PIML) can enhance reliability in infrastructure assessment and construction management. Previous studies are classified based on state estimation, digital twin updating, performance prediction, deterioration prediction, multi-hazard response analysis, and maintenance and inspection decision support. Embedding governing physical laws in the learning process ensures that models adhere to mechanical principles. The analysis shows that PIML can enhance prediction stability, decrease data needs, and allow for the identification of concealed structural and construction parameters through inverse methods. Importantly, integrating mechanics into data-driven models transforms machine learning from a curve-fitting tool into a verification-compatible analysis method. Constraining predictions with physical laws reduces unrealistic outputs; enables extrapolation to unobserved hazard scenarios such as earthquakes, winds, and floods; and facilitates estimation of deterioration states needed for risk-informed maintenance planning. The reviewed literature shows that these capabilities enable operational digital twins that continuously update infrastructure conditions using real-time monitoring data. However, there are persistent challenges, including computational expenses, inadequate uncertainty quantification, limited multi-physics integration, and the lack of benchmark datasets and regulatory approval. This review concludes that PIML offers a pathway to next-generation artificial intelligence in construction and infrastructure systems by bridging monitoring data and engineering mechanics. As a reliability engine within digital twin frameworks, PIML supports predictive maintenance, performance-based design, and resilience-oriented management of existing and future infrastructure systems. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Training LLMs with Reinforcement Learning over Digital Twin Representations for Reasoning-Intensive Surgical VideoQA
Affiliations: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States
Authors with affiliations: Shen Y., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States; Zhang H., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States; Unberath M., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States
Abstract: Surgical video question answering requires multi-step reasoning across semantic, spatial, and temporal dimensions. Existing methods architecturally compress videos into discrete token representations and couple visual perception with reasoning. This approach fragments continuous spatial-temporal relationships and has been shown to restrict multi-step reasoning capabilities. We introduce a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains large language models (LLMs) to decouple perception from reasoning by operating over digital twin representations constructed from surgical foundation models. Additionally, we introduce hierarchical representations across frame, temporal window, and procedure levels with probabilistic uncertainty estimates. Finally, we propose a novel reward that combines format validation with accuracy assessment through clinical plausibility evaluation and uncertainty-aware calibration for training. To demonstrate the capabilities of this approach, we introduce REAL-Colon-Reason, a colonoscopic benchmark with 2000 question-answer pairs across three complexity levels. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on REAL-Colon-Reason and two existing surgical VideoQA benchmarks REAL-Colon-VQA and EndoVis18-VQA. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Research on edge-intelligent IoT collaborative perception and adaptive spatial design optimization for urban digital twins
Affiliations: Institute of Marxism, Hubei Institute of Fine Arts, Wuhan, 430000, China
Authors with affiliations: Ruan Y., Institute of Marxism, Hubei Institute of Fine Arts, Wuhan, 430000, China
Abstract: Edge collaborative perception for urban digital twins requires timely state maintenance under constrained communication resources. Existing collaborative perception methods mainly optimize detection accuracy and communication compression, whereas urban-scale 3D reconstruction methods generally assume that observations have already been acquired or transmitted. Neither directly addresses how limited edge communication resources should be allocated according to their expected contribution to persistent twin-state maintenance. To address this gap, this paper proposes a twin-update-aware communication-allocation framework for edge-enabled urban digital twins. Candidate perception queries are selected under a fixed bandwidth budget according to their predicted twin-state variation, uncertainty reduction, spatial-feedback relevance, and communication cost. An event-driven semantic Gaussian backend then performs localized semantic and identity-preserving updates in event-affected regions, while a spatial-feedback estimator derives protocol-defined operational indicators and sensitivity signals from the updated twin state. The propagated sensitivity is explicitly used in the next time step to adjust subsequent query priorities, forming a feedback-coupled communication process rather than a post-hoc feedback module. Under a multi-dataset hierarchical proxy protocol, the proposed method achieves a favorable perception–communication trade-off and improved twin-maintenance utility. On V2X-Real, it achieves 72.4% 3D mAP and 77.6% recall at 4.4 Mb/frame, while the fixed-backend evaluation yields a TSUG of 0.312 and a DSCE of 0.103. Sequential experiments further show that dynamic sensitivity propagation reduces cumulative twin-state error relative to static or sensitivity-free variants. These results concern protocol-defined twin maintenance and feedback-aware communication utility and should not be interpreted as evidence of complete urban spatial-design optimization. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: From smart sensing to adaptive remediation: artificial intelligence and Internet of Things for persistent organic pollutants

Abstract: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) remain a major environmental challenge because of their persistence, long-range transport, bioaccumulation, and resistance to degradation. Conventional monitoring and remediation systems provide reliable analytical performance but are largely fragmented, laboratory dependent, and unable to deliver the continuous, predictive, and adaptive management required for complex, dynamic contamination scenarios. Recent literature reports substantial advances in biosensors, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) for pollutant detection, forecasting, source identification, and remediation optimization. However, these developments often operate separately, with limited coordination between environmental sensing, data analytics, treatment processes, and decision-making. The literature further highlights persistent barriers to field deployment, including limited and geographically heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent sensor performance and calibration, restricted model transferability, insufficient independent validation, uncertainty in AI predictions, and the lack of mature regulatory frameworks for AI-assisted environmental assessment. From our perspective, the next advance in POP management should move beyond isolated AI applications toward integrated, closed-loop AI–IoT architectures that continuously connect sensing, prediction, remediation, and feedback control. Such systems could transform POP management from reactive assessment to proactive and adaptive environmental governance. Future progress will depend on standardized, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) environmental datasets, explainable and uncertainty-aware AI, robust field validation, and interoperable sensing infrastructures. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Multi-granularity and negotiation model updating method for satellite digital twin; [卫星数字孪生模型多粒度协商修正方法]
Source title: Journal of Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Affiliations: School of Astronautics, Beihang University, Beijing, 100191, China; Beijing Institute of Spacecraft System Engineering, Beijing, 100094, China

Abstract: The uncertainty of the model should be statistically assessed as the foundation for model selection, as there are errors between the digital twin model and the actual system that must be reduced. However, the satellite digital twin model exhibits multi-dynamic, multi-spatial scale, and multi-physical field coupling properties. Additionally, the numerical solution will reveal the stiffness problem of ordinary differential equations and the multiscale problem of partial differential equations. If many telemetry parameters are updated at the system level, the results will not converge. A multi-granularity and negotiation model updating framework for satellite digital twin method was proposed. The parameters were grouped by correlation analysis and frequency domain analysis. Multi-granularity digital twin models were built based on the requirements, and various granularity models of satellite subsystems and components were produced. The coupling relationship between the satellite structure of different levels was studied, and a negotiation updating method was proposed. Real on-orbit telemetry data were used to verify the framework. According to the research findings, the proposed method updating approach outperforms the unused one by over 50% in terms of accuracy, and the updating results are more thorough and methodical. © 2026 Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics (BUAA). Title: Application of digital modeling tools for the design and development of infrastructure facilities in the extractive industry; [Применение инструментов цифрового моделирования для проектирования и развития объектов инфраструктуры добывающих активов]

Authors with affiliations: Savelyev S.V., LUKOIL-Engineering LLC, Moscow, Russian Federation
Abstract: This paper presents a methodological approach to pre-investment and conceptual design of infrastructure for production assets based on an integrated digital model. The relevance of the study is driven by high uncertainty in initial data during early development stages, the need for coordinated consideration of production dynamics, hydraulic constraints, power supply parameters, spatial positioning of facilities, and technical-economic criteria. A sequential process is proposed for developing a spatiotemporal asset model, simulating production gathering and transportation networks, electrical grids, and conducting multi-scenario comparison of development concepts. The methodology was tested on an asset comprising several separate fields unified under common infrastructure. It is demonstrated that when final geological targets for production drilling are not yet defined, the digital model enables estimation of projected production levels, locations of gathering centers, pipeline routes and diameters, as well as options for placement of processing facilities. Based on calculation results, a scheme was justified involving construction of a central processing facility at licence block (LB) LB-2; installation of a DN 250 oil pipeline connecting to an existing field; and connection of LU-3 via a DN 250 pipeline in 2051. Integration of engineering calculations with financial-economic models enables creation of a decision tree and elimination of technologically unfeasible or economically inefficient alternatives. © 2026, Neftyanoe Khozyaistvo. Title: From Descriptive to Predictive Analytics in Healthcare Service Operations: A Strategic Analysis of AI-Driven Digital Twins for Emergency Department Capacity Management
Affiliations: SiMLQ, Toronto, Canada; Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada; Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel; Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel
Authors with affiliations: Baron O., SiMLQ, Toronto, Canada, Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel; Azaria S., Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel; Krass D., SiMLQ, Toronto, Canada, Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada
Abstract: Many modern business processes operate under congestion: stochastic demand, shared and limited resources, complex routing, and tight service-level constraints. From healthcare and public services to logistics, financial operations, and large-scale customer support, these systems exhibit nonlinear behavior where small disruptions propagate quickly and performance deteriorates sharply. This paper examines how Business Process Management (BPM) can evolve to address congestion-driven environments by integrating process mining, queueing theory, simulation, and machine learning and artificial intelligence (ML&AI) into digital twins. We discuss how descriptive analytics must move beyond static dashboards toward data-driven process models that reveal how processes actually unfold in practice—capturing routing variability, rework loops, synchronization delays, and resource contention. Process mining provides structural visibility; queueing-aware modeling explains performance; ML&AI supports prediction under uncertainty. Building on these foundations, predictive and comparative analytics enable counterfactual “what-if” evaluation of staffing, routing, prioritization, and scheduling policies before implementation. Finally, prescriptive analytics embedded within real-time digital twins allow organizations to intervene proactively—anticipating congestion, reallocating capacity, and mitigating cascading delays. Drawing on industrial deployments through SiMLQ, we demonstrate how combining process intelligence with congestion-aware operational modeling transforms BPM from retrospective analysis into continuous, real-time decision support. The implications extend across service industries where variability and resource contention define performance, resilience, and competitiveness. Emergency departments are not failing because clinicians lack commitment; they are failing because the operating system that coordinates demand, staffing, beds, diagnostics, specialist consultation, and inpatient transfers remains largely reactive. Digital twins that are based on extensive descriptive analytics can transform fragmented event data into a safe, continuously updated environment for prediction, counterfactual evaluation, and prescriptive action. The managerial implication is blunt: modern businesses, such as hospitals that rely only on after-the-fact statistics will remain trapped in decision blind spots. Businesses that build validated digital twins would move capacity management upstream, detect failure before it occurs, and redirect scarce resources to the highest-leverage bottlenecks in real time. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Validation by design: Model-informed validation design (MIVD) as a quantitative design science
Affiliations: Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing (CAAT), Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, MD, United States; CAAT-Europe, University of Konstanz, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Hartung T., Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing (CAAT), Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, MD, United States, CAAT-Europe, University of Konstanz, Germany
Abstract: Validation underpins confidence in test methods and integrated testing strategies, yet while the methods under evaluation have been transformed, the design of validation studies remains gov-erned by convention and feasibility rather than prospective optimization. I propose model-informed validation design (MIVD), a quantitative framework that treats a validation study as a decision problem to be designed before resources are committed. This expands on our e-validation concept from 2024. Inspired by model-informed drug development, MIVD represents the pathway from target substance population and reference construct through biological and laboratory variability, analysis, and decision rules as an executable computational model, a digital validation twin. Can-didate designs are then compared by simulation using assurance, information economics, adaptive rules, and multi-objective optimization, with the aim of maximizing the probability of the correct, appropriately scoped validation decision rather than minimizing effort or maximizing the chance that a method will pass. Because reference standards are imperfect and contexts of use evolve, a validation becomes cumulative and can be updated along a lifecycle. A mean-based proxy recon-struction of the 1996-1997 EPISKIN skin corrosion validation shows how the preferred validation design shifts with the acceptance criteria, reference uncertainty, and chemical selection, while dem-onstrating that additional testing does not necessarily produce proportionately greater decision value. MIVD reframes validation from the evaluation of methods to the prospective design of the evidence by which those methods are judged.; Before a new safety test can be used, it must be checked, or validated, to show that it produces reliable and correct results. Such validation studies are expensive, because many chemicals are tested in several laboratories. Today validation studies are mostly designed based on past practice, rather than by working out in advance which experiments would settle the important questions. This article proposes a way to design validation studies deliberately. A digital twin imitates and compares different study designs before the laboratory work begins. Revisiting a skin corrosion vali­dation study done in 1996-1997, the approach shows that the amount of testing needed depends strongly on how much confidence in the results is required, how reliable the reference classifications are, and which chemicals are selected. Designing validation studies, rather than assembling them from templates, is the next step for safety science.

Abstract: The Dynamic Data Driven Applications Systems (DDDAS) paradigm has endured since its inception in 1980, and starting in 2000, science and technology (S&T) developments have exploited the key tenet of DDDAS of combining executing models with instrumentation data estimation as well as augmented data from other models. More recently, similar paradigms have been adopted by the artificial intelligence (AI) community such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), with the difference being that, in GANs, the seeded augmented data comes from a corpus of represented data versus DDDAS, wherein data augmentation results from first-principle physical modeling. In the preceding DDDAS handbooks, various theoretical and strategic approaches were shown that integrate augmented data from models with that of real-time data or targeted data from archival collections. This introductory chapter highlights recent advances by the DDDAS community such as physics-enhanced machine learning (PEML), uncertainty-aware digital engineering, and edge computing. Each of these methods utilizes the DDDAS paradigm, such as PEML applying the traditional DDDAS methods with a high-fidelity systems model orchestrated with an instrumented system. Digital engineering with “dynamic” digital twins (DTs) utilizes the advances in the past decade to process large amounts of data to provide augmented data for analysis. As from the first handbook, edge computing includes instrumentation systems to control the uncertainty by incorporating computed knowledge to maintain a system’s function when real-time data is incomplete. This introductory chapter highlights some of the broader scopes of the science and technology developments under the rubric of DDDAS as well as the DDDAS impact over time in challenging application areas and in emerging directions of artificial intelligence, digital twins, edge computing, communication networks, and related advances based on the DDDAS paradigm tenets. Title: From state estimation to active intelligence: safety-aware battery management for electric vehicles

Abstract: Battery management systems (BMSs) are increasingly required to convert incomplete electrical and thermal measurements into safe control actions rather than merely report battery states. This Mini Review focuses on two deployment questions that connect electrochemistry with control: how electrochemical states can be made observable with affordable diagnostics, and how charging, thermal, balancing, and health objectives can be arbitrated when their constraints conflict. We compare physics-based, equivalent-circuit, and data-driven representations using reported quantitative benchmarks, and show why cross-dataset accuracy alone is insufficient evidence of deployability. Particular attention is given to electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), distribution of relaxation times (DRT), galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT), and active pulse diagnostics as routes for linking measurable responses to interfacial kinetics, resistance growth, and transport limitations. A layered vehicle–edge–cloud architecture is proposed in which a deterministic safety supervisor enforces voltage, temperature, lithium-plating, power, imbalance, and uncertainty limits before performance optimization. The same framework is then examined for solid-state, lithium–sulfur, and sodium-ion batteries, where pressure, observability, and chemistry-specific calibration introduce new constraints. We conclude with a testable short-, mid-, and long-term roadmap centered on uncertainty calibration, pack-level validation, electrochemical observability, version-controlled learning, and safety-case evidence.
