Authors with affiliations: Fei J., China Southern Power Grid Company Limited Extra-High Voltage Transmission Company, Guangdong, Guangzhou, China; An S., China Southern Power Grid Company Limited Extra-High Voltage Transmission Company, Guangdong, Guangzhou, China; Caiyan L., China Southern Power Grid Company Limited Extra-High Voltage Transmission Company, Guangdong, Guangzhou, China; Luyang L., China Southern Power Grid Company Limited Extra-High Voltage Transmission Company, Guangdong, Guangzhou, China; Ning Z., China Southern Power Grid Company Limited Extra-High Voltage Transmission Company, Guangdong, Guangzhou, China; Daming H., China Southern Power Grid Company Limited Extra-High Voltage Transmission Company, Guangdong, Guangzhou, China
Abstract: This paper proposes a digital twin-based cost prediction and multi-objective optimization framework for power transmission projects under uncertainty. The proposed framework integrates GIS and BIM information within the digital twin to represent the spatial and engineering characteristics of transmission projects. The framework integrates GIS spatial constraints, BIM engineering objects, construction progress, resource consumption, market prices, and risk event data to establish a multi-level digital twin model. Dynamic cost prediction is combined with uncertainty-aware forecasting to identify evolving cost conditions and project risks. A probabilistic prediction and similar-condition clustering approach enables dynamic interval forecasting of staged costs and explains deviations through risk-event mapping. In addition, a multi-objective optimization mechanism jointly considers cost, schedule, and risk exposure to support project-level decision analysis, including resource allocation, procurement adjustment, construction sequencing, and contingency planning. The evaluation results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework for dynamic cost prediction, uncertainty assessment, high-risk line-section identification, and decision support for whole-process project cost control. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Computational Sustainability for Climate-Resilient Materials: AI-Driven Decarbonization Pathways for Cement and Industrial Systems
Affiliations: Department of Electrical Power Engineering, Durban University of Technology, Durban, 4001, South Africa
Authors with affiliations: Ige O.E., Department of Electrical Power Engineering, Durban University of Technology, Durban, 4001, South Africa; Kabeya M., Department of Electrical Power Engineering, Durban University of Technology, Durban, 4001, South Africa
Abstract: Cement production remains a major industrial source of anthropogenic CO₂ because emissions arise from both limestone calcination and high-temperature fuel combustion. This review examines how computational sustainability can support climate-resilient and low-carbon cement production by integrating artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), digital twins, optimization, life cycle assessment (LCA), techno-economic analysis, and industrial systems modeling. An interdisciplinary scoping review was conducted using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) informed procedures to synthesize evidence across materials discovery, cement and concrete mix optimization, plant operations, LCA integration, and system-level decarbonization planning. The review identifies computational sustainability as a multi-scale decision-support framework that links materials design, plant operations, supply-chain coordination, and policy/system planning. The synthesis shows that supervised learning, ensemble models, physics-informed neural networks, explainable AI, multi-objective optimization, digital twins, and system dynamics can support low-carbon binder screening, SCM optimization, kiln control, predictive maintenance, environmental-impact assessment, and infrastructure planning. SCM-based clinker substitution and energy-efficiency improvements are the most mature near-term options, while alternative binders, electrification, hydrogen integration, and cement-specific carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) require further validation, cost reduction, infrastructure development, and alignment with standards. Critical gaps remain in open and representative datasets, external model validation, uncertainty quantification, long-term durability evidence, multi-plant field trials, and integrated prospective LCA–techno-economic–system modeling. The review concludes that computational sustainability can accelerate cement-sector decarbonization when data-driven prediction, physical constraints, environmental assessment, economic evaluation, and policy-aware systems planning are integrated into transparent and validated decision frameworks. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Circular manufacturing in sustainable production systems for building materials: A systematic scoping review of emerging pathways

Abstract: Circular manufacturing is gaining attention as the construction sector seeks to reduce resource extraction, construction and demolition waste, and environmental burdens from building material production. The current evidence, however, remains fragmented across material pathways, digital tools, assessment methods, and implementation barriers. A PRISMA based systematic scoping review was conducted using Scopus and Google Scholar for English language publications from 2015 to 2026. The review synthesized evidence on waste streams, circular manufacturing strategies, building material applications, environmental assessment, technical performance, digital tools, challenges, and future research needs. The findings indicate that circular manufacturing pathways may enable sustainable production of building materials, as long as feedstock quality, processing conditions, substitution rates, and the contexts in which materials are applied are rigorously managed. Alkali activated and geopolymer systems, recycled aggregate concrete, waste glass and ceramic based materials, bio-based composites, and polymer based products show potential to reduce reliance on virgin resources while maintaining functional material performance in selected applications. Digital and analytical tools, including LCA, BIM, GIS, digital twins, machine learning, sensor monitoring, and material characterization, can support environmental assessment, traceability, performance prediction, and decision making. Nevertheless, adoption remains constrained by material variability, incomplete LCA comparability, limited external validation of predictive models, durability uncertainty, leaching and safety concerns, fragmented standards, and weak integration between research evidence and industrial practice. Future studies should strengthen comparable LCA protocols, performance based standards, leaching and durability verification, externally validated predictive models, interoperable circular material data systems, and cross-sector collaboration. These priorities are essential for moving circular manufacturing from isolated material feasibility toward reliable and scalable construction practice. Title: SHINE: An Entropy-Guided Digital Twin Framework for 3D Myocardial Scar Reconstruction from Sparse CMR

Abstract: Accurate reconstruction of the arrhythmogenic myocardial substrate—specifically the conducting isthmuses essential for ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation—depends on capturing fine-scale scar topology from sparse, anisotropic Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) MRI. Given the pronounced anisotropy (e.g., 1.2 × 1.2 × 8.0 mm) and limited slice sampling, volumetric reconstruction constitutes a highly ill-posed inverse problem, often leading to aliasing artifacts and discontinuous “staircase” geometries under discrete interpolation schemes. To address this challenge, we propose substrate reconstruction as a continuous function learning task defined on a patient-specific anatomical manifold. We introduce SHINE (Scar Heterogeneity via Implicit Neural Encoding), a framework that constructs a mathematically consistent “Digital Twin” of the diseased myocardium. The pipeline integrates automated biventricular segmentation with a Statistical Shape Model (SSM) to establish a continuous anatomical prior. To reconstruct detailed scar morphology, we employ a Bayesian SIREN architecture with sinusoidal activation functions, enabling the representation of high-frequency geometric structures and mitigating the spectral bias persistent in conventional Neural Fields. Importantly, we introduce an Entropy-Weighted Dirichlet Energy loss, which uses epistemic uncertainty to adaptively enforce smoothness in data-sparse regions while preserving high-fidelity details in data-rich regions. Evaluated on a clinical VT cohort of 40 patients, SHINE significantly outperformed discrete interpolation and weakly supervised benchmarks, achieving a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.93 and a volumetric error of 3.1%. Notably, our method effectively addresses the Nyquist sampling gap, enabling recovery of sub-voxel conducting channels within a unified, topology-preserving 3D framework to support precision electrophysiology planning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A data-driven dynamic Bayesian network for health monitoring and maintenance decision support of marine diesel engines

Abstract: Performance monitoring and maintenance decision-making are critical components of machinery management for ensuring the safety, reliability, and operational efficiency of maritime systems. Recent advances in sensor technologies, data transmission capabilities, machine learning, and knowledge management have accelerated the transition from traditional fixed-interval maintenance towards condition-based and predictive maintenance strategies in the maritime industry. However, the health assessment of large two-stroke marine diesel engines remains challenging due to the presence of multiple interdependent operational parameters and their temporal uncertainties under varying sea and operational conditions. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel data-driven Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) framework for the health monitoring and maintenance decision support of large two-stroke marine diesel engines. The proposed framework integrates 15 operational parameters within a unified probabilistic model to capture temporal degradation and quantify health uncertainty through dynamic probabilistic reasoning. The framework was validated using operational data from a six-cylinder MAN B&W 6S50MC-C main engine. A five-day case study showed that cylinders 4 and 6 remained in the AMBER health state, while cylinder 5 was predicted to deteriorate from GREEN to AMBER after two days of operation, demonstrating the model's capability to predict health degradation trends. Sensitivity analysis identified Total Base Number (TBN) and iron content as the most influential indicators affecting engine health. Furthermore, water mist catcher performance, fuel viscosity, and exhaust temperature deviation exhibited the largest temporal variations, with average deviations of 4.31%, 3.91%, and 3.37%, respectively. The results demonstrate that the proposed DBN framework effectively captures temporal dependencies and operational uncertainty, enabling dynamic health assessment and risk-informed maintenance decision-making. By integrating multiple interdependent degradation factors within a unified probabilistic framework, the proposed approach provides an effective tool for condition-based maintenance and establishes a practical foundation for future maritime digital twin and intelligent maintenance applications. Abstract: Aging reinforced concrete (RC) bridges are susceptible to complex deterioration, yet conventional visual inspections yield qualitative condition ratings that cannot be directly translated into remaining service life predictions. Meanwhile, standard theoretical fatigue models often overestimate damage accumulation when site-specific loading and material degradation histories are not accounted for. To bridge this gap between physical inspection and numerical simulation, this study proposes an integrated assessment framework that synergizes Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry with nonlinear Finite Element Analysis (FEA). Applied to an 80-year-old RC bridge in Thailand exhibiting extensive cracking, the methodology features a novel two-stage calibrated fatigue assessment. In the calibration phase, an uncertainty-based matching algorithm systematically compares UAV-derived crack topologies (including flexural crack spacing and shear crack inclination) against simulated failure patterns across the full FEA loading history to determine the structure's equivalent fatigue age and current damage index. In the prediction phase, a structure-specific S-N curve is derived from multi-level cyclic FEA simulations and combined with Miner's rule to project the remaining service life under variable traffic scenarios. The calibration revealed that the bridge has consumed approximately 83.3% of its fatigue life, with the uncalibrated model overestimating the damage rate by predicting the same damage state at 54 years versus the actual 80-year service life. Scenario analyses estimate a remaining service life of approximately 7.5 years under baseline traffic conditions, while a load restriction policy prohibiting heavy trailers is estimated to extend operational life by approximately 0.8 years, within a range of 0.4–1.3 years reflecting the confidence interval on the fitted S-N exponent. The sign of this benefit is robust across that range; its magnitude is not tightly determined. While the calibration inputs, namely crack pattern, load history assumptions, and material properties, are specific to the case-study bridge, the underlying two-stage procedure, comprising uncertainty-based crack-pattern matching followed by structure-specific S-N characterization and Miner's-rule projection, is a generic pipeline applicable to any RC bridge for which UAV crack data and a nonlinear finite element model can be obtained, including structures with incomplete historical load records. The proposed framework thus demonstrates a transferable methodology for converting field-observed crack data into quantitative fatigue life predictions for aging RC structures. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of Institution of Structural Engineers.

Abstract: Food Packaging 4.0 represents a paradigm shift in packaging systems, driven by the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies that transform packaging from a passive containment solution into an intelligent, connected, and data-enabled component of the food supply chain. This chapter examines the opportunities, limitations, and future perspectives of Food Packaging 4.0, with a focus on key enabling technologies, including artificial intelligence, big data analytics, blockchain, the Internet of Things and smart sensors, robotics, nanotechnology, digital twins, additive manufacturing, and augmented and immersive interfaces. These technologies offer significant potential to enhance food safety, real-time quality monitoring, traceability, operational efficiency, and sustainability, while reducing food waste and strengthening consumer trust. However, their large-scale adoption remains constrained by technical challenges related to, for example, data quality, interoperability, and scalability, as well as economic barriers, regulatory uncertainty, safety concerns, and variable consumer acceptance. By synthesizing recent advances and identifying persistent gaps, this chapter highlights critical considerations for the responsible and effective implementation of Food Packaging 4.0, paving the way for more human-centric, transparent, and resilient packaging strategies in the emerging context of Food Packaging 5.0.s © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Abdo Hassoun; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Recent advances and emerging trends in CFD applications for disinfection in water and wastewater treatment: A decade in retrospect
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Kennesaw State University, Marietta, 30060, GA, United States; Carollo Engineers, Seattle, 98101, WA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Zhang J., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Kennesaw State University, Marietta, 30060, GA, United States; Neogi B., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Kennesaw State University, Marietta, 30060, GA, United States; Wicklein E., Carollo Engineers, Seattle, 98101, WA, United States
Abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is widely used to analyze and optimize water and wastewater disinfection. This targeted structured review synthesizes approximately 110 peer-reviewed studies published during 2014–2025, with selected earlier studies retained for historical context. Applications spanning UV and UV-LED reactors, chlorination, ozonation, peracetic acid (PAA), advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), and emerging systems are evaluated using a decision-oriented right-fidelity framework that links the engineering quantity of interest to model fidelity, validation evidence, dominant uncertainty, and application readiness. Major advances include multiphysics coupling of hydrodynamics with radiation, reactive transport, and gas–liquid mass transfer; higher-fidelity turbulence treatment; uncertainty-aware validation; and CFD-trained surrogate models. Direct CFD–AI evidence is currently concentrated in surrogate and optimization studies, whereas physics-informed neural networks and digital-twin applications remain emerging or prospective for disinfection. Across technologies, the dominant uncertainty is process specific: optical and dose-response assumptions for UV, matrix-dependent kinetics for chlorine and PAA, and multiphase mass-transfer closures for ozone. The review provides practitioner guidance on model selection, minimum validation requirements, current reliability limits, and evidence needed for routine design, regulatory assessment, and operational decision support. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A Hybrid physics-informed digital twin for offshore wind-farm flow prediction: integrating CFD simulations with deep regression forest and probabilistic surrogate models
Source title: Journal of Engineering and Applied Science
Affiliations: Department of Smart O & M and IoT, Nantong Institute of Technology, Jiangsu, Nantong, 226002, China; Nantong Huarong Construction Group Co., Ltd, Jiangsu, Nantong, 226002, China

Abstract: The marine-atmosphere dynamics are nonlinear and multiscale, which poses a computational challenge for accurately describing the flow field around offshore wind turbines. Using advanced data-driven surrogate models and CFD simulations, this study presents a hybrid physics-informed digital twin framework to predict wind farm behavior under stochastic environmental conditions with high accuracy. In this work, we propose a framework that simultaneously integrates spatiotemporal dependencies, physical constraints, and probabilistic uncertainties by combining Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), Deep-Gaussian Process Regression (Deep-GPR), Extreme Gradient Boosting Algorithm (XGBoost), and a transformer-based regression model called CFD-Former. PINNs incorporate Navier–Stokes equation residuals into the training process to ensure physical consistency, while XGBoost and Deep-GPR improve model generalizability to different inlet flow conditions. Hybrid surrogate models are trained on data from CFD calculations with different wind direction and speed conditions. The generated digital twin is able to predict the velocities measured at the meteorological tower within an uncertainty of 10% and reproduce the high resolution flow patterns due to CFD with a mean absolute deviation below 1%. This novel approach uses deterministic simulation and intelligent inference to predict offshore wind farm performance in a scalable and physically based manner, possibly enabling adaptive operation and reliability assessment. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Despite major advances in analytical sensitivity, resolution, molecular recognition, and computational analysis, reliably discriminating target analytes remains a fundamental challenge in modern analytical chemistry. High sensitivity or instrumental sophistication does not necessarily prevent molecular ambiguity, matrix interference, cross-reactivity, or analytical misidentification. This review critically evaluates analytical selectivity as a systems-level property by integrating molecular recognition, matrix complexity, cross-reactivity, signal discrimination, validation, and computational interpretation, while identifying limitations that prevent reliable selectivity under real-world conditions. Current evidence indicates that high affinity does not guarantee molecular discrimination, matrix composition can dynamically alter analyte recognition and response, and cross-reactivity remains largely identified retrospectively rather than predicted. Engineered receptors, selective sample preparation, multidimensional separations, HRMS/ion mobility, chemometrics, and machine learning reduce specific sources of ambiguity but cannot ensure true selectivity on their own. Importantly, computational discrimination may classify overlapping signals without establishing unique molecular identity, while current validation frameworks insufficiently capture dynamic, matrix-dependent selectivity. Future analytical systems should shift from static selectivity testing toward predictive, adaptive, and uncertainty-aware selectivity management. Integrating matrix monitoring, predictive cross-reactivity modeling, explainable AI, adaptive recognition, digital twins, orthogonal data fusion, and closed-loop quality control may enable intelligent systems to detect and correct selectivity failure before analytical decisions are made. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to the Institute of Chemistry, Slovak Academy of Sciences 2026.

Abstract: Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), as core devices for hydrogen energy utilization, play an increasingly strategic role in transportation electrification, distributed power generation, and large-scale energy storage. However, the inherent strong multi-physics coupling, complex nonlinear degradation, and high sensitivity to operating conditions of PEMFC impose significant challenges on its cost, durability, and efficiency. Machine learning (ML) provides new opportunities to address these challenges and accelerate intelligent PEMFC development. This review examines ML applications across the full lifetime of PEMFCs, covering material design, manufacturing and quality control, system state management and control, and digital twin (DT) development. Beyond summarizing recent progress, it critically compares ML approaches in terms of data requirements, interpretability, computational cost, robustness, generalization, and uncertainty quantification, while highlighting emerging physics-informed ML, hybrid physics-data-driven models, self-adaptive DTs, and deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Three major challenges are identified: (1) data scarcity, heterogeneity, and insufficient standardization; (2) limited physical consistency, interpretability, generalization, and uncertainty quantification; and (3) computational, real-time, and safe-deployment requirements. Overall, integrating data, physical knowledge, and intelligent decision-making can advance ML-enabled PEMFCs from isolated prediction and optimization toward reliable, adaptive, and full-lifetime intelligent operation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Two-stage fundamental Bayesian model updating method based on MCMC algorithm

Abstract: Model updating plays an important role in obtaining a more accurate finite element model (FEM) based on measured vibration data. Based on the updated FEM, it is more convenient to carry out further analysis, e.g., structural health monitoring, digital twin, and so on. Bayesian model updating methods are attracting more attention since they can provide rigorous models and evaluate the uncertainty of the updated results. However, in the real application, it still has some problems such as computational efficiency and accuracy. In this paper, a two-stage Bayesian function combined with MCMC algorithm is proposed and used to perform model updating of a real complicated long-span cable-stayed bridge. The two-stage Bayesian function can automatically consider the heteroscedasticity of each utilized modal degree and it allows for incomplete modal information for model updating. Before conducting model updating, two different sensitivity analysis functions are used for local and global sensitivity analysis of bridge model. A set of interaction process between different computation tools has been established to improve computational speed by using an improved stopping criterion. The updated results are demonstrated for both model classes, and ultimately a Bayesian model class evidence was used to judge their superiority. The proposed method was verified by a numerical example and then applied in the updating of the bridge. The experimental results show that the model updating method successfully corrects initial FEMs with reverse mode order errors using incomplete modal information. Simultaneously, the results exhibit a relatively low level of uncertainty. Furthermore, the Bayesian model class selection algorithm proves that new sensitivity analysis functions are superior. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of Institution of Structural Engineers.

Title: Design and implementation of a dual-driven digital-twin for PWR-core; [压水堆堆芯的双核驱动数字孪生体设计与实现]

Abstract: [Background] As a key technology for the deep integration of cyber-physical systems, the digital twin concept has demonstrated significant potential in the nuclear field. It aims to address the complex mechanisms, challenging parameter measurement, and stringent safety requirements of reactor cores. Currently, digital twin technology in the nuclear power field is in its initial stage, with system-level and component-level solutions emerging. [Purpose] This study aims to enhance the capability of nuclear industrial software in supporting the safe and economical operation of reactor cores by proposing the concept of a mechanism-data dual-driven digital twin for PWR cores with emphasis on the component-level reactor core. [Methods] Firstly, in accordance with the principles of full-domain monitoring, real-time interaction, and self-evolution, a high-precision digital core model was constructed with the autonomous core physics analysis software NECP-Bamboo serving as the mechanism-driven core. Then, a dedicated neural network was built as the data-driven core, with this integrating measured and simulated data to dynamically correct the measurement uncertainty of operating condition parameters. Finally, the BEAVRS benchmark, a general standard for such validation using data from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) public dataset, was employed to validate this method. [Results] The validation results show that calculation errors of parameters driven by the abovementioned mechanism are within the acceptable limits. Under typical operating conditions at the beginning of the cycle life, with a fuel consumption depth of 38.7 MWd·tU−1, the relative power error is reduced from 0.29% to 0.28% by this dual-drive method. The detector response currents deviation range is reduced from −3.41%~3.14% to −2.99%~3.05%, and the root mean square value is decreased from 1.74% to 1.62%. The digital virtual core and the physical core are evolving in tandem, achieving preliminary dual evolution. [Conclusions] The dual-driven digital-twin solution for PWR-Core proposed in this study is feasible, capable of reducing errors during the transfer of physical target core to the digital virtual core, facilitating the evolution of the twin between the digital virtual core and the physical entity core. © 2026 Science Press. Abstract: Nonviral nanocarrier delivery remains a major translational bottleneck for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based genome editing because functional outcome emerges from coupled losses across biodistribution, cell uptake, intracellular trafficking, endosomal escape, access to the relevant cellular compartment, editing and tolerability. This Perspective develops three complementary conceptual tools. The Delivery-Specificity-Toxicity (DST) framework treats formulation design as a constrained multi-objective problem. The Composite Nanobio Delivery Efficiency (CNBDE) framework represents functional delivery as a chain of conditional probabilities rather than a product of statistically independent barriers, with shared formulation and biological variables allowed to alter multiple stages simultaneously. We explicitly distinguish the chain-rule formulation from the simpler independence approximation and clarify that the novelty of CNBDE lies in CRISPR-specific mechanistic decomposition and its linkage to measurable state variables, not in multiplication itself. Heterogeneous literature values are reclassified by evidence maturity instead of being treated as universal cross-platform constants. An explicitly hypothetical in silico stress test is added to demonstrate uncertainty propagation and structural sensitivity; importantly, it shows that the bare multiplicative form cannot by itself prove that any single stage, including endosomal escape, is universally dominant. A worked hepatic Lipid-Nanoparticle (LNP) example, contrasted with lung-targeted LNP studies, illustrates why organ-specific parameterization is required. Finally, the Nanobio Digital Twin System (NB-DTS) is defined as a digital-twin-ready multiscale architecture requiring a biological counterpart, iterative data assimilation, uncertainty-aware state updating, prediction and feedback. CNBDE and NB-DTS remain hypothesis-generating frameworks and require prospective experimental and external validation before predictive or clinical use. © 2026 World Scientific Publishing Company

Title: LLM-augmented semantic edge intelligence in wireless sensor networks and IoT: a review-led evidence synthesis and conceptual framework
Affiliations: Department of Computing and Information Technology, Faculty of Science and Technology, The University of the West Indies, St. Augustine, Trinidad and Tobago
Authors with affiliations: Khan K., Department of Computing and Information Technology, Faculty of Science and Technology, The University of the West Indies, St. Augustine, Trinidad and Tobago
Abstract: Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) increasingly support sensing-to-decision loops in which the value of a transmission depends on task utility, freshness, uncertainty, privacy, and safety rather than on bit fidelity alone. This article presents a review-led evidence synthesis and, as a secondary contribution, an author-proposed conceptual framework; it does not report a validated control algorithm. The review analyzes a 178-record evidence corpus, complemented by seven separately logged mathematical-outlook references, across WSN and IoT foundations, semantic communication, TinyML and split inference, federated learning, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), digital twins, wireless foundation models, and language-model-assisted operations. The supplementary materials release a machine-readable extraction sheet with one row per record, a field codebook, a reference and screening ledger, qualification and completeness audits, and an integrity manifest. A work qualifies as LLM-augmented semantic edge intelligence only when an identifiable large language model (LLM) consumes task-relevant WSN/IoT state or operator intent and can affect sensing, communication, diagnosis, resource allocation, or control through a typed and auditable path. Under this boundary, only one retained work supplies direct E2 simulation evidence of an LLM-mediated communication or control path. Most LLM/RAG evidence is bridging or adjacent and remains at E0–E2. The synthesis therefore distinguishes the roles and maturity of the component technologies instead of treating them as an interchangeable stack. It identifies bounded examples of LLM/RAG utility in communication-policy generation, cross-task networking adaptation, global evidence synthesis, tool orchestration, and natural-language formulation for an external solver. It does not support a general claim of superiority over rules, exact optimization, structured retrieval, or task-specific machine learning and reinforcement learning. To translate the documented gaps into testable requirements, the article proposes an IoT-native reference architecture, a seven-axis taxonomy, a threat model, a formal synthesis and selection/cost model, typed cross-layer interface contracts, and an eight-phase benchmark protocol. These normative artifacts are proposed by the author. They are not established methods extracted from the corpus, consensus standards, a deployable solver or controller, or experimentally validated results. An explicitly hypothetical wildfire-monitoring case makes the formalism inspectable: it defines semantic distortion, normalizes and elicits the penalty weights, evaluates a finite candidate set under hard constraints, applies the non-dominance and LLM-admission rules, reports switch-point sensitivity, and exercises one LLM-to-optimizer interface contract. Its values are tutorial inputs, not measurements. A provenance audit separates cited evidence, author-defined review and coding constructs, conventional notation, and proposed framework artifacts. Each contribution is linked to measurable outcomes and a minimum support condition, but these quantities define future tests rather than imply new performance gains. An LLM is retained only when it closes a declared open-vocabulary or heterogeneous-knowledge capability gap, satisfies hard energy, deadline, privacy, safety, and verifier constraints, and provides positive incremental value over the strongest feasible simpler baseline. Resource-constrained nodes continue to handle sensing, routing, medium access control, and lightweight inference. Grounded LLM/RAG components operate at gateway, edge, cloud, or digital-twin tiers, and their outputs are limited to evidence-linked, tool-checked, reversible proposals. The review remains the evidentiary core; the conceptual framework converts its gaps into falsifiable design and evaluation requirements for future semantic IoT systems. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: A physics-assisted digital twin of a village-scale solar dryer: Cross-site validation and propagated calibration uncertainty in rural Tripura, India
Affiliations: Department of Renewable Energy, NB Institute for Rural Technology (NBIRT), Tripura & West Bengal, India; International Solar Innovation Council, Helsinki, Finland; Department of Environmental Studies, Siksha-Bhavana, Visva Bharati, West Bengal, Santiniketan, 731235, India; Geetanjali Solar Enterprise, Kasba Industrial Estate, West Bengal, India

Abstract: Post-harvest losses remain a persistent burden for smallholder spice producers in humid tropical regions, where open-sun drying degrades both yield and quality. This work presents a physics-assisted machine learning digital twin for a forced-convection solar dryer deployed at four Self-Help Group sites in West Tripura, India, for turmeric drying. Five thermal models were calibrated on 105 multi-site field records and evaluated under a leave-one-group-out protocol that withholds entire sites, where Random Forest reached a cross-site R2 of 0.430. A latent-heat correction couples the thermal model to a calibrated Lewis drying-kinetics model in a closed hourly loop and constrains cumulative thermal exposure rather than peak temperature. For a rated 50 kg batch, the twin predicts a peak cabinet temperature of 84.9 °C, a moisture-based thermal efficiency of 21.3 % and a drying duration of 276 h to 372 h depending on start month. Because the rated load exceeds the mean operated field load by about sixteen times, these are reported as model projections, with calibration uncertainty propagated through to the outcomes. A triple-bottom-line assessment gives a payback period of 2.3 to 5.0 years, a benefit-cost ratio of 1.35 to 2.87 and 99 kg to 195 kg of CO2-equivalent avoided per unit annually, with benefits shared predominantly among women members. Uncertainty in the kinetic calibration, derived from a single 27 h window, lengthens every batch by about a quarter and, unlike seasonal variation, does not average out over the year, making a full-load drying trial the highest-value measurement. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Toward Self-organizing Production Logistics: A Multi-agent Approach
Source title: IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology
Affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Klein J.-F., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Jeong Y., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Flores-García E., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Wiktorsson M., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden
Abstract: Production logistics is increasingly exposed to variability, dynamic interdependencies, and operational disturbances that challenge conventional centralized planning and control approaches. Following a Design Science Research Methodology, this paper establishes a conceptual foundation for the design, implementation, and evaluation of Self-Organizing Production Logistics (SOPL) systems. First, key technological and systemic drivers motivating SOPL are identified, including autonomous logistics resources, advances in distributed AI-based decision-making, and the transition toward circular production systems, which further amplify operational uncertainty and complexity. Based on these drivers, system-level objectives and design requirements for SOPL are derived. Building on these requirements, the paper proposes an initial multi-agent architecture that integrates embodied and non-embodied agents, event-driven coordination, semantic knowledge structures, and digital twins. In addition, a three-phase demonstration roadmap is presented, progressing from an initial laboratory demonstrator toward increasingly distributed and adaptive SOPL systems. The Phase I demonstrator provides an experimental environment for investigating disturbance handling, human involvement, and supervisory coordination within an order-driven kitting and supply scenario. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Abstract: Autonomous vehicles operating near handling limits are vulnerable to sensor and actuator faults. A single biased measurement or a degraded steering actuator can turn a small tracking error into a loss of control. Existing fault-tolerant Model Predictive Control (MPC) methods usually assume perfect fault classification, treat one fault type at a time, or rely on offline digital twins that cannot adapt during a fault episode. This paper proposes a hybrid physics–data digital twin coupled with a robust MPC formulation. The data-driven part is an online Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) model that updates every 20 control cycles from a rolling window of recent state–input pairs. Fault detection and classification act on the raw measurements, upstream of any state reconstruction, through four mechanism-matched signature tests: a high-pass energy ratio of the speed signal (sensor noise), a latched step in the measured speed (sensor drift), a steering-feedback residual between the applied and commanded angle (actuator fault), and a sustained lateral-error offset (sensor bias). All thresholds are adapted from a 200-step fault-free baseline. Because the drift and actuator tests identify the fault magnitude at detection, the corresponding corrections are applied before the MPC rather than learned afterwards. The classifier separates the four fault classes at 97.2% accuracy (bias 93.2%, drift 100%, actuator 99.2%, noise 94.6%) with a mean cost of 0.7 ms per cycle. A confidence-weighted constraint-tightening scheme maps the real-time twin uncertainty into the size of the MPC tube. The framework is evaluated in simulation on a 1:10 scale autonomous racing platform (mass 1.98 kg, wheelbase 0.25 m, top speed 5 m/s) that follows the Verschueren racing circuit for 15.8 s at Ts = 20 ms under a fixed sequential fault schedule in which the bias and noise faults overlap for 56 cycles. Relative to uncompensated faulty operation the framework cuts lateral root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 0.164 m to 0.031 m (81%) and velocity RMSE from 0.157 m/s to 0.060 m/s (62%), bringing both to within 3% of the fault-free run; a per-window decomposition shows that the residual difference is confined to the 56 noisy speed samples, while the drift window is tracked at the fault-free level because the identified offset is removed before the speed loop sees it. Mean computation time stays below 10 ms per 20 ms control cycle. The paper also discusses what is needed to migrate the framework from the desktop-CPU simulation platform to a production automotive electronic control unit. © 2020 IEEE.

Abstract: Gasification provides a flexible route for converting coal, biomass, plastics, and waste-derived feedstocks into syngas, hydrogen, fuels, chemicals, power, and carbon materials. Its modeling and operation remain difficult because feedstock composition, reaction regimes, multiphase transport, reactor configuration, sensor availability, and downstream integration vary simultaneously. Machine learning (ML) has consequently expanded from static performance prediction to CFD surrogate modeling, soft sensing, fault diagnosis, predictive control, digital twins, and sustainability assessment. However, the literature remains dominated by application-specific accuracy reports, and R2, RMSE, and MAE values are often compared without accounting for sample size, data provenance, validation strategy, domain shift, uncertainty, or deployment conditions. This review combines a broad Web of Science corpus of 951 records with a 417-record direct-topic sensitivity subset and a separately screened technical evidence layer. It reorganizes the evidence through a system-level framework linking gasification science, descriptor engineering, task–model matching, trustworthy validation, cyber–physical integration, and sustainability-oriented decision making. Representative studies demonstrate large reductions in surrogate-computation time and credible industrial optimization, but few establish closed-loop deployment. In an adjacent solar-thermochemical membrane-reactor study, a learning-assisted feedforward–feedback controller reduced the control integral error by 82.4%, increased hydrogen recovery and yield by 43% and 33%, respectively, and reduced the input preheat ratio by 30%; these results are informative for controller architecture but are not direct gasification evidence. The review proposes gasification-specific descriptor classes, a task–data–model selection matrix, evidence levels for validation and deployment, and a decision chain coupling uncertainty-aware prediction with scenario evaluation, robust Pareto optimization, risk filtering, governed execution, and feedback learning. The central conclusion is that progress depends less on marginal in-distribution accuracy than on transferable, physically consistent, uncertainty-aware, and governed ML systems that convert predictions into verifiable operating and sustainability decisions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Monte Carlo–Informed Surrogate Model for the Analysis of Decay Heat Behavior in Molten Salt Reactors
Affiliations: Department of Energy, CeSNEF - Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Iaselli N., Department of Energy, CeSNEF - Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, Italy; Lorenzi S., Department of Energy, CeSNEF - Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, Italy
Abstract: Noble metal fission products in molten salt reactors (MSRs) deposit on primary loop surfaces, where their decay heat becomes safety-relevant during drain scenarios: Once the salt is discharged, the deposit remains without active cooling and can drive localized overheating. Predicting it requires tracking the full nuclide inventory across core, bulk, and deposition regions, for which repeated Monte Carlo (MC) depletion is prohibitive. This work develops a MC-informed surrogate built on a sparse transition operator spanning neutron-induced reactions, decay, advection, and deposition, with region-wise mass transfer correlations setting the deposition rates. The neutron-induced rates are extracted from a single MC simulation and rescaled with power under a constant-spectrum assumption, so that the ordinary differential equations (ODEs) system is solved without further transport runs, for a substantially larger nuclide set than historical zero-dimensional models. Applied to the Molten Salt Reactor Experiment (MSRE) fuel loop, the predicted mass transfer coefficients reproduce the original MSRE values, and the calculated 132Te distribution is comparable across surfaces for both the 233U and 235U campaigns without per-nuclide tuning. Benchmarked against a self-consistent MC workflow on a simplified generic MSR case, the surrogate reproduces the total decay heat of both the bulk and deposition nodes from sub-second to yearly time scales, to within ±0.3% at fixed power and ~2% under sinusoidal modulation. It does so at a cost low enough for design exploration and for a digital-twin representation of the primary loop. An uncertainty quantification shows that fission yields dominate the nuclear data budget and that the deposited inventory is markedly more uncertain than the bulk, partly due to non–noble-metal precursors in the yield normalization constraint. © 2026 American Nuclear Society.

Abstract: The digital twin (DT) of battlefield environment is a cornerstone for real time, high fidelity decision support in modern joint operations. Traditional numerical simulation methods face inherent trade offs between computational speed, accuracy for nonlinear multi scale phenomena, and robust uncertainty quantification. This paper investigates physics informed machine learning as a paradigm to overcome these limitations, focusing on two representative techniques: adaptive physics informed neural networks (PINNs) for underwater acoustic field reconstruction, and graph neural network (GNN) based weather forecasting (GraphCast) for global atmospheric simulation. For underwater acoustics, we analyze an adaptive PINN framework that dynamically balances data fidelity and physics constrained losses, enabling accurate reconstruction of multimodal pressure fields from sparse hydrophone measurements; the method reduces inference time by two orders of magnitude compared to traditional parabolic equation solvers while maintaining relative errors below 5% in complex shallow water environments. For global weather, GraphCast generates 10 day deterministic forecasts at 0.25° resolution in under one minute, outperforming the ECMWF high resolution system in more than 90% of atmospheric variables when verified against operational analyses. A side by side comparison highlights complementary strengths, applicability boundaries, and common challenges including forecast smoothness, bias accumulation, and lack of intrinsic uncertainty quantification. Drawing on recent advances in conformal prediction and adversarial uncertainty quantification, we discuss pathways to produce statistically valid prediction intervals. Finally, we propose a layered simulation architecture for military digital twin environments that integrates global GNN based forecasting with local PINN based high resolution refinement, and we address verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A) considerations based on DoD and U.S. Navy guidelines. The results demonstrate that physics guided artificial intelligence provides a viable, scalable path toward intelligent, real time battlefield environment digital twins. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Abstract: Humans can navigate an unfamiliar city and gradually form a coherent spatial mental map spanning tens of square kilometers. Can AI build spatial representations at a comparable scale? Although recent foundation models have advanced scene reconstruction and embodied intelligence, scaling to entire cities remains an open challenge, primarily due to the lack of city-scale data. To bridge the gap, we introduce WildCity, a real-world multimodal dataset collected by autonomous fleets traversing complex urban environments. Our dataset includes 18 trajectories, each averaging 83.7 km in length, and preserves the core challenges of in-the-wild perception, e.g., dynamic objects, lighting variations, and imperfect camera poses. We further establish an urban-tailored reconstruction baseline and convert the reconstructed environments into a closed-loop simulator. Beyond the dataset and baseline, we systematically analyze the key challenges on the path to simulation-ready urban digital twins: scalability, extrapolation, and uncertainty. Ultimately, WildCity aims to catalyze progress not only in city-scale rendering, but more broadly in the pursuit of AI that can perceive, remember, and reason across space at a scale comparable to human cognition. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Abstract: The increasing complexity of anaerobic digestion processes, characterized by nonlinear biochemical interactions, delayed dynamics, and sensitivity to feedstock variability, necessitates the development of advanced control and prediction systems. This study proposes an adaptive digital twin framework that integrates a physics-based anaerobic digestion model (ADM1) with a data-driven long short-term memory (LSTM) network and a delay-aware model predictive control (MPC) strategy. The proposed framework incorporates an adaptive residual synchronization mechanism that continuously updates the hybrid model parameters based on deviations between simulated and measured methane production, supported by an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for state estimation. Unlike conventional approaches that treat prediction and control as separate tasks, the proposed framework unifies these components within a single cyberphysical architecture, enabling real-time optimization of methane production. Experimental evaluation based on synthetic ADM1-consistent datasets and validated operational profiles demonstrates improved predictive reliability with an F1-score reaching 0.92 and a methane yield increase of up to 23.4% compared to baseline methods. The results confirm that the integration of temporal learning and predictive control significantly enhances process stability and efficiency under uncertain and time-delayed conditions. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Digital twin technology enables real-time monitoring and predictive analysis of complex structural systems. However, traditional finite element analysis (FEA) remains computationally expensive for real-time applications, while existing deterministic machine learning models often lack robust uncertainty quantification. This paper presents a Twin-Branch Probabilistic Stress Estimator (TB-PSE) specifically designed for digital twin-enabled large-scale structural static responses analysis, with application to liquid rocket engine frame static testing. The TB-PSE architecture employs a dual-branch neural network structure in which each branch utilizes multi-layer residual connections to independently predict the mean and standard deviation of stress distributions across all structural nodes. By formulating stress prediction as a probabilistic process rather than deterministic estimation, the proposed method captures inherent uncertainties in structural response and provides confidence intervals for critical stress assessments. Experimental validation conducted on a 24-step static test of rocket engine frame structures demonstrates that TB-PSE improves stress-field estimation accuracy while providing uncertainty information for risk-informed assessment of safety–critical aerospace structures. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Digital-twin-driven Adaptive Distance Protection for FACTS-compensated Transmission Lines under High Photovoltaic Penetration
Source title: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems
Affiliations: Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Wasit University, Iraq; Department of Cyber Security, College of Computer Science and Information Technology, Wasit University, Iraq; Department of Renewable Energy Techniques, Technical Institute-Kut, Middle Technical University, Baghdad, Iraq
Authors with affiliations: Abbas Z.H., Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Wasit University, Iraq; Jabbar A.K., Department of Cyber Security, College of Computer Science and Information Technology, Wasit University, Iraq; Ahmed M.S., Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Wasit University, Iraq; Mahmood H.R., Department of Renewable Energy Techniques, Technical Institute-Kut, Middle Technical University, Baghdad, Iraq
Abstract: When synchronous generation is replaced by grid-following photovoltaic plants, series-compensated lines lose distance-protection dependability: the metal-oxide varistor conducts during faults, and the converter's current-limited contribution corrupts the remote-infeed term at high fault resistance. This paper proposes a digital-twin-driven adaptive scheme in which the compensator drop is subtracted from direct measurement rather than from a model, and the infeed ratio is extracted from a superimposed-current Kirchhoff balance across synchronized terminals. Fault distance and fault resistance are separated by closed-form solution of a two-by-two real system, exact for an ideal two-source line, with the residual on the simulated line quantified against a fault-node ammeter. A first-order sensitivity law is applied online as the relay's own confidence bound, calibrated on data held strictly out of the evaluation grid. Over 250 enumerated fault episodes under a declared instrument chain (1% phasor-measurement-unit total vector error, 1.4% end-to-end per channel), the scheme is compared with four re-implemented methods published between 2021 and 2026, one of them from 2025, each run on the identical episodes, chain and two-cycle decision instant. Median reach error is lower by a factor of 3.0 than the strongest of them, dependability is 93.3% against 87.3%, and operating time is the same 44.8 ms at the median. That factor is pooled; stratified it ranges from 7.0 to 0.35, and at zero fault resistance the strongest comparators are as accurate, so the advantage lies in the resistive band. Across twelve measurement chains, high-resistance accuracy is shown to be instrument-limited rather than method-limited for the models tested. Title: Knowledge-Driven Parameter Optimization for Combat Experimentation Simulation Models: Evolution, Mechanisms, and Application Prospects
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Affiliations: Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; People’s Liberation Army Unit 63677, Xinjiang, Urumqi, 830000, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiang D., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China, People’s Liberation Army Unit 63677, Xinjiang, Urumqi, 830000, China; Lyu M., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; Liu Z., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; Wen M., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China
Abstract: With the transition of combat experimentation from scheme demonstration to intelligent decision support, the computational efficiency and credibility of simulation model parameter optimization have become key bottlenecks in system-of-systems wargaming. Traditional black-box optimization methods face severe challenges, including high computational cost, high-dimensional mixed-variable spaces, and deep battlefield uncertainty. To address these challenges, knowledge-driven parameter optimization integrates military domain knowledge, physical mechanisms, tactical rules, and historical simulation data into the optimization process, thereby reducing ineffective search spaces and improving the feasibility of candidate solutions. This paper systematically reviews knowledge-driven parameter optimization methods for combat experimentation simulation models. First, it clarifies the conceptual boundaries between parameter calibration and parameter optimization, and summarizes a four-stage technological evolution from offline heuristic search to surrogate-assisted optimization, online closed-loop assimilation, and cognitive optimization assisted by large models. Second, it analyzes the core mechanisms of heuristic and evolutionary optimization, high-dimensional Bayesian optimization, multi-fidelity surrogate modeling, physical-prior injection, Kalman-filter-based data assimilation, reinforcement learning, and large-language-model-assisted semantic reasoning. Third, it compares the advantages, limitations, applicable scenarios, and validation requirements of different mechanisms, and summarizes their applications in simulation experiment design, combat entity behavior modeling, system-of-systems effectiveness evaluation, and digital twin battlefield construction. Finally, it discusses future research directions, including multimodal foundation models, simulation resource sharing, heterogeneous multi-task collaborative optimization, and human-machine hybrid cognitive simulation. The review aims to provide a structured reference for method selection and trustworthy application of parameter optimization in combat experimentation simulation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Production planning with digital twins
Affiliations: IMT Atlantique, LS2N-CNRS, La Chantrerie, Nantes, France
Authors with affiliations: Luo D., IMT Atlantique, LS2N-CNRS, La Chantrerie, Nantes, France; Thevenin S., IMT Atlantique, LS2N-CNRS, La Chantrerie, Nantes, France; Dolgui A., IMT Atlantique, LS2N-CNRS, La Chantrerie, Nantes, France
Abstract: In Industry 4.0, manufacturers increasingly use digital twins (DTs) to develop real-time representations of shop floors. However, the application of DTs in production planning remains limited. This paper proposes a DT-driven methodology for production planning that integrates planning engines, simulation, forecasting, and data-driven models. The decision model is formulated as a multi-echelon, multi-item capacitated lot-sizing problem (MMCLSP). The DT improves model fidelity by extracting key parameters and characterizing uncertainties from historical and real-time data. We extend the deterministic MMCLSP to a stochastic formulation for demand uncertainty, and, introduce a closed-loop mechanism that updates production lead times using simulation feedback. Two industrial case studies demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively integrates aggregate production planning with shop-floor execution. Compared with deterministic approaches, the stochastic model with data-driven lead times yields more effective and operationally feasible production plans, enhancing decision support for manufacturing systems. © 2026 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.

Abstract: The background of this study addresses the persistent challenges in traditional inventory management systems, which often suffer from demand uncertainty, stockouts, and excess holding costs in dynamic retail supply chains. This research leverages the Retail Store Inventory Forecasting Dataset (a publicly available Kaggle dataset comprising exactly 73,100 rows of daily synthetic yet realistic retail data across multiple stores and products, including date, store ID, product ID, sales demand, and inventory levels) to develop a novel framework. The methodology integrates a digital twin (DT) simulation layer with LSTM-based predictive analytics for real-time demand forecasting and optimized replenishment policies. Results demonstrate a 25% reduction in total inventory costs, 18% improvement in forecast accuracy (MAE reduced to 12.5 units on a normalized per-product daily demand scale), and enhanced service levels compared to conventional methods, validated through simulation and comparative analysis. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Offshore wind energy is a cornerstone of the global transition to clean and sustainable power. Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) is crucial for the safety and proper operation of Offshore Wind Turbines (OWTs) as these systems are prone to damage, faults, and deterioration due to their dynamic sensitivity and continuous loading. However, foundations have received limited attention compared to other components, such as blades and gearboxes, despite supporting the entire system, and the fact that SHM must be comprehensive to provide reliable insights about the system condition. This contribution addresses this issue by examining the use of the Random Walk Metropolis (RWM) method in the finite element model updating of OWT foundations. It focuses on monopiles because they are the most widespread and deterioration-prone supporting system. The performance of RWM is assessed in the inference of Soil-Structure Interaction parameters of an OWT finite element model under noisy data, modeling errors, and varying deterioration. Results from a case study demonstrate that the RWMmethod can estimate the soil parameters with acceptable accuracy and construct proper digital twins of monopile-supported OWTs. Furthermore, it is able to provide uncertainty metrics about the updating results. © 2026 American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME). All rights reserved.

Title: Mapping Emerging Trends in Artificial Intelligence for Quality Control and Management: A Large-Scale Computational Literature Review Using Semantic Natural Language Processing
Affiliations: Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco
Authors with affiliations: Afassi O., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco; Benaya N., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco; Dib F., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco
Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into industrial quality control (QC) and management encompassing automated defect detection, real-time process monitoring, and zero-defect manufacturing has generated a rapidly expanding yet fragmented research landscape. This study addresses the need for comprehensive mapping of quality and reliability engineering practice through a computational systematic review of 9618 publications spanning the 2020–2025 period. A hybrid natural language processing (NLP) pipeline combining FlashText, Sentence-BERT, KeyBERT, and spaCy performs semantic extraction of AI architectures, learning paradigms, defect typologies, and deployment contexts. The review pursues three objectives: mapping the architectural evolution of deep learning in industrial inspection, characterizing operational challenges of AI-driven manufacturing, and identifying methodological frontiers for improving production reliability and supporting intelligent quality assurance (QA) systems. Results reveal that AI-based quality control advances through coevolution of neural architectures, learning paradigms, and deployment requirements. CNNs remain central to discriminative visual inspection, while Transformers extend capabilities for multimodal reasoning. The field exhibits strong bias toward surface defects while overlooking safety-critical internal defects. Emerging trends show transition from algorithm-centric research toward deployment-oriented paradigms including Uncertainty Quantification, Edge AI, Explainable AI, and Digital Twins. This work provides practitioners with an evidence-based foundation for developing reliable, scalable AI quality systems aligned with Industry 4.0 principles. © 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Karigowda; Pandey S.K.; Habib G.
Title: Emission Inventories to Artificial Intelligence-Based Prediction for Air Pollutants
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India; Department of Electrical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India
Authors with affiliations: Karigowda, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India; Pandey S.K., Department of Electrical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India; Habib G., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India
Abstract: Advanced computer techniques combining numerical modeling, statistical methodologies, and artificial intelligence (AI) are needed to evaluate and predict air pollution. Conventional air quality models, including Gaussian dispersion, Eulerian, and Lagrangian models, provide a fundamental understanding of the movement of pollution and chemical modification over time. However, these models sometimes demand extensive source-specific emission inventories and meteorological data, thus introducing uncertainty about spatial and temporal resolution, chemical reaction mechanisms, long-range transport, boundary conditions, and model parameterizations, and hence possible differences between expected and observed pollution concentration levels. The merging of machine learning and deep learning approaches has improved forecast accuracy using large-scale datasets from ground-based monitoring, satellite observations, and reanalysis sources. Moreover, computational fluid dynamics methods allow high-resolution pollutant dispersion calculations, especially in complicated metropolitan settings. This chapter covers data pretreatment, emission inventory building, and model-based predictions and offers a complete computational approach to studying air pollution. Case studies on fine particulate matter (PM2.5) prediction, source apportionment, and policy impact evaluations were also discussed. Furthermore, important constraints such as model validation, uncertainty quantification, and data integration difficulties were investigated. The chapter emphasizes new developments, including AI-driven real-time forecasting, Internet of Things-based air quality monitoring, and digital twins’ role in air pollution control. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: RECONSTRUCTION OF DEFORMATION AND STRESS IN SHIP STRUCTURES SUBJECTED TO WAVES USING AN INVERSE FINITE ELEMENT METHOD
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference on Offshore Mechanics and Arctic Engineering - OMAE
Affiliations: The University of Tokyo, Chiba, Japan; National Maritime Research Institute, Tokyo, Japan; The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
Authors with affiliations: Mikami K., The University of Tokyo, Chiba, Japan; Komoriyama Y., National Maritime Research Institute, Tokyo, Japan; Ma C., National Maritime Research Institute, Tokyo, Japan; Murayama H., The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract: In hull stress monitoring systems currently used for structural health monitoring of ships, structural integrity is assessed using measurements from only a limited number of sensors, which introduces uncertainty in the evaluation. To overcome this limitation, the inverse finite element method (iFEM) has gained attention as a technique for reconstructing displacement and stress fields over the entire structure from limited strain measurements. In this study, the displacement and stress fields of a ship structure subjected to head, oblique, and beam waves are reconstructed using iFEM. Strain data obtained from numerical simulations are used as inputs to iFEM, and the reconstructed results are compared with the reference solutions from finite element analysis applying hydrodynamic loading. By analyzing the spatial distribution of reconstruction errors in displacement and stress, the influence of wave direction on reconstruction accuracy is investigated. The results show that iFEM successfully reconstructs hull-girder deformations, including vertical and horizontal bending and torsion, under various wave conditions. These findings demonstrate the potential of iFEM as a practical tool for real-time structural monitoring of ships in waves and for digital-twin applications. Copyright © 2026 by ASME.

Title: The right to uncertainty: strategic indeterminacy and the queering of algorithmic governance
Affiliations: School of Public Administration, Hubei University, Wuhan, China
Authors with affiliations: Wang J., School of Public Administration, Hubei University, Wuhan, China
Abstract: This research note interrogates the crisis of predictive algorithmic governance in 2026 through the lens of quantum international relations. Integrating the no-cloning theorem with post-colonial and queer theory, it argues that digital twin technologies utilised in contemporary conflict constitute a form of ontological error and necropolitical violence. The paper challenges the Newtonian assumption of the atomistic actor, proposing instead that the global order is an entangled wave function where algorithmic measurement forces a violent ‘collapse’ of political possibility. By engaging with Glissant’s right to opacity and Butler’s ethics of non-violence, it outlines a quantum cosmopraxis, a strategy of strategic indeterminacy designed to resist the epistemic violence of algorithmic coloniality in the Global South. Ultimately, it posits that the refusal to be cloned–or predicted–is the fundamental condition of sovereignty in an entangled world. © 2026 Global South Ltd.

Abstract: Accurate modelling of the performance of a vapor-compression cycle across broad operating ranges is essential for the design, optimization and supervisory control of refrigeration systems. But traditional data-driven surrogate models can perform poorly out of training distribution and do not guarantee thermodynamic feasibility. Here we introduce a physics-guided Fourier-transformer surrogate model to model a single-stage vapor-compression cycle with R1234yf and nano-lubricant additives, such as alumina, graphene, and carbon nanotubes. The model leverages Fourier feature lifting for smoother non-linear interactions, Transformer blocks to learn interactions across the four thermodynamic states, and physics-guided soft penalties designed to encourage physically plausible predictions by penalizing violations of output bounds and a prescribed monotonicity prior, without explicitly enforcing the governing thermodynamic conservation equations. To facilitate a systematic evaluation, a Koopman-inspired physics-guided state-space model is also proposed and compared with ANN, PIML, PGML, and PG-FNT models. The novelty of this study lies in its combination of spectral, relational, and physics-guided learning within a single compact architecture and its comparison with a specially designed state-space model under explicit distribution shift testing. To the authors’ knowledge, this combination has not been previously investigated for vapor compression refrigeration systems using nanolubricants with low GWP refrigerants. In the original five-fold cross-validation benchmark, PG-FNT[full] achieved a mean validation RMSE of 0.005202 and MAE of 0.003895, corresponding to reductions of approximately 55.5% and 55.7%, respectively, compared with the conventional ANN baseline under the same evaluation protocol. PG-KSSM also demonstrated competitive predictive performance, achieving up to 28.7% lower RMSE than ANN in the corresponding benchmark. Furthermore, under a high-condenser-temperature operating-envelope shift within the same experimental campaign, PG-FNT achieved a mean R2 of 0.9541 ± 0.0082 across five initialization seeds following few-shot adaptation with 10 labelled observations. Performance was evaluated on a separate 20-sample held-out test set, with no overlap between adaptation and test observations. These findings demonstrate the strong predictive capabilities of the proposed architectures and highlight the effectiveness of limited-data adaptation for maintaining accurate thermodynamic performance prediction under changing operating conditions. This work presents a transferable benchmarking and cross-validation, out-of-dispersion assessment, perturbation analysis, and significance testing protocol applicable to other thermofluidic systems with limited small and noisy datasets for the scientific community. The proposed framework provides a physics-guided, data-driven approach for predicting vapor-compression-cycle performance, demonstrating improved accuracy relative to the evaluated machine-learning baselines. Its comparative performance against conventional thermodynamic cycle solvers remains to be established. Looking ahead, this framework provides a foundation for fault-tolerant digital twins and real-time supervisory control, while the competitive performance of PG-KSSM points to reduced-order, control-oriented thermodynamic models for future closed-loop applications. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Abstract: Urban congestion affects fatigue in people with a mobility constraint, but the majority of the available digital twins is deterministic and lacks the ability to calculate counterfactuals with an uncertainty that is sensitive to individuals. Our generative causal digital twin, which combines high-frequency urban measurements: congestion, weather, and air quality, and digital gait biomarkers, co-models fatigue patterns and predicts the critical role that congestion plays. The twin combines a multimodal foundation encoder with a conditional diffusion simulator of probabilistic forecasting and structural causal engine of estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATE). As indicated in experiments, predictive performance is strong, with a close correlation between predicted and observed values, there are stable distributions of residual values, and subject-level RMSE are low (2058). The model has well-behaved uncertainty through narrow predictive intervals and strong causal behavior with values of the CATE lying in 0.06 to 0.10 range and monotonic dose-response curve with a range lying between 0.03 to 0.07 with respect to congestion levels. The gait variability (r = 0.93) and baseline disability (r = 0.71) are verified as the key predictors through feature-outcome correlations. Collectively, these results indicate that the generative causal twin offers credible, decipherable, and personalized fatigue risk estimates and is useful in offering custom mobility assistance and policy responsive to congestion. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: INVERSE ESTIMATION OF DIRECTIONAL WAVE SPECTRUM AND STRESS RESPONSE RECONSTRUCTION AT UNMEASURED LOCATIONS OF A 9,000 TEU CLASS CONTAINER SHIP USING FULL-SCALE MEASUREMENT DATA

Authors with affiliations: Son J., INHA University, Incheon, South Korea; Kim Y., INHA University, Incheon, South Korea; Lee J., HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Gyeonggi, South Korea; Jung B., HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Gyeonggi, South Korea
Abstract: Ensuring the structural integrity of a vessel during operation is a critical yet challenging task, as the structural response to ocean waves involves significant uncertainties arising from complex environmental and operational conditions. The digital twin technology, which integrates real measurement data with a vessel’s digital design model, has been increasingly recognized as an effective means of ensuring structural integrity under operational conditions. Within this framework, accurate estimation of the directional wave spectrum plays a key role, as it enables the characterization of sea states and supports the estimation of structural responses at unmeasured locations. This study employs a regularized optimization formulation combined with a cubic B-spline surface representation to estimate the directional wave spectrum from onboard measurement data. The proposed approach minimizes the discrepancy between the measured and reconstructed response spectra while maintaining the smoothness and continuity of the estimated surface. An adaptive quadrature scheme is also introduced to address the singularity that arises in the encounter-to-absolute frequency conversion due to the Doppler effect. The methodology is applied to long-term onboard measurement data obtained from a 9,000 TEU CLASS container vessel. The estimated directional wave spectra were statistically analyzed to evaluate their consistency across varying sea states, and the reconstructed response spectra were compared with the measured counterparts to validate the accuracy of the estimation procedure. These results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed approach to structural integrity assessment under operating conditions. Copyright © 2026 by ASME.

Title: A PHYSICS-BASED DIGITAL TWIN FOR WAVE ELEVATION AND SEABED MOMENT ESTIMATION OF OFFSHORE MONOPILES

Abstract: In this work, we present a proof of concept of a physics-based digital twin for a monopile structure (with overhead inertia) subjected to wave loading. The digital twin is formulated using reduced-order models derived from first principles and combined with a Kalman filter for state estimation. The proposed framework estimates the monopile top motion, the wave elevation, and the section forces and moments along the pile using primarily acceleration measurements at the monopile top. Key innovations include the use of a hydrodynamic shape function to represent distributed wave loading in a compact and computationally efficient manner and the introduction of a shaping filter to augment the state-space with wave kinematics. Synthetic measurement data are generated using OpenFAST and used as a reference to assess the performance of the digital twin. Results demonstrate that the wave elevation can be accurately reconstructed without direct sea-state measurements as long as the wave regime is inertia-dominated. Under the ideal tested conditions, the total hydrodynamic force and seabed bending moment are estimated with relative errors on the order of 1% and correlation coefficients exceeding 96%. Future work will evaluate the estimator’s performance under operational uncertainties and more complex loading conditions. Copyright © 2026 by ASME.
