Abstract: Subsea pipeline leaks and their underwater releases remain a major challenge in understanding leak fate, release rate, and plume geometry. As the bubble plume rises towards the sea's surface, it poses substantial risks to offshore operations and marine ecosystems. This study presents a hybrid approach that combines high-speed imaging and non-dimensional modeling to develop a nomograph that considers bubble size, rise velocity, and dispersion parameters, along with developing non-dimensional numbers for predicting leak release fate in multiphase flow pipelines. In a closed-loop transparent tank system, a controlled experiment was conducted to simulate subsea leaks, with high-speed videography capturing plume dynamics under varying leak diameters (1.8–2.5 mm), liquid flow rates (134–397 kg/min), gas flow rates (10–50 g/min), and operating pressures (1.1–1.5 bar). Imaging and image processing techniques were used to analyze the bubble trajectory, rise, and plume dispersion pattern. Image analysis results show that the bubble diameters ranged from 3-8 mm and that the size increases with ascent, suggesting strong coupling between gas expansion and liquid flow regimes. The resulting non-dimensional nomograph, and non-dimensional number bridges laboratory-scale findings with field-scale applications, allowing for improved monitoring, early detection, and predictive modeling of leak transit time, dispersion behavior, and plume geometry, as well as supporting digital twin development and real-time decision making for offshore production systems. Title: A Broadcasting-Based Approach to Create Distributed Situational Awareness in Construction Projects
Source title: IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science

Authors with affiliations: Prabhu P., Department of Design and Manufacturing, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India; Sahadevan D.V., School of Construction, NICMAR university, Pune, India; Singh V., Department of Design and Manufacturing, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India
Abstract: Construction projects operate as temporary socio-technical systems in which interdependent actors must coordinate under uncertainty, making situational awareness (SA) essential for effective decision-making. Although digital technologies such as BIM, IoT, drones, and digital twins improve data visibility, they often centralise information within hierarchical structures, producing uneven awareness across organisational roles. Existing research largely assumes that improved access to information leads to improved awareness, yet limited attention has been given to how communication practices enable distributed actors to develop aligned understanding. This study examines broadcasting as a communication practice through which interpreted project information is simultaneously disseminated to participants to support distributed situational awareness (DSA). Drawing on a qualitative case study of a digitally enabled construction project, the findings show that awareness depends not only on data availability but also on how interpretations are synchronised through communication structures. Broadcast-oriented practices supported shared comprehension and anticipation by reducing delays associated with sequential reporting while complementing existing digital systems. The study contributes to DSA research by demonstrating how communication architecture shapes the emergence of aligned awareness in temporary project environments and highlights broadcasting as a coordination mechanism for improving collective interpretation in digitally enabled construction projects. © 2026, Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd. Abstract: Nuclear power plants (NPPs) generate virtually carbon-free baseload electricity and occupy a strategic role in the global energy transition, yet their potential as a context for sustainable data-driven innovation remains underexplored in the energy analytics literature. This paper presents a comprehensive integrative review grounded in the 2026 IAEA technical report NR-T-1.22 as its primary authoritative source, enriched by 78 peer-reviewed studies (2018–2026) spanning the full NPP lifecycle across sixteen query clusters. The review delivers: (i) a seven-paradigm AI/ML/DS taxonomy with explicit boundary definitions, a hierarchical structure, and regulatory compatibility ratings under IEC TR 63468:2023; (ii) a cross-domain performance evidence synthesis across fourteen application domains, classified under a four-level data-environment scheme (synthetic / simulator / integral test facility / operating plant) that separates laboratory results from genuine field validation; (iii) a six-barrier adoption analysis with quantified mitigation pathways and a mechanism-level account of why the simulator-to-field gap persists; (iv) a reliability-oriented synthesis of uncertainty quantification, false-positive behaviour, and robustness reporting; and (v) a five-layer AI-NPP integration framework applied diagnostically across domains. Reported performance is strong in simulator settings—high simulator-based classification accuracy in anomaly detection and fault diagnosis, large thermal–hydraulic simulation speed-ups, and economically material fuel-optimisation benefits—and fleet-scale field deployments are documented across 68 NPP units in the IAEA annexes. Critically, however, 53 of the 78 peer-reviewed studies (68%) report synthetic or simulator-only results and only 12 (15%) use operating-plant data; the high headline metrics therefore evidence simulator-stage feasibility rather than demonstrated real-world readiness, and the IAEA field figures are practitioner-reported without an independent non-AI baseline. The paper establishes that systematic AI/ML/DS deployment can advance SDG 7 and SDG 13 through four quantified mechanisms—extended plant lifetimes, improved fuel efficiency, reduced unplanned outages, and accelerated advanced-reactor development—while arguing that the binding constraints are regulatory and institutional rather than algorithmic. Ethical dimensions including algorithmic bias, liability allocation, and safety–critical deployment thresholds are addressed with concrete regulatory and operational specifics. © 2026

Title: SYSTEM-BASED MODELING OF A TWO-STROKE MARINE ENGINE FUEL EFFICIENCY AND ITS UNCERTAINTIES

Affiliations: Department of Mechanics and Maritime Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology, Göteborg, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Hosseini A., Department of Mechanics and Maritime Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology, Göteborg, Sweden; Mao W., Department of Mechanics and Maritime Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology, Göteborg, Sweden; Lang X., Department of Mechanics and Maritime Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology, Göteborg, Sweden
Abstract: This study develops a high-fidelity zero-dimensional thermodynamic model of a large two-stroke marine diesel engine, utilizing an advanced molding environment. To bridge the gap between the computational cost of CFD and limited resolution of Mean Value Engine models, this study incorporates a phenomenological Dual Flame Model enabling near real-time engine performance evaluation. This approach resolves in-cylinder processes on a crank angle basis, explicitly differentiating between premixed and diffusion combustion phases to generate predictive thermodynamic states. Specific calibration strategies are considered to parameterize engine subsystems, including heat transfer, mechanical friction, and turbocharger performance, using limited standard engine shop test data. Simulation demonstrated good agreement with physical measurements, successfully capturing the characteristic non-linear efficiency trends across the operational envelope. Crucially, when applied to scenarios simulating added resistance from adverse weather, the model identifies the operational states characterized by increased thermal and mechanical loads and quantifies the resulting specific fuel consumption penalty relative to baseline conditions, which are often missed by quasi-steady estimation methods. The shift toward rigorous decarbonization standards exposes the limitation of conventional steady-state polynomial fuel consumption maps, which often fail to account for the complex, non-linear engine responses essential for accurate efficiency prediction under dynamic environmental loads. This system-level simulation is capable of being integrated with other models, serving as a comprehensive decision-support tool for optimizing propulsion system interactions and evaluating the operational viability of energy-saving technologies in real-world conditions. Abstract: The global ocean carbon sink is a critical component of the Earth’s climate but current ocean models are limited in their predictive capabilities because of the high computational cost that a biogeochemical (BGC) model, required to simulate air-sea CO2 fluxes, entails. Our research investigates the reconstruction of ocean CO2 flux focusing on local physical oceanographic drivers, such as sea surface temperature, salinity, and sea-ice coverage, which are outputs of the simulations conducted with a global ocean BGC model. We frame the flux estimation problem as a temporal sequence problem and evaluate the efficacy of both Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) architectures augmented with attention mechanisms. The models ingest eight different physical parameters over a six-month sliding window at each grid point without explicit spatial information, and are designed to identify and weigh the historical physical states that most strongly influence current ocean-atmosphere carbon fluxes. Our framework employs LSTMs to capture sequential dependencies through recurrent hidden states. Moreover, we evaluate TCNs as a distinct alternative that uses dilated convolutions to identify multi-temporal patterns. Besides, we build a probabilistic framework utilizing Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss to account for aleatoric uncertainty in the dynamical drivers of ocean CO2 flux. To ensure credible reconstructions, we apply Conformal Prediction as a post-hoc calibration layer. This methodology yields calibrated uncertainty intervals with guaranteed 95% coverage. Our results show that for most oceanographic regimes deep temporal models can function as reliable digital twins for point-wise carbon flux estimates. The proposed framework provides a data-driven foundation for reconstruction of air-sea carbon fluxes through an AI emulator built upon dynamic physical parameters. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Purpose of the research: Particle therapy is rapidly evolving beyond highly conformal dose delivery toward biologically informed, image-guided, and patient-specific treatment strategies. Materials and methods: Selected preclinical and translational advances presented at the 64th Annual Meeting of the Particle Therapy Co-Operative Group (PTCOG 64) are reported with emphasis on their potential impact and expected timeline for clinical implementation. Results: Recent developments span accelerator technologies, treatment delivery, dosimetry, imaging, radiobiology, and predictive modeling. Near-term innovations include compact accelerator concepts, software-driven treatment acceleration, photon-counting computed tomography, prompt-gamma range verification, linear energy transfer-aware quality assurance, and uncertainty-aware normal tissue complication probability models for proton therapy selection. Emerging approaches such as optically stimulated luminescence detectors, nanodroplet ultrasound imaging, radioactive and mixed-ion beams, and mechanistic digital twins expand capabilities for biological dosimetry, adaptive imaging, and prediction of late toxicity events. Carbon-ion research is simultaneously progressing toward biologically optimized treatment through advances in immunoradiobiology, flash irradiation, predictive biomarkers, functional imaging, and multi-ion optimization. Quantum technologies represent a longer-term perspective for imaging, dosimetry, and treatment planning. Conclusion: Particle therapy is transitioning from a dose-centered discipline to an integrated framework combining advanced imaging, radiation quality, biological modeling, and patient-specific decision support. Several technologies are sufficiently mature for near-term clinical translation, with digital twins, biologically optimized multi-ion therapy, and quantum-enabled systems represent innovations likely to shape the next generation of precision particle therapy and guide future priorities within the RadioTransNet network. © 2026 Société française de radiothérapie oncologique (SFRO). Abstract: Agricultural robots have been increasingly recognized as the key intelligent equipment for high productivity and quality in sustainable farming. It is often required to integrate environmental perception, autonomous decision-making, and precise execution in a complex field. However, spatiotemporal variations in soil conditions, crop morphology, terrain landscapes, loading, and meteorological factors have introduced substantial uncertainty into robotic perception, decision-making, and control systems, particularly for the open, dynamic, and unstructured scenarios. Agricultural robots can be extended into the crop-robot-environment coupling system. As a result, their intelligent operation is still restricted by incomplete sensing information, insufficient model accuracy, limited adaptability of control strategies, low repeatability of field validation, and weak coordination among robots, tasks, and environments. Digital twin can be expected to provide a promising potential approach for the dynamic connection between physical entities and virtual models, according to real-time data interaction, model updating, and predictive simulation. Virtual representations can be constructed to integrate agricultural robots, operating environments, and task processes. Therefore, digital twins can support state monitoring, process prediction, strategy evaluation, and control optimization, thereby reducing the dependence on costly and time-consuming field trials. In this study, a systematic review was presented on the technical pathways and prospects of digital twins in agricultural robots. Agricultural machinery evolved from conventional equipment to intelligent robotic systems. Agricultural robots were summarized from the perspectives of perception, decision-making, and control systems. Furthermore, the concept, system elements, and functional value of digital twins were analyzed to clarify their applicability to agricultural robotic systems under complex field conditions. Empowerment pathways of digital twins were summarized within a perception-decision-control framework. In perception enhancement, dynamic virtual mapping was realized to integrate digital twins with the robot state data, environmental information, historical data, and mechanisms. Multi-source data fusion, virtual sensing, state reconstruction, and anomaly correction were used to improve the reliability and interpretability of sensing information. In decision optimization, controllable and evaluable virtual environments were provided for process simulation, multi-strategy comparison, intelligent algorithm training, and policy iteration. Path planning, task allocation, parameter matching, and risk avoidance were shifted from experience-based decision-making into prediction and optimization. In control improvement, digital twins were used to connect decision outputs, execution, external disturbances, and control constraints using online updating, disturbance prediction, and adaptive parameter tuning, thereby supporting control compensation, parameter adaptation, and closed-loop optimization. Representative scenarios were then analyzed, including fault and health prediction, autonomous operation, as well as scheduling and coordination. In fault and health prediction, real sensing was integrated with virtual simulation data for the key component and anomaly detection, degradation prediction, and maintenance. In autonomous operation, virtual testing and optimization of motion and operation-control algorithms were adjusted to trajectories, parameters, and execution strategies in agricultural robots, according to field conditions. In scheduling and coordination, field environments, robot fleets, tasks, and environmental constraints were simulated to evaluate scheduling and then optimize task allocation, path coordination, and resource deployment. Digital twins enhanced the role of agricultural robots as information hubs in the production chain. Transition conductions were accelerated from mechanical into data-driven intelligent systems. Finally, the challenges were summarized from the current application of the digital twin. Their future directions were also proposed in agricultural robotics. This finding can contribute to the theoretical and practical guidance of digital twins in agricultural robots. © 2026 Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering. All rights reserved.

Abstract: Continuous cardiovascular monitoring creates a distributed scientific workflow in which Internet of Things (IoT) devices acquire physiological streams while patient-level records remain local. This paper presents PhysioFed-Discover, a physiological-constraint federated learning (FL) framework for cardiovascular representation modeling and cross-client knowledge discovery. Sensor-aware tokens and latent cardiovascular proxies support task prediction together with soft constraints for heart-rate consistency, ECG–PPG timing, Windkessel pressure dynamics, monotonic blood-pressure relations, and plausible ranges. The server combines sample support, predictive uncertainty, update drift, and physiological residuals to weight compressed updates; label-conditioned prototypes summarize recurring representation patterns. Experiments on real patient recordings cover ECG diagnosis on PTB-XL, blood-pressure estimation on PulseDB, and hypotension forecasting on VitalDB. Relative to Transformer-FL, the PTB-XL macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve increases from 0.899 to 0.914, PulseDB systolic-pressure mean absolute error decreases from 8.18 to 7.48 mmHg, and VitalDB area under the curve increases from 0.862 to 0.881. Module-level ablations support further study of the combined framework but do not isolate each physiological mechanism. The evaluation retrospectively analyzes patient recordings from the three public datasets, with these records partitioned among federated clients. Knowledge discovery denotes exploratory inspection of task-conditioned prototypes, not validated clinical phenotypes or a patient-specific mechanistic digital twin. © 2014 IEEE.

Abstract: Electric vehicles are crucial in the transition to sustainable transportation. Specifically, in the coming years, the number of electric trucks is expected to increase significantly due to regulations and an anticipated lower total cost of ownership (TCO). As a result, electric truck adoption is growing, bringing challenges to fleet managers due to range limits and uncertain energy usage. This work introduces an AI-powered Digital Twin (DT) framework, TwinERGY, to predict the energy consumption for battery-electric trucks at the pre- and intra-trip stages. Three sequence-to-sequence models are compared for the pre-trip scenario to determine trip-level energy consumption. We utilize a conditional diffusion model for real-time probabilistic estimation of power and time elapsed, initialized on the pre-trip model’s output and conditioned on historical intra-trip inputs. Combined with the pre-trip model’s output using Bayesian fusion, it aims to reduce end-trip energy consumption estimation uncertainty with every lapsing segment. The results show that the framework can aid in reducing uncertainty and contribute to more confident decision making during fleet management. Going a step ahead, we also provide explanations of the obtained results, uncovering the important features affecting energy consumption. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: High-dimensional non-intrusive surrogate modeling for multi-physics computation: white box tensor structure vs black box deep learning
Affiliations: Univ. Lille, Arts et Métier Institute of Technology, Centrale Lille, Junia, ULR 2697-L2EP, Lille, F-59000, France; Wuhan University of Science and Technology, School of Artificial Intelligence and Automation, Wuhan, China

Abstract: Digital twins in practical engineering demand accurate predictions of high-dimensional system responses. These responses typically arise from coupled multiphysics fields, where multi-parametric dependencies further intensify the system’s nonlinearity. While a single forward simulation is usually manageable, the repetitive nature of digital twins can amplify the computational burden beyond the capabilities of traditional numerical solvers. Non-intrusive surrogate modeling provides a practical solution to speed up these evaluations. Beyond rapid forward prediction, these surrogate models offer significant potential to handle many-query tasks, such as design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and inverse problems, which require thousands of field evaluations. In this study, we propose a non-intrusive tensor-structure-exploiting (TSE) framework and evaluate its performance against two deep learning baselines: the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and the deep operator network (DeepONet). We test these methods within a multiphysics framework, focusing on an electromagnetic-thermal problem to assess their accuracy in capturing complex, high-dimensional responses. © 1965-2012 IEEE.

Abstract: The uncertainty of the soil conditions, non-uniform ageing and the challenge of safe testing of adaptive controllers on live underground assets restrict the use of real-time thermal management of underground electrical networks. This study presents an adaptive electro-thermal network model, a fuzzy cognitive map (FCM) for causal risk aggregation, tabular reinforcement learning and a predictive safety shield to realize closed-loop digital twins. The framework was tested on a repeatable simulation of three thermally coupled XLPE cable circuits with a time resolution of 5 min. Two learning agents were each trained on 100 randomized simulated days and then compared with fixed allocation, threshold control, a one-step FCM controller and temperature-only reinforcement learning under nominal and disturbed sensing and soil conditions over 20 held-out days per condition. When the FCM–SafeRL was applied in nominal conditions, it maintained the maximum conductor temperature at 88.62 ± 0.19 ℃, without ever exceeding 90 ℃, and with 0.41 ± 0.50% unserved energy. It also reduced daily dispatch movement by 79.2% compared with the more conservative one-step FCM controller. There was no thermal-limit violation for FCM–SafeRL in all of the scenarios of high sensor noise, 20% sensor loss, a 25% increase in soil resistance and a compound disturbance (+ 20% soil resistance, 20% sensor loss and 1.0 ℃ sensor noise). These results are useful for the feasibility analysis of the fusion of fuzzy causal-risk reasoning and shielded learning in all of the evaluated simulation scenarios, but do not imply a formal safety guarantee; field calibration and HIL validation still need to be performed. © Akadémiai Kiadó Zrt 2026.

Title: A Safety-Aware Agentic LLM–Digital Twin Framework for Fuzzy Multi-Objective Control of Industrial Fed-Batch Bioreactors
Affiliations: Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Nozari H., Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Yordanova Z., Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Abstract: This study develops a safety-aware supervisory framework for industrial fed-batch bioreactors by integrating an adaptive digital twin, fuzzy multi-objective optimization, Agentic LLM reasoning, and an independent Safety Governor within a closed-loop architecture. The digital twin continuously reconstructs process states and updates sensitive parameters, while α-cut fuzzy intervals preserve biological and operational uncertainty throughout prediction and optimization. The Agentic LLM coordinates prediction, optimization, process knowledge, and candidate evaluation, and supports context-dependent reevaluation and replanning as operating conditions evolve. The framework was evaluated using data from 12 industrial 72 h fed-batch runs, together with 600 uncertainty-aware simulated trajectories. Across three fully independent validation batches, the digital twin achieved an average NRMSE of 4.7%, MAPE of 4.4%, and R2 of 0.985. Closed-loop operation achieved a volumetric productivity of 0.347 g/L·h while maintaining a positive minimum dissolved-oxygen margin of 5 percentage points and zero hard-constraint violations. Across nominal and stressed scenarios, the Safety Governor preserved feasible operation with no residual hard-constraint violations, while the Agentic LLM successfully activated reevaluation and replanning following changes in process conditions. The ablation results further showed that the complete architecture provided the strongest overall balance among productivity, biological risk, robustness, and disturbance recovery. These findings demonstrate the value of combining adaptive process representation, uncertainty-aware optimization, agentic supervisory reasoning, and independent safety validation for reliable intelligent bioprocess operation. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Forest Land Use Intensity (F-LUI) is a multidimensional and dynamic property of forest ecosystems that cannot be directly observed by Remote Sensing (RS). Existing approaches commonly quantify individual management activities, forest attributes or ecological responses and therefore capture only specific dimensions of forest-use intensity. This concept-driven narrative review proposes a trait-based conceptual framework in which forest traits constitute the common observational interface linking anthropogenic forest use, ecosystem responses and RS observations. Based on this principle forest traits and their spatial, temporal and functional expressions are interpreted within six complementary F-LUI indicator families: Trait, Genesis, Structure, Taxonomy, Function and Socio-economics. Rather than defining a universal F-LUI index, the framework provides a multidimensional, sensor-independent architecture for integrating RS with in situ observations, forest inventories, management information and environmental data. Emerging approaches including Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Foundation Models, multi-sensor data fusion, semantic technologies, Knowledge Graphs and Digital Twins may support its operationalisation. Key challenges remain in standardisation, uncertainty quantification, attribution of management effects and transferability across forest types, management regimes and spatial and temporal scales. The proposed framework provides an open and extensible basis for harmonised, reproducible and operational trait-based monitoring of F-LUI. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: From Geometry to Behavior: A Smoothness-Certified Digital-Twin Framework for Information Management, Sustainability, and Resilience in Built Heritage Conservation
Affiliations: International Business School, Qingdao Huanghai University, Qingdao, 266427, China; School of Smart City Engineering, Qingdao Huanghai University, Qingdao, 266427, China
Authors with affiliations: Xu C., International Business School, Qingdao Huanghai University, Qingdao, 266427, China; Zhao Y., School of Smart City Engineering, Qingdao Huanghai University, Qingdao, 266427, China; Kong Y., International Business School, Qingdao Huanghai University, Qingdao, 266427, China
Abstract: Existing heritage digital twins document geometry and monitor condition with high fidelity, but rarely model the behavioral process through which owners, authorities, and peer-exchange networks jointly determine the long-run conservation profile of a historic district, and therefore cannot answer the subsidy-design questions heritage authorities face. This paper supplies that missing behavioral layer. We formalize heritage conservation credit systems (indivisible credits, capped holdings, balanced aggregate stock) as a matching model and establish four analytical guarantees for twin operation: predictions exist, are unique, are globally stable, and vary continuously differentiably with policy parameters. Global stability acts as a resilience certificate, guaranteeing recovery from any shock within roughly twenty annual cycles, and smoothness bounds prediction uncertainty in closed form. These certificates are properties of the behavioral engine, established analytically; they are not claims about field-validated operation. A three-layer architecture embeds the engine behind a state-synchronization loop that re-estimates behavioral parameters from registry observables at a cadence set by the data source rather than by the model; in a controlled in silico sensing experiment the synchronized twin reduces post-disruption tracking error by 71% relative to a static twin, and a window-length sweep shows the loop dominates the static twin by 62–71% at every cadence tested. Calibrated to a traditional village in the Mount Tai Piedmont and verified against an agent-based Monte Carlo counterpart, the twin yields three model-dependent policy results: a subsidy trap (higher subsidy rates activate conservation exchange yet reduce steady-state top-tier counts), the dominance of within-tier cooperation over cross-tier mentorship, and an inverted-U sustainability frontier locating Mount Tai villages in the under-funded regime. All outputs consolidate into a single HBIM-compatible information-management deliverable. We report the framework as a specified and in-silico-verified behavioral twin whose sensing interfaces await field deployment, and we state explicitly which components remain conceptual. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Digital Twin Construction and Simulation Technologies for Urban Organism; [城市生命体数字孪生构建与模拟推演技术框架]
Affiliations: Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China; School of Architecture, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China

Abstract: [Significance] As a complex organism characterized by self-organization, metabolism, and adaptive evolution, a city exhibits highly systematic and dynamic behaviors in both its operation and long-term development. With rapid urbanization and increasing system complexity, contemporary cities are confronted with persistent and intertwined challenges, such as environmental degradation, traffic congestion, resource imbalance, and public safety risks. Traditional urban governance paradigms, which often rely on static planning and reactive interventions, are increasingly inadequate for addressing these non-linear and multi-scale urban problems. This situation calls for a fundamental shift toward a full life-cycle governance paradigm that treats the city as an integrated and evolving organism. Digital twin technology, serving as a bridge between the physical city and its virtual counterpart, offers a promising technical pathway for realizing such a paradigm. By enabling continuous interaction between real-world observations and computational models, digital twins provide new possibilities for finegrained perception, system-level understanding, and proactive governance. Against this background, this paper focuses on digital twin technologies from the perspective of the urban organism, aiming to establish a methodological foundation that supports perception, understanding, inference, and decision-making throughout the entire life cycle of future urban organisms. [Analysis] This paper systematically analyzes the core functionalities and development pathways of digital twins for urban organisms, with a particular focus on urban modeling, operational simulation, and intelligent decision-making. First, acknowledging the inherent incompleteness and uncertainty of urban data, we explore data completion strategies based on Bayesian inference and graph diffusion models. These approaches enable the reconstruction of missing or sparse observations and support the construction of digital twin models that span multiple interconnected subsystems of the urban organism. Second, to capture the coupled dynamics of physical infrastructure and social behaviors, we integrate dynamic system models with agent-based simulation methods, and propose a co-simulation mechanism that enables coordinated modeling of physical and social urban elements. This mechanism is designed to be continuously updated through real-time monitoring data, ensuring consistency between simulated states and real-world urban conditions. Furthermore, to support the early warning and governance of urban diseases, we introduce a spatiotemporal foundational modeling approach for urban indicator prediction and counterfactual inference. This approach allows different governance strategies to be simulated, evaluated, and iteratively optimized within the digital twin environment before real-world implementation. [Prospect] From the perspective of the urban organism, this study establishes a systematic technical framework and research approach for urban digital twins that goes beyond static physical mapping. By emphasizing data completion, multi-system co-simulation, and predictive inference, the proposed framework aims to enhance the capability of digital twins to support perception, understanding, inference, and decision-making across the full life cycle of urban governance. This work provides methodological insights for developing next-generation urban digital twins that are better aligned with the complexity, dynamics, and evolutionary nature of real cities. © 2026, Science Press. Title: Cyber-Resilient Digital Twin Architectures for Smart Grids: A Review of Attack Modeling, Detection, Mitigation, and Secure Control Strategies
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States
Authors with affiliations: Ogiesoba-Eguakun O.C., Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States; Rath S., Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The https://ror.org/04wn28048University of Tulsa, Tulsa, 74104, OK, United States
Abstract: The digitalization of smart grids has expanded the cyberattack surface of critical energy infrastructure, creating a need for security mechanisms that integrate communication behavior, physical-system dynamics, and resilient control. Digital twins provide a promising foundation for this integration, but existing research remains fragmented across system architectures, threat models, defense methods, and validation environments. The aim of this review is to identify, classify, and critically compare how cyber-resilient DT architectures support the smart-grid cybersecurity lifecycle across DT architecture, cyber–physical attack modeling, detection and mitigation, secure control and recovery, and experimental validation. A structured multi-database search of Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library identified 1627 records. After duplicate removal, publication-type exclusions, and eligibility assessment, 149 publications were retained for thematic synthesis and quality appraisal. The evidence indicates that a qualifying cyber-resilient digital twin is distinguished not merely by the presence of a virtual model, but by bidirectional physical–virtual synchronization combined with explicit cyber-resilience functions. Cyberattack studies span measurement, communication, control, device and infrastructure, and coordinated attack surfaces, although study-specific assumptions regarding attacker access and compromised interfaces frequently limit direct comparison. Physics-based detectors offer strong interpretability and real-time suitability but remain sensitive to model and topology errors, whereas data-driven methods capture complex attack patterns but depend on representative data and may generalize poorly. Federated learning preserves data locality but introduces privacy, poisoning, and communication concerns, while moving target defense and deception provide complementary proactive capabilities. No detection or mitigation strategy is uniformly superior across attack coverage, interpretability, false-alarm behavior, latency, scalability, and computational burden. DT-enabled secure control and self-healing further require safety-constrained mitigation under detection uncertainty, communication delay, model mismatch, and partially compromised information. Validation is dominated by simulation, with comparatively little hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) or utility-scale field evidence. Key research gaps include inconsistent digital twin terminology, limited benchmark datasets, synchronization and model-fidelity challenges, inadequate interoperability, and insufficient validation of autonomous mitigation. This review contributes an integrated taxonomy and decision-oriented framework for evaluating and selecting cyber-resilient digital twin strategies for smart grids. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Feedback-enabled digital twin and explainable artificial intelligence framework for predictive resilience and adaptive decision-making in disrupted supply chains
Affiliations: Industrial and Production Engineering Department, Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, Nigeria; Department of Engineering Management, School of Engineering, University of the West of England, Bristol, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Nwamekwe C.O., Industrial and Production Engineering Department, Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, Nigeria; Igbokwe N.C., Industrial and Production Engineering Department, Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, Nigeria; Unigwe I.B., Department of Engineering Management, School of Engineering, University of the West of England, Bristol, United Kingdom
Abstract: Supply-chain disruptions are increasingly difficult to manage with conventional monitor–respond–recover approaches because they provide limited early-warning, explanation, uncertainty assessment and adaptive recovery support. This study developed a feedback-enabled digital twin and explainable artificial intelligence framework for predictive resilience and adaptive decision-making in disrupted supply chains. A quantitative modelling, simulation and multi-objective optimization design was applied to a hybrid dataset containing 3,500 de-identified operational shipment records from CarryGo Logistics Company, Awka, Nigeria, and 1,500 simulation-generated rare-disruption observations. The data were divided into 3,500 training, 750 validation and 750 testing observations, with validation and testing conducted entirely on operational records. Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM and Bayesian Neural Network models were evaluated, while 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo simulation, SHAP analysis and normalized multi-objective optimization supported uncertainty assessment, explanation and recovery selection. Random Forest achieved 0.79 accuracy, 0.61 precision, 0.99 recall, 0.75 F1 and 0.85 AUC, whereas XGBoost achieved 0.62 precision, 0.86 recall, 0.85 AUC and the lowest MAE of 0.27. The framework classified 353 normal, 61 watch, 333 warning and 3 critical states. Disruption severity increased from 22% at supplier failure to 83% customer-service loss across the simulated network. Supplier reliability and lead time contributed 41.49 and 39.97% of disruption risk, respectively. Inventory redistribution ranked first under equal weights with J = 0.26 and remained preferred under service and risk priorities, while supplier switching became optimal under cost and delay priorities. The framework demonstrates company-level operational utility for transparent, uncertainty-aware and feedback-enabled supply-chain resilience, while wider multi-company validation remains necessary. Abstract: Accurate prediction and inversion of time-dependent gap deformation between a passenger aircraft door and its frame remain difficult under slowly varying pressurization because the response is governed by coupled geometry, lock restraint, and nonlinear contact. This study develops a digital-twin-driven inversion framework for door–frame gap deformation. A physics-based parametric twin is established using feature associations and a unified assembly datum, and the outer skin, stiffeners, load-bearing frame, inner panel, locks, and door frame are represented in a nonlinear quasi-static finite-element model. Geometric nonlinearity and a separable door–frame contact are retained so that load-dependent opening, local slip, and constraint effects can be captured. A full-scale test platform with binocular vision provides three-directional relative-displacement measurements. The numerical model is updated through equivalent-stiffness correction, local nodal adjustment, and global scaling, with physical restrictions imposed on the adjustable region and correction amplitudes to avoid unconstrained point-wise fitting; corrected simulation and experimental data are then fused for surrogate training. An improved Gaussian process regression model uses the normalized pressure level, spatial coordinates of the registered key-point pairs, and displacement-direction encoding as inputs and the corresponding fused directional gap displacement as the output; a squared-exponential kernel and input-dependent noise model represent nonlinear response and uncertainty. Under an identical within-profile training–validation partition, the reported GPR implementation yields lower aggregate error than the corresponding RBF-NN and random-forest benchmark runs, with a root-mean-square error of 0.21, a mean relative error of 2.8%, and a coefficient of determination of 0.985. These metrics quantify interpolation within the calibrated slowly varying quasi-static loading domain rather than validated extrapolation to an independent unseen load history. The framework provides a mechanism-consistent route for virtual–physical updating and surrogate-based inversion of aircraft door–frame gap states. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twins, and Cyber-Resilience in Water Distribution Systems: A Critical Narrative Review with a WDT Benchmark Case Study
Affiliations: Research Group of Advanced Control Systems, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Rambla Sant Nebridi 22, Terrassa, 08222, Spain
Authors with affiliations: Pérez-Pérez E.-J., Research Group of Advanced Control Systems, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Rambla Sant Nebridi 22, Terrassa, 08222, Spain
Abstract: Water-infrastructure digitalization increasingly couples hydraulics with sensing, communication, artificial intelligence (AI), and supervisory control, while digital twins support operational decisions. This article combines a critical narrative review with structured full-text evidence mapping of 50 water cyber-physical systems (CPS) studies and an accompanying reproducible Water Distribution Testbed (WDT) benchmark case study. The review synthesizes model-based, data-driven, and physically informed methods across detection, localization, mitigation, and recovery, distinguishing anomaly evidence, cyber attribution, and closed-loop resilience. The WDT case study compares nominal-only detectors and alarm policies under a common chronological protocol. Across five primary neural runs, cumulative policies increase sample-level recall but sustain alarms and detect fewer event onsets than the fixed-threshold policy. These numerical findings characterize the declared protocol and evaluated records; they do not establish a general ranking of detection algorithms. They motivate interpreting classification metrics alongside event performance and held-out nominal alarm burden. Priorities include trustworthy digital-twin updating, causal localization, uncertainty-aware intervention, independent validation, and verified recovery for intelligent water-infrastructure operation. © 2026 by the author.

Abstract: Anaerobic fermentation converts crop residues, livestock manure, and other agricultural wastes into energy-rich products, particularly methane and hydrogen, simultaneously enabling waste treatment and resource recovery. However, stable operation and industrial scale-up remain difficult because feedstock properties, microbial metabolism, fluid behavior, and mass transfer vary continuously throughout fermentation. Their interactions generate nonlinear, time-varying, and multiscale dynamics that are difficult to observe, predict, and regulate using conventional methods. This review synthesizes progress in modeling and intelligent control for the anaerobic fermentation of agricultural wastes, with particular attention to biochemical hydrogen production. The reviewed advances are organized around a hierarchical data-mechanism-control framework that connects process characterization, hybrid modeling, online estimation, optimization, and system-level decision support. First, the review examines heterogeneous data generated during feedstock characterization, pretreatment, reactor operation, microbial conversion, and product formation. Laboratory and pilot-scale datasets are often sparse, noisy, imbalanced, and dependent on specific feedstocks or reactor configurations. Second, the review compares major modeling strategies and clarifies their respective roles. Random forests and support vector machines are effective for modeling feedstock characteristics and pretreatment responses, whereas artificial neural networks and long short-term memory networks are capable of capturing nonlinear relationships and temporal dependencies. Gaussian process regression supports uncertainty analysis under limited data, while transfer learning can reuse information across related feedstocks or operating scenarios. Despite these capabilities, purely data-driven models may generate unreliable predictions outside their training domains and may violate conservation laws, thermodynamic constraints, or microbial kinetics. Mechanistic models, including anaerobic digestion model No. 1 (ADM1), provide interpretable process descriptions but require extensive calibration and may inadequately represent complex slurry transport and microbial succession. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a gray-box modeling approach by embedding conservation relationships and microbial kinetic equations into the learning objective. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), particularly SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), complements this approach by identifying influential variables, interactions, inhibitory conditions, and potential process thresholds. These tools can translate model outputs into operationally meaningful evidence for process diagnosis and control, although their reliability under practical operating conditions remains to be validated in reactors treating agricultural wastes. Third, the review links hybrid modeling to closed-loop process control. Internet of things (IoT) sensor networks and edge computing can support local filtering, drift correction, feature extraction, communication management, and rapid fault detection. Soft sensors can estimate difficult-to-measure state variables, including volatile fatty acids, chemical oxygen demand, alkalinity, and microbial activity, from readily available online measurements. Multi-objective optimization and model predictive control (MPC) can then balance gas productivity, process stability, and energy consumption while satisfying equipment and safety constraints. At the system level, digital twins integrate biochemical kinetics, computational fluid dynamics, sensor data, equipment models, and scenario simulation. Nevertheless, applications in agricultural waste fermentation remain largely conceptual or limited to individual components because biological and hydrodynamic processes are difficult to couple efficiently. Future research should prioritize standardized multimodal databases, shared biochemical and hydrodynamic model libraries, adaptive hybrid models, robust sensing, uncertainty-aware control, and integrated device-edge-cloud architectures. Progress in these areas can advance interpretable prediction, resilient process operation, and reliable bioenergy recovery, thereby supporting the digital and intelligent transformation of agricultural waste management systems. © 2026 Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering. Abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is transitioning from a predictive flow-simulation technique into a central enabling technology for the design, intensification, scale-up, and digitalization of catalytic reactors. This review critically synthesizes advances reported across fixed-bed, packed-bed, fluidized-bed, trickle-bed, slurry bubble-column, monolithic, membrane, and microreactor systems, spanning chemical, petrochemical, environmental, and energy applications. Rather than treating reactor configurations and numerical methods independently, the review establishes a multiscale framework linking hydrodynamics, heterogeneous reaction kinetics, porous-media transport, heat and mass transfer, radiation, catalyst-scale phenomena, and reactor-scale performance. Particular emphasis is placed on the evolving integration of Large Eddy Simulation, Direct Numerical Simulation, Population Balance Models, artificial intelligence, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, digital twins, and high-performance computing. Their capabilities are critically compared in resolving conversion, selectivity, pressure drop, thermal gradients, species transport, catalyst utilization, and multiphase interactions, with explicit consideration of the trade-offs among predictive fidelity, computational cost, scalability, and industrial relevance. The influence of turbulence closure, mesh resolution, reaction-mechanism complexity, reactor geometry, boundary conditions, parameter uncertainty, and experimental validation on model credibility is systematically assessed. Key unresolved barriers include multiscale coupling, catalyst deactivation, numerical stiffness, uncertainty propagation, computational expense, and reliable scale-up from laboratory reactors to industrial systems. Emerging opportunities in AI-assisted CFD, GPU-accelerated simulation, uncertainty-aware modelling, autonomous optimization, and continuously updated digital twins are critically evaluated. The review ultimately proposes a pathway toward physics-informed, data-augmented, and decision-oriented CFD frameworks capable of accelerating the development of safer, more efficient, flexible, and sustainable catalytic reactor systems. © 2026 the author(s), published by De Gruyter, Berlin/Boston 2026.

Abstract: Smart drying has emerged as a research field that combines drying science, sensing, process systems engineering, and artificial intelligence. This review critically synthesizes a deliberately bounded 2021–2025 evidence corpus to assess the recent technological maturity of machine learning, digital twins, soft sensors, and predictive control in food, agricultural, biomass, and pharmaceutical drying. Using a screened Scopus-based evidence base, the article evaluates predictive modeling, sensing and inferential state estimation, optimization and control, representative implementation cases, and application-specific deployment. The synthesis indicates that moisture and drying-kinetics prediction are among the most mature components, whereas cross-product generalization, uncertainty-aware validation, industrial deployment, closed-loop control, and dynamically synchronized digital-twin operation remain less consistently demonstrated. The review distinguishes digital monitoring, digital shadows, and validated digital-twin operation; identifies implementation levels from laboratory prediction to pilot and operational control; and analyzes practical barriers including scale-dependent nonuniformity, sensor fouling, calibration drift, domain shift, latency, actuator constraints, maintenance, interoperability, and economic burden. Overall, progress depends on validated, transferable, maintainable, and control-relevant architectures rather than algorithmic accuracy alone. This journal is © The Royal Society of Chemistry, 2026.

Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) workflows for partial differential equations (PDEs) often require repeated simulations over many initial conditions, boundary conditions, or physical parameters. Although a single high-fidelity solve may be tractable on modern computing systems, large ensembles, optimization loops, uncertainty quantification studies, and digital-twin applications can make the aggregate computational cost substantial. This study presents a neural operator augmented with dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). The architecture combines a DeepONet-style branch–trunk mapping with additional branches that encode DMD modes and modal dynamics. The resulting model is intended as a trajectory-informed surrogate: DMD features are computed from states available before the prediction point and the subsequent state is reserved as the target. The method is evaluated for the Laplace, heat, and Burgers equations on 64×64 grids. On the heat benchmark, controlled five-seed comparisons include DeepONet, a parameter-matched DeepONet, FNO, and a KNO-style baseline; a capacity-controlled input ablation additionally evaluates the contribution of the DMD inputs without changing the trainable parameter count. Computational measurements separate classical solution time, DMD preprocessing, training, and network inference. The trained network has low evaluation latency, while case-specific DMD preprocessing dominates the present end-to-end path. Thus, the results support DMD-NO as a structured operator-learning approach for trajectory-conditioned prediction and identify modal preprocessing as the principal target for future parallel optimization, without claiming an end-to-end speedup over the classical solver. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: PHYSICS-GUIDED PROBABILISTIC DIGITAL TWIN FOR UNDERWATER NOISE PREDICTION
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference on Offshore Mechanics and Arctic Engineering - OMAE
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Deo I.K., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada; Venkateshwaran A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada; Jaiman R., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada
Abstract: The underwater radiated noise (URN) from commercial shipping is a growing environmental and regulatory concern, particularly in coastal waters, where marine mammals are exposed to elevated sound levels. This paper presents a physics-guided and uncertainty-aware surrogate model for the rapid prediction of three-dimensional transmission loss (TL) in range-dependent marine environments, allowing real-time digital twins for operational noise mitigation. The proposed approach combines a low-order physics-based representation of geometric spreading and frequency-dependent absorption with a data-driven correction that captures bathymetry- and environment-induced variability. The framework is trained on large-scale hydroacoustic simulations for the Salish Sea across seasonal sound-speed conditions and one-third-octave frequency bands from 12.5 Hz to 8 kHz. Results demonstrate sub-dB mean prediction error and substantially reduced spatial variability relative to baseline surrogate models, while achieving prediction times on the order of hundreds of milliseconds. The model is embedded within a digital-twin workflow to support voyage-level speed optimization and assimilation of sparse acoustic measurements. The proposed framework provides a practical pathway for integrating fast and uncertainty-aware acoustic prediction into marine engineering design and operational decision-making for URN mitigation. Authors: Yang J.
Title: GAN-enhanced digital twins for biomarker-guided cancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy: a mini review
Affiliations: Shandong University of Technology, Shandong, Zibo, China
Authors with affiliations: Yang J., Shandong University of Technology, Shandong, Zibo, China
Abstract: Cancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy have transformed modern oncology, yet durable benefits remain limited by tumor heterogeneity, immune escape mechanisms, biomarker variability, and the dynamic remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment. Current biomarker strategies, including PD-L1 (programmed death-ligand 1) expression, microsatellite instability (MSI), tumor mutational burden (TMB), immune gene signatures, liquid biopsy measurements, and target antigen profiles, provide clinically useful information but are often static and insufficient to capture longitudinal tumor–immune–therapy interactions. Digital twin technology offers a computational paradigm for integrating multi-omics, immune profiling, clinical variables, imaging, and treatment-response data into patient-linked virtual models. Generative artificial intelligence, including generative adversarial networks (GANs), may enrich sparse biomarker-defined state spaces and support the simulation of underrepresented treatment response or toxicity trajectories. This mini review critically compares mechanistic quantitative systems pharmacology, spatial and agent-based modeling, data-driven prediction, and emerging digital twin approaches and proposes a platform-agnostic architecture that can be implemented in MATLAB/Simulink or other computational environments. The adoptive cell therapy scope focuses on chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T), chimeric antigen receptor natural killer cell (CAR-NK), and T-cell receptor-engineered T-cell (TCR-T) therapies, with related principles applicable to tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy. We describe conditional and longitudinal GAN strategies, dynamic tumor–immune state modeling, biomarker integration, validation metrics, governance, and prospective implementation pathways. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not yet been clinically validated; synthetic data are treated as methodological support rather than clinical evidence. Its intended near-term uses are hypothesis generation, virtual-cohort enrichment, trial design, and uncertainty-aware decision support. Copyright © 2026 Yang.

Title: Just-in-Time Material Delivery Optimization in Multi-Site Construction through BIM–IoT-Enabled Digital Twin-Based Fourth-Party Logistics
Source title: International Journal of Industrial Engineering and Production Research
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering, Iran University of Science & Technology, Tehran, Iran
Authors with affiliations: Karimi B., Department of Industrial Engineering, Iran University of Science & Technology, Tehran, Iran; Mohammadpour Omran M., Department of Industrial Engineering, Iran University of Science & Technology, Tehran, Iran; Sahebi H., Department of Industrial Engineering, Iran University of Science & Technology, Tehran, Iran
Abstract: Construction material delivery across multiple sites faces uncertain demand, changing site readiness, limited logistics capacity, restricted storage, and transport-related emissions. This study develops a BIM–IoT-driven digital twin for fourth-party logistics (4PL) orchestration of just-in-time material delivery under uncertainty. The framework integrates BIM information with operational data on project progress, shipment status, inventory, site readiness, and logistics availability. A scenario-based multi-objective MILP uses rolling-horizon optimization to minimize logistics cost, delivery deviation, site congestion, and carbon emissions. It distinguishes implemented decisions from immediate decisions and scenario-dependent recourse. Transportation uncertainty is addressed by separating dispatch from arrival and incorporating conditional value at risk. For large instances, an Event-Aware Rolling-Horizon NSGA-II uses scenario-linked encoding, Pareto warm starts, event-affected gene masks, adaptive operators, and hierarchical feasibility repair. In the case application, BIM–IoT digital-twin updating with JIT control reduced delivery deviation by 36.1% and site congestion by 32.2%, while the complete policy achieved 90.6% on-time delivery. Across benchmark classes, ERH-NSGA-II increased hypervolume by 8.4–88.2% and reduced IGD+ by 30.9–85.8% relative to conventional NSGA-II. The framework also provides quantitative decision rules for logistics capacity, storage, data quality, consolidation, and carbon restrictions. © Iran University of Science and Technology 2026.

Title: Algorithms for Coupled Electrified Transportation and Power Networks: From Grid Services to Real-World Deployment—A Systems-Oriented Review
Affiliations: Department of Electrical, Computer, and Software Engineering, The University of Auckland, 20 Symonds Street, Auckland CBD, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand
Authors with affiliations: Liu Y., Department of Electrical, Computer, and Software Engineering, The University of Auckland, 20 Symonds Street, Auckland CBD, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand; Massier T., Department of Electrical, Computer, and Software Engineering, The University of Auckland, 20 Symonds Street, Auckland CBD, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand; Nair N.-K.C., Department of Electrical, Computer, and Software Engineering, The University of Auckland, 20 Symonds Street, Auckland CBD, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand
Abstract: Electrified transport introduces loads whose location, timing, and flexibility depend on vehicle movement and user behavior. Its operation therefore links road networks, charging infrastructure, distribution grids, communication systems, and electricity markets. However, many studies examine these components separately or represent interactions through fixed demand profiles and simplified forecasts. This review examines electrified transportation and smart-grid analytics from a system-level perspective. It presents a five-layer framework covering transportation, charging, power, information, and market-governance systems, and compares models across spatial scales and decision horizons. The review evaluates traffic–power network coordination, managed charging, vehicle-to-grid services, fleet operation, infrastructure planning, forecasting, optimization, and distributed control. It also considers reliability, cybersecurity, privacy, battery degradation, emissions, resilience, and equitable access as integral design requirements. Four limitations recur across the literature: unequal modeling detail between transportation and power networks, limited validation of operational decisions, insufficient representation of user and institutional responses, and a lack of reproducible cross-domain benchmarks. Priorities for future work include modular digital twins, uncertainty-aware learning and optimization, multi-timescale coordination, interoperable flexibility markets, and field validation under realistic operating conditions. Electrified mobility should consequently be planned and operated as an integrated transportation–energy system rather than treated solely as an additional category of electricity demand. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: An Intelligent LLM–Fuzzy Decision Support and Digital Twin Framework for Adaptive Agricultural Robotics Systems
Affiliations: Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Nozari H., Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Yordanova Z., Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Abstract: This study develops an integrated LLM–fuzzy decision-support and digital twin framework for adaptive agricultural robotics, combining semantic reasoning, fuzzy inference, multi-objective optimization, and feedback-driven state updating. Numerical sensor data, operational information, and textual field knowledge are transformed into validated decision rules and model-ready parameters, enabling coordinated decisions across economic, operational, crop-stress, and sustainability-related objectives. The framework is evaluated as a simulation-based proof of concept calibrated with real observations from a semi-smart tomato farm, while controlled digital twin scenarios are used to assess its behavior under environmental and operational disturbances. Compared with numerical optimization alone, the complete LLM–fuzzy framework reduces operational cost by 3.35% and crop stress by 7.98%, while improving operational performance by 4.45%. Ablation, repeated-run, scenario, sensitivity, and dynamic-adaptation analyses further demonstrate consistent computational performance under the evaluated conditions. Sustainability is assessed through a model-based measure integrating water use, energy consumption, and soil-compaction-related impacts. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining semantic reasoning, uncertainty processing, optimization, and digital-twin feedback for adaptive agricultural decision support. However, the results represent a calibrated simulation-based proof of concept rather than validation through a full-scale autonomous field deployment; broader multi-season and field-scale validation is therefore required before generalizing the reported operational and sustainability benefits. © 2026 by the authors.

Authors: Jia X.; Zhou D.
Author full names: Jia, Xingyun (57449291100); Zhou, Dengji (56150854500)
Title: Toward reliable physics-informed neural networks under degradation uncertainty: An implicit-volume framework for dynamic modeling of gas turbine engines
Affiliations: The Key Laboratory of Power Machinery and Engineering of Education Ministry, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, China; Shanghai Jiao Tong University Sichuan Research Institute, Chengdu, 610213, China
Authors with affiliations: Jia X., The Key Laboratory of Power Machinery and Engineering of Education Ministry, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, China; Zhou D., The Key Laboratory of Power Machinery and Engineering of Education Ministry, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, China, Shanghai Jiao Tong University Sichuan Research Institute, Chengdu, 610213, China
Abstract: Accurate dynamic modeling of gas turbine engines under real-operating conditions is important for digital-twin assessment and system monitoring. Traditional component-level models rely on repeated nonlinear iterations for dynamic simulation, while standard physics-informed neural networks may suffer robustness degradation when ideal physical priors are inconsistent with degradation-affected data. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes the Implicit Volume Physics-Informed Neural Network (IVP-PINN) to improve dynamic modeling reliability for gas turbine engines under degradation uncertainty. First, a statistical error-tolerance mechanism employing a divergence metric relaxes the zero-residual constraint imposed on the flow-matching relation of the non-degraded reference model, thereby accommodating degradation-induced model mismatch without relaxing the physical mass-conservation law. Second, an implicit-volumetric architecture considering unsteady wave coupling utilizes neural network nonlinear mapping to bypass traditional iterative solvers. This simultaneously substantially reduces the computational cost and preserves authentic volumetric hysteresis effects. Validations under diverse transient disturbances and actual operational data show that IVP-PINN closely captures complex trajectories. Within the validated outside-training degradation range of [−10%, −6%), 87.75% of healthy-state predictive performance was retained at −10%. Compared with PI-LSTM, PINN, and MLP, IVP-PINN reduces peak MaxAE by 58.5%, 71.2%, and 68.0%. The proposed IVP-PINN shows potential for digital-twin dynamic assessment of gas-turbine systems. Title: The airframe digital twin: Some challenges to realization

Abstract: A new structural modeling concept, the Airframe Digital Twin, for designing and maintaining airframes is proposed. The Airframe Digital Twin is a tail number specific computational model of an individual aircraft. It has the potential to improve the way U.S. Air Force aircraft are managed over their entire lifecycle by creating individualized structural management plans. The Airframe Digital Twin can provide configuration control for each aircraft in the inventory. Through computational simulations performed with an Airframe Digital Twin, it can serve as a virtual health sensor, and provide a forecast of future maintenance needs for an individual aircraft. The Airframe Digital Twin concept is considered possible because of advances in high performance computing. An essential part of the Airframe Digital Twin is the ability to reduce the uncertainty in the model with increasing service experience through Bayesian updating.

Title: Error quantification and confidence assessment of aerothermal model predictions for hypersonic aircraft
Source title: 53rd AIAA/ASME/ASCE/AHS/ASC Structures, Structural Dynamics and Materials Conference 2012
Affiliations: Air Force Research Laboratory, Structural Sciences Center, Wright-Patterson AFB, OH, 45433, United States; Air Force Research Laboratory, Universal Technology Corporation, Wright-Patterson AFB, OH, 45433, United States; Vanderbilt University, Civil and Environmental Engineering Department, Nashville, TN, 37235, United States
Authors with affiliations: Smarslok B.P., Air Force Research Laboratory, Structural Sciences Center, Wright-Patterson AFB, OH, 45433, United States; Culler A.J., Air Force Research Laboratory, Universal Technology Corporation, Wright-Patterson AFB, OH, 45433, United States; Mahadevan S., Vanderbilt University, Civil and Environmental Engineering Department, Nashville, TN, 37235, United States
Abstract: Assessing prediction confidence and enabling its use as a decision-making metric for autonomous model fidelity selection is essential to the USAF's vision of a 'Digital Twin' as a viable approach for condition-based fleet management by tail number. Significant strides have been made in modeling complex interactions of the multi-physics, fluid-thermal-structural coupling applicable to hypersonic flow conditions. However, validation of these models remains a challenge due to limited experimental data for hypersonic conditions. This research addresses quantifying errors and assessing the confidence in aerodynamic pressure and heating predictions for a spherical dome protruding from a flat ramp. Well-characterized aerothermal test data from hypersonic wind tunnel experiments are used to calibrate uncertain model parameters and quantify errors through Bayesian techniques. A Bayesian hypothesis testing-based confidence metric is employed to compare the accuracy in various model predictions. A model selection study is performed for 1st-, 2nd-, and 3rd-order piston theories. The results showed that the greatest confidence in model predictions does not necessarily correspond to the highest-order model.

Abstract: Assessing prediction confidence and enabling its use as a decision-making metric for autonomous model fidelity selection is essential to the USAF's vision of a 'Digital Twin' as a viable approach for condition-based fleet management by tail number. Significant strides have been made in modeling complex interactions of the multi-physics, fluid-thermal-structural coupling applicable to hypersonic flow conditions. However, validation of these models remains a challenge due to limited experimental data for hypersonic conditions. This research addresses quantifying errors and assessing the confidence in aerodynamic pressure and heating predictions for a spherical dome protruding from a flat ramp. Well-characterized aerothermal test data from hypersonic wind tunnel experiments are used to calibrate uncertain model parameters and quantify errors through Bayesian techniques. A Bayesian hypothesis testing-based confidence metric is employed to compare the accuracy in various model predictions. A model selection study is performed for 1st-, 2 nd-, and 3rd-order piston theories. The results showed that the greatest confidence in model predictions does not necessarily correspond to the highest-order model. © 2012 AIAA.

Title: A framework to establish credibility of computational models in biology
Source title: Progress in Biophysics and Molecular Biology
Affiliations: School of Engineering, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom; European Commission Joint Research Centre, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Patterson E.A., School of Engineering, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom; Whelan M.P., European Commission Joint Research Centre, Italy
Abstract: Computational models in biology and biomedical science are often constructed to aid people's understanding of phenomena or to inform decisions with socioeconomic consequences. Model credibility is the willingness of people to trust a model's predictions and is often difficult to establish for computational biology models. A 3 × 3 matrix has been proposed to allow such models to be categorised with respect to their testability and epistemic foundation in order to guide the selection of an appropriate process of validation to supply evidence to establish credibility. Three approaches to validation are identified that can be deployed depending on whether a model is deemed untestable, testable or lies somewhere in between. In the latter two cases, the validation process involves the quantification of uncertainty which is a key output. The issues arising due to the complexity and inherent variability of biological systems are discussed and the creation of ‘digital twins’ proposed as a means to alleviate the issues and provide a more robust, transparent and traceable route to model credibility and acceptance. © 2016 The Authors

Abstract: The increasingly pervasive usage of robotic automation not only calls for a high performance of physical robot manipulators, but also implies challenging requirements on 3D robot simulators. A skillful reaction of simulated robots to unpredicted contact forces has become an especially stringent necessity to support the development of emerging applications for which a compliant robotic manipulation is indispensable. This paper focuses on the simulation of physics-based virtual testbeds in which simulated robots are made capable of accommodating external forces exerted by the environment on their manipulators. For this, we integrate methods from multi-body dynamics modeling, advanced robotics, and virtual reality to develop a robotics simulation basis that facilitates the employment of compliant robotic manipulations in simulated applications. The validation of this basis in joint space indicates that a physics-based simulation of robots endowed with active physical interaction control can capture and reflect significant effects which characterize the interactive behavior of physical compliant robots.We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach to unlock competitive advantages in fully simulated applications prone to position uncertainty. Furthermore, we show the potential of using compliant digital twins of physical robots to introduce compliant robotic manipulations into real applications. © 2016 IEEE.

Abstract: Current airframe health monitoring generally relies on deterministic physics models and ground inspections. This paper uses the concept of a dynamic Bayesian network to build a versatile probabilistic model for diagnosis and prognosis in order to realize the digital twin vision, and it illustrates the proposed method by an aircraft wing fatigue crack growth example. The dynamic Bayesian network integrates physics models and various aleatory (random) and epistemic (lack of knowledge) uncertainty sources in crack growth prediction. In diagnosis, the dynamic Bayesian network is used to track the evolution of the time-dependent variables and calibrate the time-independent variables; in prognosis, the dynamic Bayesian network is used for probabilistic prediction of crack growth in the future. This paper also proposes a modification to the dynamic Bayesian network structure, which does not affect the diagnosis results but reduces the time cost significantly by avoiding Bayesian updating with load data. By using a particle filter as the Bayesian inference algorithm for the dynamic Bayesian network, the proposed approach handles both discrete and continuous variables of various distribution types, as well as nonlinear relationships between nodes. Challenges in implementing the particle filter in the dynamic Bayesian network, where 1) both dynamic and static nodes exist and 2) a state variable may have parent nodes across two adjacent networks, are also resolved. © 2016 by the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Inc.

Title: Near real-time probabilistic damage diagnosis using surrogate modeling and high performance computing

Abstract: This work investigates novel approaches to probabilistic damage diagnosis that utilize surrogate modeling and high performance computing (HPC) to achieve substantial computational speedup. Motivated by Digital Twin, a structural health management (SHM) paradigm that integrates vehicle-specific characteristics with continual in-situ damage diagnosis and prognosis, the methods studied herein yield near real-time damage assessments that could enable monitoring of a vehicle’s health while it is operating (i.e., online SHM). High-fidelity modeling and uncertainty quantification (UQ), both critical to Digital Twin, are incorporated using finite element method simulations and Bayesian inference, respectively. The crux of the proposed Bayesian diagnosis methods, however, is the reformulation of the numerical sampling algorithms (e.g., Markov chain Monte Carlo) used to generate the resulting probabilistic damage estimates. To this end, three distinct methods are demonstrated for rapid sampling that utilize surrogate modeling and exploit various degrees of parallelism for leveraging HPC. The accuracy and computational efficiency of the methods are compared on the problem of strain-based crack identification in thin plates. While each approach has inherent problem-specific strengths and weaknesses, all approaches are shown to provide accurate probabilistic damage diagnoses and several orders of magnitude computational speedup relative to a baseline Bayesian diagnosis implementation. © 2017, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics Inc, AIAA.
